- **How many people the shortage actually covers.** Ranked by people rather than places, where do the most actual humans go without care, and how far is each place from its provider-ratio goal? — estimated underserved population and ratio goals (fed_hrsa_hpsa_primary_care, fed_hrsa_shortage_areas). *Harm:* the gap between the ratio goal and reality is the number of people with no doctor; ranking by people puts urban shortage back into the conversation. · caveat: underserved population estimates are formula-derived, not counted; ratio fields may be text.
- **Where poverty and doctor shortage stack.** Do the deepest care shortages sit on the poorest populations? — poverty percentage vs shortage score (fed_hrsa_hpsa_primary_care, fed_hrsa_shortage_areas). *Harm:* where poverty and shortage stack, people get sicker before they ever see a doctor. · caveat: poverty may be a designation input — partial circularity; poverty column name mangled in one mart (header parsing problem).
- **The border corridor care gap.** How do shortage scores, provider ratios, and clinic coverage compare in the US–Mexico border corridor versus the rest of the same states? — border-county indicators (fed_hrsa_hpsa_primary_care, fed_hrsa_shortage_areas, fed_hrsa_uds_service_delivery_sites). *Harm:* border communities combine the worst provider ratios with the largest uninsured population — and the least attention. · medium · caveat: border indicator flags may be sparsely set.
- **Many payouts, zero discipline.** How many practitioners have a stack of paid malpractice claims and no license action at all — and when discipline comes, is it a slap or a stop? — NPDB prior-report counts vs adverse actions (fed_hrsa_npdb). *Harm:* practitioners with repeated payouts and no discipline keep treating patients. · caveat: the NPDB public file is deliberately de-identified — practitioner identity is not recoverable; prior-report counts are as-of-report snapshots.
- **States that pay claims but never discipline.** Which states show many malpractice payments per adverse licensure action? — NPDB actions per payment by state (fed_hrsa_npdb). *Harm:* patients in never-discipline states are exposed to practitioners other states would have stopped. · caveat: state fields may be masked in low-count states.
- **The people behind the malpractice record.** Who are the injured — by age, sex and allegation type — how are their injuries valued, and how many years pass between injury and payment? — NPDB demographics, allegations, payments (fed_hrsa_npdb). *Harm:* years between injury and payment is time spent uncompensated. · caveat: ages and payments may be banded in the public-use file; allegation codes need the source codebook.
- **How the federal ban hammer gets used.** What conduct drives federal healthcare exclusions, and does enforcement intensity vary wildly by state and specialty? — OIG exclusion list (fed_hhs_oig_leie). *Harm:* if identical bad actors face different odds by state, enforcement itself is the inequity. · caveat: exclusion date may be YYYYMMDD text (epoch-cast trap); per-capita rates need a provider-count denominator.
- **Bans that are pauses.** Which exclusion types get reinstated and how often? — OIG exclusion reinstatement fields (fed_hhs_oig_leie). *Harm:* providers reinstated after patient-harm exclusions return to the same population. · caveat: reinstatement derivation unverified; the snapshot may drop reinstated parties entirely.
- **Which vulnerable populations have funded care.** State by state, which health centers are funded to serve migrant workers, homeless patients and public-housing residents — and where do whole populations have zero dedicated funding? — UDS health-center funding streams (fed_hrsa_uds_health_center_info). *Harm:* an empty cell is a state where a whole vulnerable population has no dedicated funded care. · caveat: funding-field semantics unconfirmed (flags vs dollars); 1,356 rows suggests a single reporting year.
- **Who the safety net actually serves.** What is the age and sex mix of each health center's patients — which are effectively pediatric practices, which serve aging communities? — UDS patient age/sex tables (fed_hrsa_uds_table3a_patients, fed_hrsa_uds_health_center_info). *Harm:* who a clinic serves determines which services it must have and often does not. · medium · caveat: columns are opaque line numbers with no labels — map them to age bands from the UDS manual first or the question collapses; likely a single reporting year.
- **The Indian Health Service, mapped.** Where does the IHS physically exist — facilities, beds, status by service area — and which tribal communities are furthest from any care? — IHS facility inventory (fed_ihs_facilities, fed_ihs_scb_facility). *Harm:* areas with almost no inpatient beds send patients hundreds of miles. · caveat: ~1,006 facility rows; the two tables' grains differ (8,733 vs 1,006) and their relationship is unverified; per-population normalization needs external data.
- **Missing services on tribal land.** Which IHS service areas have no behavioral health, dental, or pharmacy service at all? — IHS facility service flags (fed_ihs_facilities). *Harm:* an area with no behavioral-health facility means tribal citizens in crisis have nowhere to go. · caveat: service flags may be inconsistently maintained.
- **Handed to tribes, with or without the money.** How much of the Indian health system is now tribally operated versus federally operated — and does the shift transfer resources or just burden? — IHS operator/owner types (fed_ihs_facilities, fed_ihs_scb_facility). *Harm:* handing operations to tribes without matching funding transfers the burden, not the resources. · medium · caveat: no time axis in the tables — the shift itself cannot be shown over time.
- **Where veterans die faster than everyone else.** On which causes do veterans die at higher rates than comparable civilians, and which causes steal the most life-years? — VA all-cause mortality by cohort and cause, 2018-2023 (fed_va_allcause_mortality). *Harm:* causes where veterans die faster point at what service or VA care did to them. · caveat: only 2,808 rows across six years — coarse cohorts; presence of a non-veteran comparison cohort unverified.
- **The veteran suicide gap.** How large is the veteran-vs-civilian suicide gap since 2001, and do VHA users fare better than veterans outside the system? — VA national suicide series (fed_va_suicide_national, fed_va_suicide_appendix). *Harm:* if VHA users fare no better, the care system is not reaching those at risk. · caveat: VHA users are a selected, sicker population — confounded, not causal; VA methodology changes mid-series; the appendix mart is 144 rows of unnamed columns — unusable until rebuilt.
- **Women veterans, buried in the averages.** How much higher is women veterans' suicide and mortality risk relative to civilian women? — female vs male veteran rates indexed to civilians (fed_va_suicide_national, fed_va_allcause_mortality). *Harm:* women veterans' excess risk is routinely buried inside the male-dominated total. · caveat: small female counts make rates unstable or suppressed in some years.
- **The geography of veteran suicide.** Where do veterans die by suicide at the highest rates, and where is the veteran-specific excess over the state's population largest? — VA state-level veteran suicide rates (fed_va_suicide_state). *Harm:* where a veteran lives changes their odds of dying by suicide. · caveat: suppressed small-count cells read as gaps, not zeros; the two rate bases may not be age-standardized the same way; small-state rates swing on a handful of deaths.
- **Who is in the new specialty payment model.** Which states and organizations dominate the new ambulatory specialty payment model, and are small practices designated out over its life? — model participant lists (fed_cms_ambulatory_specialty_model_participants). *Harm:* patients in states with no participating specialists are excluded from whatever the model improves. · medium · caveat: forward-looking designation flags, not observed behavior; future-year columns may be blank at ingest.
- **Lead in tap water: how bad, where, improving?** How do lead and copper samples distribute against the federal action level, which systems recorded the worst taps, and has the 90th-percentile lead level actually fallen? — SDWA lead and copper rule samples (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_LCR_SAMPLES). *Harm:* every sample above the action level is a household drinking leaded water. · caveat: sample measure left uncast (may be text) and units vary — normalize or the ranking is nonsense; protocol changes can fake a trend.
- **Lead testing gaps.** Which water systems have gone years without a lead sample? — SDWA lead and copper samples (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_LCR_SAMPLES). *Harm:* an untested system has no idea whether its pipes are leaching lead. · caveat: sampling requirements vary by system size — a long gap can be legal.
- **Non-detect gaming.** Do some systems report suspiciously many non-detect lead results — sample selection gamed to hide exposure? — SDWA lead sample result-sign codes (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_LCR_SAMPLES). *Harm:* gamed sampling hides real lead exposure from residents. · wild · caveat: result-sign encoding unverified; non-detects can be entirely legitimate.
- **Schools and daycares on their own water.** Where do schools and daycares run their own small water systems? — SDWA public water systems school/daycare flag (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS). *Harm:* children are most vulnerable to lead and pathogens and often drink from the smallest, weakest systems. · caveat: school/daycare flag fill rate unverified, may be sparse.
- **Health-based drinking water violations: the core count.** How many health-based violations occur per year, by rule family — contaminants above legal limits in people's taps? — SDWA violations and enforcement (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT). *Harm:* health-based violations are contaminants above the legal limit in real taps. · caveat: 15.4M rows are quarterly snapshots — dedupe by violation ID or counts inflate wildly.
- **How far over the legal limit.** When water systems violate, are they barely over the maximum contaminant level or ten times over? — SDWA measured values vs federal MCL (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT). *Harm:* ten times over the limit is a different harm from barely over — the data can say which. · caveat: measure and MCL columns left uncast, possibly text with mixed units.
- **Debarred providers, live licenses.** How many federal debarments carry a healthcare provider identifier — barred providers who may still hold a working provider number? — federal contractor exclusions list, provider-ID column (fed_sam_exclusions). *Harm:* A debarred healthcare provider still holding a working provider number is a patient-safety failure with a name attached. · caveat: fix: the NPI column risks being blank or sentinel-masked — run COUNT(DISTINCT) plus a value sample before any claim; mart is a partial slice (2,940 of ~9k).
- **Product injuries that fall unevenly by race.** Do specific consumer products injure some racial groups far more than others once survey weights are applied? — CPSC NEISS emergency-room injury survey (fed_cpsc_neiss). *Harm:* a product that injures one group far more is a distribution and design failure, not bad luck. · caveat: race coding changed over the survey's history and is often unknown; no population denominator in the table.
- **Injury curves rising before recalls.** Which products show injury counts bending sharply upward years before any recall — the early-warning signal nobody acted on? — CPSC NEISS weighted injury counts by product over years (fed_cpsc_neiss). *Harm:* catching the curve early is the difference between warning people and counting them. · caveat: rising curves can reflect product popularity without a sales denominator; statistical weights must be applied correctly.
- **Products that maim versus products that scrape.** Which products produce hospital admissions rather than treat-and-release visits, and how often are fire, alcohol, or drugs part of the picture? — CPSC NEISS disposition and involvement flags (fed_cpsc_neiss). *Harm:* admission rate is the honest measure of how badly a product hurts people; context flags separate a defect from an unwarned hazard. · caveat: disposition codes need the lookup table; involvement flags are often unrecorded rather than negative.
- **Fertility collapse and the coming care gap.** How fast is fertility collapsing where, when did each country cross below replacement, and is the global spread narrowing? — OWID fertility rate (xc_owid_fertility). *Harm:* countries crossing earliest face care-worker shortages first, and the shortfall lands on unpaid family carers. · medium · caveat: entity column mixes countries and aggregates — filter on valid ISO codes.

### environment-and-pollution (131)
- **How chemicals get onto the warning list.** How fast does California list cancer and reproductive toxicants, through which pathways, and are reproductive toxicants listed at a fraction of the carcinogen rate? — California Prop 65 chemical list (st_oehha_proposition_65_list). *Harm:* every year a chemical sits unlisted is a year of exposure with no warning label; under-listing reproductive toxicants leaves pregnant workers unwarned. · caveat: only 952 rows; date_listed may be text; a few chemicals span multiple toxicity types and double-count.
- **Warnings with no usable threshold.** Which listed toxic chemicals have no safe-harbour exposure level at all — so businesses over-warn or ignore the listing? — Prop 65 NSRL/MADL columns (st_oehha_proposition_65_list). *Harm:* without a threshold the warning system collapses into noise and consumers get no real signal. · caveat: the safe-harbour column may be mostly blank — itself the finding, but it makes a chart thin.
- **Absentee owners of polluting infrastructure.** How far do the owners and decision-makers of plants and toxic facilities sit from the communities that host them? — EIA-860 utility and owner schedules plus TRI mailing addresses (FED_EIA860_1_UTILITY, FED_EIA860_4_OWNER, FED_EPA_TRI_FACILITY). *Harm:* communities host the pollution while ownership income, tax base, and decisions sit elsewhere. · caveat: owner/mailing state is often a registered agent or law firm — build an address-type classifier before the flow map is honest.
- **Unlined coal ash next to communities.** Where do unlined or failing coal-ash impoundments sit, and who lives next to them? — EIA-860 plant schedule (FED_EIA860_2_PLANT). *Harm:* unlined ash ponds leach arsenic and heavy metals into groundwater of nearby, usually poor, communities. · caveat: impoundment fields may be sparse or oddly coded; single 2024 snapshot.
- **Plants stacked on one stressed water source.** How many power plants draw on the same named river or water source? — EIA-860 plant schedule (FED_EIA860_2_PLANT). *Harm:* multiple plants drawing and heating one river hit fisheries and drinking water downstream. · medium · caveat: water-source names are free text — normalize to group the same river; no withdrawal volumes in this table.
- **Carbon capture: claims vs deployed reality.** How much carbon capture is actually operating — flagged capacity, and captured tonnage versus emissions? — EIA-860 generator schedule plus EPA greenhouse gas facility file (FED_EIA860_3_1_GENERATOR, FED_EPA_GHGRP_FACILITY). *Harm:* capture claims justify keeping plants open next to neighborhoods; near-absence is a broken promise to the people breathing the exhaust. · caveat: flag semantics unverified; capture columns likely populated for a tiny handful of facilities.
- **Plants that can switch to oil next to neighborhoods.** Which communities live next to plants that can flip to oil burning on short notice — with an air-permit limit (or nothing) as the only brake? — EIA-860 multifuel schedule (FED_EIA860_3_5_MULTIFUEL). *Harm:* neighbors breathe oil-burn emissions during gas price spikes with no notice or say. · caveat: blank limit fields may mean not-reported rather than no-limit — that would invert the read.
- **The cofire fuel menu.** What unusual waste-derived fuels get cofired in what equipment, and which host communities get the exotic emissions? — EIA-860 multifuel schedule (FED_EIA860_3_5_MULTIFUEL). *Harm:* waste-derived cofire fuels concentrate exotic emissions in whichever community drew the plant. · wild · caveat: fuel codes are unlabeled — land the EIA fuel-code lookup as a reference table; six cofire slots must be unpivoted.
- **The boiler-generator tangle.** Which plants have the most tangled boiler-to-generator wiring, where emissions attribution is hardest? — EIA-860 environmental association bridge (FED_EIA860_6_1_ENVIROASSOC). *Harm:* complex plants are where regulators lose the thread on which unit caused which exceedance. · medium · caveat: pure bridge table; needs boiler/generator tables to say anything about quantities.
- **Boilers with no mercury control.** Where do boilers report no existing mercury control strategy at all? — EIA-860 environmental equipment schedule (FED_EIA860_6_2_ENVIROEQUIP). *Harm:* mercury from uncontrolled boilers lands in local water and food and hits children hardest. · caveat: blank strategy may mean not-applicable rather than none-installed.
- **Pollution controls perpetually promised.** How many pollution controls exist only as proposals with compliance years that keep sliding? — EIA-860 environmental equipment schedule (FED_EIA860_6_2_ENVIROEQUIP). *Harm:* every year of deferred compliance is another year of measured pollution on a real population. · caveat: single-year snapshot can't see proposals made and dropped; compliance-year columns may hold sentinel values like 9999.
- **New Source Review never triggered.** Which utilities run active boilers with no New Source Review permit ever recorded? — EIA-860 environmental equipment schedule (FED_EIA860_6_2_ENVIROEQUIP). *Harm:* skipping NSR locks a community into 1970s emissions. · caveat: absence of an NSR record is not proof of avoidance; many boilers legitimately never triggered review.
- **Unequal legal pollution ceilings.** Are two identical boilers allowed to emit several times different amounts depending on the permitting state? — EIA-860 environmental equipment schedule (FED_EIA860_6_2_ENVIROEQUIP). *Harm:* two identical boilers, two legal ceilings — one community is simply worth less. · wild · caveat: emission-rate standards carry per-row units and averaging periods — a unit-normalization build must come first; cross-state comparison invalid until then.
- **Who got solar and who got diesel behind the meter.** Which sectors and states got distributed solar versus combustion backup? — EIA-861 non-net-metering distributed (FED_EIA861_NON_NET_METERING_DISTRIBUTED). *Harm:* households stuck with combustion backup breathe the exhaust in their own neighborhood. · caveat: ten unlabeled technology slots — decode against the EIA form.
- **How much water fracking takes.** How much water does each frack job draw, where, which operators drill the thirstiest wells, and is per-well use rising in arid basins? — FracFocus disclosure list (FED_FRACFOCUS_DISCLOSURE_LIST). *Harm:* water drawn per job in drought counties is water not available to households. · caveat: volume units unverified; mixed coordinate datums possible; outliers may be data-entry errors.
- **The disclosure regime going dark.** When the fracking disclosure format changed versions, what stopped being reported? — FracFocus disclosure list (FED_FRACFOCUS_DISCLOSURE_LIST). *Harm:* version changes that drop fields are how disclosure regimes quietly go dark. · medium
- **Trade-secret frack chemicals.** Which operators withhold the most ingredients as proprietary? — FracFocus registry (FED_FRACFOCUS_REGISTRY). *Harm:* you cannot test your water for a chemical whose name the company refuses to disclose. · caveat: trade secret inferred from missing identifiers; the source may encode it differently.
- **What got pumped under which counties.** Which chemicals — and how much cumulative hazardous mass — have been pumped into the ground under each county? — FracFocus registry (FED_FRACFOCUS_REGISTRY). *Harm:* cumulative chemical mass under a county is exposure residents never consented to. · caveat: ingredient names are free text with many spellings; selecting "hazardous" needs a CAS-keyed hazard reference (CAS is not a verified key) — land a CAS-normalized reference and measure the match; mass column may be sparse.
- **Operator chemical recipes differ.** Do different operators pump materially different chemical cocktails? — FracFocus registry (FED_FRACFOCUS_REGISTRY). *Harm:* different recipes mean different exposures nobody has compared. · medium · caveat: purpose and ingredient are free text needing grouping.
- **The suppliers claiming the secrecy.** Are service companies, not well operators, the ones claiming chemical secrecy? — FracFocus registry (FED_FRACFOCUS_REGISTRY). *Harm:* the party hiding the chemical identity may not even be the one your state regulates. · wild · caveat: supplier/claimant fields are free text and possibly mostly blank.
- **Frack water: fresh versus recycled.** How much fracking water is drinking-water-grade fresh, which operators rely on it hardest, and is recycling growing? — FracFocus water source table (FED_FRACFOCUS_WATER_SOURCE). *Harm:* fresh groundwater used for fracking is drinking water permanently removed from the aquifer. · caveat: source descriptions are free text needing fresh/recycled classification; only 23,747 rows against 248k disclosures — partial, possibly non-random coverage.
- **Where the orphaned wells are and who inherited them.** Where do orphaned oil and gas wells cluster, and which counties inherited the cleanup bill? — USGS orphaned wells (FED_USGS_ORPHANED_OIL_GAS_WELLS). *Harm:* orphaned wells leak methane and brine into the groundwater of whoever still lives there, with no owner left to bill. · caveat: coordinates parsed from text and county names lack FIPS — needs a county crosswalk; some records have only township-range descriptions.
- **States undercounting their orphans.** Does each state's orphan-well count reflect reality or just its willingness to report? — USGS orphaned wells (FED_USGS_ORPHANED_OIL_GAS_WELLS). *Harm:* under-reporting states leave residents next to hazards that officially do not exist. · caveat: differing state definitions make cross-state counts genuinely non-comparable.
- **Idle versus orphaned: parked liabilities.** How many wells sit "idle" rather than formally orphaned — liabilities operators park and intend never to pay? — USGS orphaned wells (FED_USGS_ORPHANED_OIL_GAS_WELLS). *Harm:* the idle-to-orphaned gap is where cleanup obligations go to die. · caveat: status vocabulary differs by reporting state — harmonize before the grid means anything.
- **Ghost operators in the notes.** Can the free-text notes reconstruct which companies abandoned wells the structured fields no longer credit? — USGS orphaned wells notes fields (FED_USGS_ORPHANED_OIL_GAS_WELLS). *Harm:* the notes are often the only surviving record of who left the mess. · wild · caveat: company extraction from free text — needs text mining plus name canonicalization; notes may be mostly null or purely locational.
- **The abandoned-mine landscape.** Where are past-producer and abandoned mineral sites, when did production end, and which towns were left holding contamination and unemployment? — USGS mineral resources (fed_usgs_minerals). *Harm:* communities built around a mine that closed forty years ago carry the cleanup and the job loss. · caveat: table mixes national statistics with site records; production years sparsely populated.
- **Toxic byproducts that travel with target metals.** Which contaminants co-occur with which valuable metals at the same sites? — USGS mineral resources (fed_usgs_minerals). *Harm:* knowing the byproducts tells mining towns what to test their water for. · wild · caveat: commodity fields are inconsistent free text.
- **Hazardous air pollution hot spots — and who grew.** Which facilities emit the most hazardous air pollutants and VOCs, and which grew emissions year over year instead of cleaning up? — EPA combined air emissions (fed_epa_air_emissions_poll_rpt_combined_emissions). *Harm:* HAP emissions map directly onto cancer and asthma in fenceline neighborhoods. · caveat: units vary by row — summing across unit_of_measure without normalizing is a fatal error; NEI years may be triennial.
- **Pollutants visible through only one program.** Which pollutants are tracked by a single reporting program — one budget cut away from public invisibility? — EPA combined air emissions (fed_epa_air_emissions_poll_rpt_combined_emissions). *Harm:* a pollutant tracked by one program vanishes from the record if that program stops. · caveat: program coverage may be uneven across years.
- **Exotic chemicals, few communities, no studies.** Which rare chemicals are emitted or permitted at only a handful of sites? — EPA combined air emissions plus ICIS-Air pollutant permits (fed_epa_air_emissions_poll_rpt_combined_emissions, FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_POLLUTANTS). *Harm:* a chemical at three plants means three communities exposed with no national study. · wild · caveat: pollutant name variants split the same chemical and CAS numbers are often blank — normalize names against a chemical reference before counting.
- **Is anyone actually measuring emissions.** How much of the pollution record is measured (monitors, stack tests) versus estimated by the polluter? — NEI-type flags, GHGRP monitoring method, ICIS-Air stack tests (fed_epa_air_emissions_poll_rpt_combined_emissions, FED_EPA_GHGRP_FACILITY, FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_STACK_TESTS). *Harm:* enforcement and health studies rest on numbers the polluter estimated for itself. · caveat: NEI-type and CEMS flag encodings undocumented; stack-test pollutant lists are packed multi-value strings.
- **Air monitoring gaps — and monitors turned off.** Which counties have no active air monitor at all, and where did states retire more monitors than they opened? — EPA AQS monitoring sites (fed_epa_aqs_sites). *Harm:* a county with no monitor cannot prove its air is bad, so it never qualifies for relief. · caveat: needs a county universe joined in; closure can be relocation; null closed-dates mean still open.
- **Monitors placed where it looks good.** Are air monitors sited in rural and residential settings rather than where the industry actually is? — EPA AQS monitoring sites (fed_epa_aqs_sites). *Harm:* monitors away from industry produce clean readings for communities not breathing clean air. · caveat: siting rules legitimately require some background sites.
- **Monitoring coverage of tribal lands.** Which tribal nations have air monitors and administered water systems, and which have no measurement infrastructure at all? — AQS tribe fields plus SDWA tribal codes (fed_epa_aqs_sites, FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS). *Harm:* tribal nations without monitors cannot document exposure from nearby industry on their own land. · caveat: tribal fields likely mostly blank; blank does not mean off tribal land.
- **Who owns the monitors.** When a polluting state runs its own air monitors, does the referee work for one team? — EPA AQS monitoring sites (fed_epa_aqs_sites). *Harm:* self-run monitoring lets a state understate its own pollution. · medium · caveat: agency strings are unnormalized free text.
- **Chronic noncompliance with no penalty.** Where do facilities sit in noncompliance for years — even flagged as significant — with zero formal action and near-zero fines? — EPA ECHO exporter with penalty-gap flag (fed_epa_echo). *Harm:* communities live next to chronically noncompliant facilities that never get fined — a regulator that stopped regulating. · caveat: 3.1M rows include inactive registrations — filter to active/major or the map is noise; action counts are lifetime totals with no date bound.
- **Enforcement inequality by neighborhood demographics.** Are facilities in minority neighborhoods inspected less often than identical facilities elsewhere? — ECHO demographics fields (fed_epa_echo). *Harm:* if inspectors visit minority neighborhoods less, enforcement itself is unequal. · caveat: agency's own area estimates; industry mix confounds; correlation is not causation.
- **Where breaking environmental law is cheap.** In which states does a quarter of noncompliance or a violation cost the least? — ECHO penalties per noncompliant quarter plus ICIS-Air penalties by state (fed_epa_echo, FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FORMAL_ACTIONS). *Harm:* identical violations priced differently by state means one community's air is legally worth less. · caveat: program delegation varies by state — needs program-level control.
- **Toxic burden on tribal land.** Which corporations and federal agencies operate polluting facilities on tribal land, and how big is the release burden? — tribal flags across ECHO, FRS, GHGRP, TRI, FracFocus (fed_epa_echo, FED_EPA_FRS_FULL, fed_epa_ghgrp_facility, FED_EPA_TRI_BASIC_2023, FED_FRACFOCUS_DISCLOSURE_LIST). *Harm:* tribal communities carry releases under a jurisdictional regime with thinner enforcement, from operations they did not permit and do not profit from. · caveat: tribal flags are coarse and sparsely populated in every source; nulls must not be read as not-tribal.
- **The most people exposed.** Which facilities release the most where the most people live? — EPA ECHO exporter (fed_epa_echo). *Harm:* highest release plus highest density is the largest number of people exposed. · caveat: release volume is not toxicity-weighted.
- **Dirtiest power per megawatt-hour.** Which plants produce little power for enormous pollution? — EPA eGRID plant file (fed_epa_egrid_plant_2022). *Harm:* a high-rate low-output plant dumps pollution on neighbors for almost no public benefit. · caveat: single-year 2022 snapshot; no trend possible alone.
- **Peakers firing on smog days.** Where do low-capacity-factor, high-NOx peaker plants sit in neighborhoods? — EPA eGRID plant file (fed_epa_egrid_plant_2022). *Harm:* peakers run on hot smog days, exactly when asthma cases spike. · caveat: lat/lon cast with try_to_double — bad rows silently drop off the map.
- **Mercury rate outliers.** Which plants emit the most mercury per megawatt-hour, and are they all coal? — EPA eGRID plant file (fed_epa_egrid_plant_2022). *Harm:* mercury accumulates in local fish and in the children who eat them. · caveat: mercury columns land as raw text; casting needed.
- **Paper adjustments to emissions.** How many tons of reported pollution disappear through biomass and combined-heat-and-power accounting adjustments? — EPA eGRID plant file (fed_epa_egrid_plant_2022). *Harm:* an accounting adjustment changes nothing about what the neighborhood inhales. · caveat: adjustments are methodologically defensible — framing must include that context.
- **Structurally dirty grid regions.** Which regional grids are structurally dirty regardless of any individual plant? — eGRID subregion fields (fed_epa_egrid_plant_2022). *Harm:* everyone in a dirty subregion carries its emissions no matter what appliance they buy. · caveat: regional averages must be generation-weighted.
- **Cumulative burden: where regulated sites stack up.** Which blocks, ZIPs, and counties carry a stacked load of regulated facilities, major air sources, waste handlers, carcinogen releases, spill calls, and enforcement cases? — FRS, ICIS-Air, RCRA, TRI, NPDES and enforcement-case locations (FED_EPA_FRS_FRS_FACILITIES, FED_EPA_FRS_FULL, FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FACILITIES, FED_EPA_RCRA_FACILITIES, FED_EPA_TRI_BASIC_2023, fed_epa_npdes_icis_facilities, FED_EPA_ICIS_FEC_CASE_ENFORCEMENT_CONCLUSION_FACILITIES). *Harm:* residents of a handful of blocks live inside clusters of dozens of regulated sites while most blocks have none. · caveat: ZIP formats need normalizing, county text lacks FIPS in several tables, coordinate quality varies (ZIP-centroid guesses fake clusters) — geocode-quality filter plus FIPS/ZIP5 normalization pass first; inactive registrations inflate counts.
- **Overloaded EPA regions.** Which of the ten EPA regional offices oversee an impossible facility caseload? — FRS facilities (FED_EPA_FRS_FRS_FACILITIES). *Harm:* an overloaded office means inspections that never happen in somebody's neighborhood. · medium · caveat: no staffing data in the table — workload read needs an outside denominator.
- **How many programs watch each facility.** Which facilities sit under many regulatory programs and which large sites are watched by only one? — FRS program links (FED_EPA_FRS_FRS_PROGRAM_LINKS, FED_EPA_FRS_FULL). *Harm:* a large facility under one program is a site nobody is fully looking at. · caveat: few links can mean a small operation; state delegation makes linkage counts imperfectly comparable.
- **The same plant under many names.** Which facilities appear under different names in different regulatory systems? — FRS program links (FED_EPA_FRS_FRS_PROGRAM_LINKS). *Harm:* name drift across systems is how a repeat violator escapes recognition. · caveat: much variation is benign spelling difference — needs a similarity threshold.
- **Regulated industry in the territories.** How much regulated industry sits in Puerto Rico, Guam, and other territories national reporting forgets? — FRS program links territory fields (FED_EPA_FRS_FRS_PROGRAM_LINKS). *Harm:* territories host regulated industry with far less public attention on it. · medium · caveat: country field may be almost entirely one value.
- **Records stranded in the retired SIC system.** How many facilities and water permits carry only a retired SIC industry code and no modern NAICS? — FRS SIC/NAICS bridges plus NPDES SIC bridge (FED_EPA_FRS_FRS_SIC_CODES, FED_EPA_FRS_FRS_NAICS_CODES, FED_EPA_NPDES_NPDES_SICS). *Harm:* a facility invisible to industry-based analysis never shows up in any sector accountability sweep. · caveat: establishing absence requires the NAICS bridge — strictly cross-table within the same family.
- **Facilities that classify themselves many ways.** Which sites claim many industry codes — able to pick the least-regulated identity when it matters? — FRS and NPDES NAICS bridges (FED_EPA_FRS_FRS_NAICS_CODES, FED_EPA_NPDES_NPDES_NAICS). *Harm:* multi-identity classification can be the least-obligation identity in practice. · wild · caveat: multiple NAICS is often legitimate multi-process operation.
- **Which industries hold the permits.** Which industries dominate the regulated universe — air, water discharge, hazardous waste — and what is each state's industrial-waste signature? — FRS NAICS, NPDES facility types and codes, RCRA NAICS (FED_EPA_FRS_FRS_NAICS_CODES, fed_epa_npdes_icis_facilities, FED_EPA_NPDES_NPDES_NAICS, FED_EPA_NPDES_NPDES_SICS, FED_EPA_RCRA_RCRA_NAICS). *Harm:* naming the dominant industries is the first step to asking who oversees them. · medium · caveat: count distinct facilities, not rows — facilities carry multiple codes.
- **Records nobody has touched in decades.** Which regulatory records have gone untouched for ten or twenty years — meaning nobody has looked? — FRS create/update dates, ICIS-Air program dates, Superfund boundary timestamps (FED_EPA_FRS_FULL, FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_PROGRAMS, fed_epa_superfund_site_boundaries). *Harm:* a record nobody updates is a facility or cleanup nobody has verified in years. · caveat: bulk migrations reset update dates en masse; Superfund GIS dates reflect data maintenance, not cleanup progress.
- **The border industrial corridor.** What kind of industry clusters specifically along the US–Mexico border strip? — FRS full border indicator (FED_EPA_FRS_FULL). *Harm:* border communities host industry sited to be near a line rather than near oversight. · medium · caveat: border indicator may be a rarely-populated legacy flag.
- **Climate emitters: ranked and concentrated.** Who are the largest reported greenhouse gas emitters, and how few sites account for most of the total? — EPA GHGRP emissions (fed_epa_ghgrp_emission). *Harm:* if a short list of sites causes most emissions, action against that list helps everyone. · caveat: gas and sector IDs are unlabeled numeric codes — land the GHGRP code lookups; subsector rows may nest inside sector rows and double count.
- **Methane versus CO2 by sector.** Which industries dominate methane and fluorinated gases rather than CO2? — EPA GHGRP emissions (fed_epa_ghgrp_emission). *Harm:* methane-heavy sectors cause near-term warming and health harm the CO2 totals hide. · caveat: same unlabeled code problem — the lookup must be landed.
- **Facilities growing against the trend.** Which facilities expanded their emissions while their whole sector cut? — EPA GHGRP emissions (fed_epa_ghgrp_emission). *Harm:* a facility expanding while peers cut is a specific, nameable actor doing specific harm. · caveat: facilities entering/leaving the program fake rises and falls.
- **Who stopped reporting greenhouse gases.** Which facilities dropped out of the greenhouse gas reporting program without closing? — EPA GHGRP facility file (fed_epa_ghgrp_facility). *Harm:* a facility that exits the program keeps emitting but stops being counted. · caveat: exit can be a legitimate drop below threshold — needs the emission table to distinguish.
- **High-priority violators still running.** Where are the air facilities flagged as high-priority violators that are still operating today? — ICIS-Air facilities (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FACILITIES). *Harm:* an HPV flag means documented serious violation — and the people next door are still breathing it. · caveat: point-in-time flag with no date; can't see how long a site has held it.
- **The industries that run the violators.** Which industries have the highest share of facilities in serious violation or named in federal environmental cases? — ICIS-Air NAICS and HPV flags plus case-facility NAICS (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FACILITIES, fed_epa_icis_fec_case_facilities). *Harm:* naming the sector shows this is systemic, not one bad plant. · caveat: NAICS fields hold multiple packed codes stored as ragged text — unpack and validate before counting.
- **Local air district patchwork.** Which local air-control districts carry the heaviest facility load and the worst compliance? — ICIS-Air facilities (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FACILITIES). *Harm:* a weak or overloaded local district is why the violation next door goes unaddressed for years. · medium · caveat: local-region fields likely populated only in a few states.
- **Zombie records in the enforcement system.** How many facilities are marked closed while still carrying active program links? — ICIS-Air facilities status plus programs tables (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FACILITIES, FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_PROGRAMS). *Harm:* zombie records let a still-operating site hide behind a closed status and skip inspections. · wild · caveat: status codes undocumented; closed is often simply accurate.
- **The uninspected.** Which facilities, permits, and water systems have gone the longest with no inspection or site visit of any kind — and which whole states are inspection deserts? — inspections across ICIS-Air, EPA cross-program, NPDES, RCRA, SDWA (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FCES_PCES, fed_epa_icis_fec_icis_fec_epa_inspections, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_inspections, fed_epa_rcra_evaluations, FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_SITE_VISITS). *Harm:* an uninspected plant is one where a violation simply never gets found. · caveat: absence of a row is not proof of no inspection — state reporting varies; inactive facilities dominate the tail without a status filter; truncated loads would fabricate gaps.
- **The federal-to-state enforcement handoff.** How much environmental oversight shifted from EPA to state agencies, statute by statute? — state/EPA flags across ICIS-Air, cross-program inspections, RCRA (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FCES_PCES, FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_STACK_TESTS, FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_TITLEV_CERTS, fed_epa_icis_fec_icis_fec_epa_inspections, fed_epa_rcra_violations). *Harm:* where enforcement moved to states with weak capacity, the people nearby lost their referee. · caveat: flags may describe the data submitter rather than the actor; state derivation from program-ID prefixes is unreliable.
- **Inspections getting shallower.** Are full on-site inspections being replaced by partial checks and desk reviews? — evaluation types, inspection durations and type mix (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FCES_PCES, fed_epa_icis_fec_icis_fec_epa_inspections, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_inspections). *Harm:* a drive-by check can be logged as an inspection while missing the process actually harming people. · caveat: type recodes mid-history can fake a trend; same-day inspections may just be poorly recorded.
- **The zero-dollar penalty.** How often does a formal enforcement action carry no fine at all? — ICIS-Air formal actions plus NPDES formal enforcement (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FORMAL_ACTIONS, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_formal_enforcement_actions). *Harm:* a penalty of nothing tells a polluter the cheapest path is to keep polluting. · caveat: zero vs null (not-yet-assessed vs waived) may be indistinguishable after text-to-number casts.
- **Repeat offenders: does the price ever rise.** Do penalties escalate for repeat violators, and who are the biggest cumulative-fine repeat defendants across air, water, and hazardous waste? — formal actions, violation cohorts, penalties per permit/handler, case defendants (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FORMAL_ACTIONS, FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_VIOLATION_HISTORY, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_formal_enforcement_actions, fed_epa_rcra_enforcements, fed_epa_icis_fec_case_enforcement_conclusion_facilities). *Harm:* if penalties never escalate, a repeat polluter has learned that harm is affordable. · caveat: the actor key is a permit/handler ID, not a company — one firm hides behind many permits; roll up to owners via the FRS/LEI crosswalk before claiming repeat-offender; partial enforcement history fabricates first-offender status.
- **Are inspections collapsing over time.** Is the volume of environmental inspections, evaluations, stack tests, and sanitary surveys falling — nationally, by region, by administration era? — inspection volumes across five programs (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_STACK_TESTS, fed_epa_icis_fec_icis_fec_epa_inspections, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_inspections, fed_epa_rcra_evaluations, FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_SITE_VISITS). *Harm:* every trough in the line is a period when facilities self-regulated by default. · caveat: dates are text casts in several tables — a bad parse fakes a collapse; coverage windows unknown.
- **Penalty dollars over the administrations.** Have enforcement actions and penalty dollars risen and collapsed with political administrations? — formal actions and enforcement amounts across air, water, waste (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FORMAL_ACTIONS, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_formal_enforcement_actions, fed_epa_rcra_enforcements). *Harm:* every trough is a period when polluters faced no consequence and neighbors faced the pollution. · caveat: settlement dates lag violations by years — the timeline shows resolution, not offense timing.
- **Which enforcement tools actually have teeth.** Which legal tools do agencies actually reach for, and which carry real penalties? — formal action types, response policy codes, informal action mix (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_FORMAL_ACTIONS, FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_VIOLATION_HISTORY, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_informal_enforcement_actions). *Harm:* when agencies mostly reach for toothless tools, harm continues while the file shows action taken. · caveat: tool mix is partly statute-driven, not agency choice; several code sets need lookups.
- **Letters instead of fines.** How much enforcement is warning letters — by statute, state, and over time? — informal actions (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_INFORMAL_ACTIONS, fed_epa_icis_fec_epa_informal_enforcement_actions). *Harm:* a warning letter costs a polluter nothing and buys the neighborhood another year of the same air. · caveat: informal counts not comparable across states with different recording practices; rates need facility denominators.
- **Facilities with dozens of warnings and no escalation.** Which specific facilities have absorbed ten, twenty, or more informal warnings with no formal action ever following? — informal actions across three programs (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_INFORMAL_ACTIONS, fed_epa_icis_fec_epa_informal_enforcement_actions, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_informal_enforcement_actions). *Harm:* a facility with twenty warning letters and nothing else is a community failed twenty times. · caveat: proving no-escalation needs the formal-action tables joined — alone this only shows warning volume.
- **Enforcement off the books.** How much enforcement activity is logged as unofficial — leaving no record a citizen could use to prove a pattern? — informal-action official flags (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_INFORMAL_ACTIONS, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_informal_enforcement_actions). *Harm:* unofficial actions leave no usable record for the harmed. · medium · caveat: official-flag semantics undocumented.
- **The permitted chemical universe.** What is each facility legally permitted to emit — the chemical list neighbors rarely see? — ICIS-Air pollutants (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_POLLUTANTS). *Harm:* the permitted list is the legal exposure envelope nobody shows the public. · caveat: permitted is not emitted — no quantities in this table.
- **The longest chemical lists, never assessed together.** Which sites are permitted for dozens of substances at once? — ICIS-Air pollutants (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_POLLUTANTS). *Harm:* twenty permitted chemicals are never evaluated as one dose for the people next door. · caveat: long lists can reflect thorough permitting.
- **Which air rules protect the most people.** Which air program subparts cover the most facilities — where would one rollback harm the most people — and which large sites sit under almost none? — ICIS-Air program subparts (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_PROGRAM_SUBPARTS). *Harm:* knowing which rule covers the most facilities shows where one rollback does the most damage. · caveat: coverage counts are program-system IDs, not necessarily distinct physical sites.
- **Late arrivals to regulation.** Which facilities came under air rules late — spending extra years emitting with no rule at all? — ICIS-Air programs (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_PROGRAMS). *Harm:* late entry means unregulated years on the same neighborhood. · caveat: begin_date parsing unverified.
- **The Title V honor system.** How often do big polluters self-report a deviation on their compliance certifications — and are the too-clean perfect records believable? — Title V certifications (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_TITLEV_CERTS). *Harm:* if almost nobody self-reports a deviation, the honor-system permit program protects nobody. · caveat: deviation flag values uncoded — blank vs N vs null may be indistinguishable; perfect records may be genuine.
- **Violations that fester.** How long do environmental violations stay unresolved — across air, water, hazardous waste, drinking water — and which never resolve at all? — violation histories across four programs (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_VIOLATION_HISTORY, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_cs_violations, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_ps_violations, fed_epa_rcra_violations, FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT). *Harm:* every unresolved month is another month a neighborhood breathes or drinks an illegal amount of pollution. · caveat: unresolved cases have null end dates and silently drop from naive distributions — the visible picture is the optimistic half.
- **Where enforcement leaks: the funnel.** At which exact stage does the enforcement pipeline lose cases — discovery, notice, resolution? — ICIS-Air violation pathway dates (FED_EPA_ICIS_AIR_ICIS_AIR_VIOLATION_HISTORY). *Harm:* the width of the drop-off between inspection and penalty is the exact measure of how safe it is to pollute. · caveat: pathway-date semantics guessed from column names; funnel order may be wrong.
- **Where federal environmental cases land — and don't.** Where do concluded federal cases concentrate, and which industrial states show almost none? — EPA case-conclusion and case facilities (fed_epa_icis_fec_case_enforcement_conclusion_facilities, fed_epa_icis_fec_case_facilities). *Harm:* places with facilities but no concluded cases are places where breaking the law has no ending. · medium · caveat: no date columns — static snapshot; raw counts need a regulated-facility denominator.
- **Mega-cases and corporate case clusters.** Which corporate families appear across the most enforcement cases, and do settlements covering hundreds of sites discount per-site accountability? — EPA case-conclusion facilities (fed_epa_icis_fec_case_enforcement_conclusion_facilities). *Harm:* a single settlement covering hundreds of sites can discount each community's claim. · caveat: facility name variants split one company — canonicalize names or use the FRS/LEI crosswalk; facility UIN population unverified.
- **Dischargers stacked on impaired waters.** Which permitted water dischargers sit on waterways already flagged as impaired? — NPDES ICIS facilities impaired-waters field (fed_epa_npdes_icis_facilities). *Harm:* communities drawing from an impaired river get more discharge, not less. · caveat: impaired-waters field population and encoding unverified; lat/lon may be widely null.
- **Missed compliance schedules across programs.** How far behind schedule do promised environmental fixes run, and which promised controls never got built? — schedule violations and milestones across NPDES, RCRA, SDWA (fed_epa_npdes_npdes_cs_violations, fed_epa_npdes_npdes_ps_violations, fed_epa_rcra_violations, FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_EVENTS_MILESTONES). *Harm:* every slipped milestone is more months of the same discharge into someone's water. · caveat: null actual dates are the worst cases and drop out of naive date-difference charts.
- **The compliance pulse.** Is significant noncompliance rising or falling — quarterly for water permits, monthly for hazardous-waste handlers? — NPDES QNCR history plus RCRA SNC history (fed_epa_npdes_npdes_qncr_history, fed_epa_rcra_viosnc_history). *Harm:* a rising share means more communities getting illegal discharge quarter after quarter. · caveat: quarter/month fields are text needing parsing; SNC code values must be confirmed before counting.
- **Stuck in noncompliance forever.** Which permits, handlers, and water systems enter violation status and never leave? — QNCR, SNC, and SDWA repeat-violation cohorts (fed_epa_npdes_npdes_qncr_history, fed_epa_rcra_viosnc_history, FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT). *Harm:* sites flagged for years running are tolerated hazards next to real households. · caveat: streak logic breaks on reporting gaps; SDWA quarterly snapshots must be deduplicated first.
- **Dumping when nobody is measuring.** Do water violations cluster in particular seasons? — NPDES quarterly noncompliance history (fed_epa_npdes_npdes_qncr_history). *Harm:* seasonal spikes point to deliberate timing of discharge. · wild · caveat: seasonality could be a reporting artifact.
- **Single-event spills: how often, how long, who catches them.** How frequent are discrete water spills, how long do they run, and who actually detects them? — NPDES single-event violations (fed_epa_npdes_npdes_se_violations). *Harm:* a spill that runs a month is a month of exposure downstream; if only polluters self-report, unreported spills are invisible by design. · caveat: end dates null for ongoing events; agency-type codes uncoded; comments may be boilerplate.
- **The penalty haircut.** How much smaller is the final collected penalty than the proposed one, and which agencies discount hardest? — RCRA enforcement amounts (fed_epa_rcra_enforcements). *Harm:* the gap between the announced fine and the collected fine is the discount polluters actually get. · caveat: amount-field meanings inferred from abbreviations; some low settlements are legitimate.
- **Projects instead of fines.** How often do supplemental environmental projects replace cash penalties — and does the harmed community end up with neither money nor cleanup? — RCRA enforcement amounts (fed_epa_rcra_enforcements). *Harm:* swapping fines for voluntary projects can leave the harmed community with nothing. · wild · caveat: the four amount-column meanings could be wrong — verify before use.
- **Inspection hit rates.** Which inspection and evaluation types actually find violations — and are cheap desk reviews replacing the ones that do? — NPDES inspection outcomes plus RCRA found-violation flags (fed_epa_npdes_npdes_inspections, fed_epa_rcra_evaluations). *Harm:* a regulator whose inspections never find anything is not looking. · caveat: outcome/flag encodings unverified; type mix shifted over time, confounding rates.
- **Where the biggest hazardous-waste generators cluster.** Where do large-quantity hazardous-waste generators concentrate? — RCRA facilities (fed_epa_rcra_facilities). *Harm:* concentrated large generators concentrate risk on those residents. · caveat: coordinates parsed from text, may be null or zero-filled; category codes need a lookup.
- **Outside the enforcement universe.** What share of hazardous-waste handlers sit outside the "full enforcement universe" — facing almost no scrutiny by design? — RCRA facilities flags (fed_epa_rcra_facilities). *Harm:* facilities outside the enforcement universe face almost no scrutiny. · medium · caveat: flag semantics inferred from column names only.
- **The regulator that downgrades.** Is the share of violations escalated to significant noncompliance falling while violations hold steady? — RCRA violation/SNC history (fed_epa_rcra_viosnc_history). *Harm:* downgrading makes harm disappear from the headline numbers without stopping it. · wild · caveat: SNC criteria may have changed definition mid-history.
- **The riskiest drinking water configurations.** Which communities drink from surface water with no treatment or filtration indicated? — SDWA facilities (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_FACILITIES). *Harm:* untreated surface water is the classic setup for an outbreak. · caveat: filtration status code is cast to a number and may be mangled; quarterly snapshots need dedupe.
- **Water resale chains.** Which wholesalers sell water to many downstream systems? — SDWA facilities seller links (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_FACILITIES). *Harm:* one contaminated wholesaler can hit dozens of downstream communities at once. · caveat: seller-PWSID population unverified — may be blank on most rows.
- **Communities losing their water infrastructure.** Where are drinking-water facilities and whole systems being deactivated, and how many people did they serve? — SDWA facilities and public water systems deactivation dates (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_FACILITIES, FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS). *Harm:* when a small system dies, its residents may end up on untested private wells. · medium · caveat: deactivation may mean a merger rather than lost service.
- **Tiny water systems, no budget, worst compliance.** How many Americans drink from tiny water systems serving a few hundred people? — SDWA public water systems plus geographic areas (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS, FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS). *Harm:* tiny systems have no budget, no staff, and the worst compliance records. · caveat: population-served counts may be stale or zero on inactive systems.
- **Fragmented patchwork water service.** Which ZIPs are served by multiple different water systems — one street on wildly different water quality? — SDWA geographic areas (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS). *Harm:* fragmented service means the same street can be on different water quality. · wild · caveat: overlap may be an artifact of imprecise geographic coding.
- **Kept in the dark: notification failures.** How often do water systems fail to tell residents their water was unsafe, for how long, and about which contaminants? — SDWA public-notification violation associations (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_PN_VIOLATION_ASSOC). *Harm:* a failure to notify means people kept drinking water they would have avoided; the length of the silence is the length of the unwitting exposure. · caveat: open periods with null end dates drop out; contaminant codes need a lookup.
- **Who owns the water.** How many Americans drink from privately owned water systems — and what changes when the water goes bad? — SDWA public water systems (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS). *Harm:* private ownership changes who answers when the water goes bad. · caveat: owner-type codes uncoded; snapshots must be deduplicated.
- **Relaxed monitoring privileges.** Where have states granted reduced monitoring or "outstanding performer" status? — SDWA public water systems flags (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS). *Harm:* relaxed monitoring means fewer chances to catch contamination before people drink it. · caveat: reduced monitoring is a legitimate reward — framing needs care.
- **Who the water systems serve.** Do systems serve residential, institutional, or transient populations — and which stop reporting service areas entirely? — SDWA service areas (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_SERVICE_AREAS). *Harm:* transient-population systems serve people who never learn the water was bad. · medium · caveat: thin table; quarter-over-quarter changes may be reporting noise.
- **What fails inside water plants.** Which parts of water systems fail sanitary surveys most — treatment, distribution, management, finance? — SDWA site-visit evaluation codes (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_SITE_VISITS). *Harm:* the failing area codes point at the exact mechanism by which bad water reaches taps. · caveat: each evaluation code has its own uncoded value set; a shared lookup may not exist.
- **Financially failing water systems.** Which water systems show financial deficiency across repeated inspections? — SDWA site-visit financial code (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_SITE_VISITS). *Harm:* a broke utility cannot fix its pipes, and its customers drink the consequence. · caveat: financial-code meaning inferred from the column name.
- **Health violations nobody enforces.** In which states do health-based drinking water violations most often carry no enforcement record at all? — SDWA violations and enforcement (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT). *Harm:* unenforced health violations are the government watching contamination and doing nothing. · caveat: null enforcement IDs may be a flattened-grain artifact.
- **States with weaker limits than federal.** Do any states set maximum contaminant levels looser than the federal limit? — SDWA state vs federal MCL columns (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT). *Harm:* a weaker state limit legalizes exposure that would be a violation one state over. · wild · caveat: state MCL may be blank or mirror federal; units may differ.
- **Superfund sites and the limbo list.** Where do Superfund sites sit, how big are their footprints, and which have been stuck in "proposed" status for decades? — EPA Superfund site boundaries (fed_epa_superfund_site_boundaries). *Harm:* people live, go to school, and drink water next to these footprints while status sits frozen. · caveat: polygon geometry not landed — centroid map only; dedupe on EPA site ID (2,114 features / 1,908 sites); status codes need a lookup.
- **Carcinogens released, mapped to the ZIP.** Where were carcinogen-flagged toxic releases made in 2023, and which ZIP codes carry the heaviest cancer-linked load? — EPA TRI basic 2023 (FED_EPA_TRI_BASIC_2023). *Harm:* every dot is a place where a known carcinogen was legally released into a neighborhood. · caveat: release-quantity columns land uncast (text) and units mix pounds/grams; single-year snapshot.
- **The PFAS leaderboard.** Which facilities release the most PFAS "forever chemicals"? — TRI basic 2023 PFAS flag (FED_EPA_TRI_BASIC_2023). *Harm:* PFAS never breaks down — today's release is permanent. · caveat: PFAS flag encoding unverified; totals need casting and unit normalization.
- **Release pathways determine exposure.** How does each industry dispose of its toxics — fugitive air, stack air, water, underground injection, landfill? — TRI basic 2023 pathway columns (FED_EPA_TRI_BASIC_2023). *Harm:* air hits lungs, water hits taps, landfill hits groundwater later. · caveat: all pathway columns are uncast text; sums require casting and unit handling.
- **The companies that keep spilling.** Which responsible companies generate release call after release call to the National Response Center — and how much of the burden is corporate versus government versus private? — USCG NRC incidents plus secondary extract (fed_uscg_nrc_incidents, fed_uscg_nrc_incident_reports). *Harm:* the same firms generate release after release while communities downwind absorb every one. · caveat: company names are free text with heavy spelling variation — canonicalize or the leaderboard fragments; the 116k secondary extract overlaps the main feed and double-counts if treated as independent.
- **Are reported releases actually falling.** Across decades of NRC calls, are chemical and fuel releases really declining — or just being recategorized? — USCG NRC incidents (fed_uscg_nrc_incidents). *Harm:* if releases are flat while regulation tightened, the public enforcement story is wrong. · caveat: multiple date fields may disagree; timestamp casts may drop rows silently.
- **Incidents that stay open.** How long do reported release incidents stay open before being marked complete? — USCG NRC incidents (fed_uscg_nrc_incidents). *Harm:* incidents open for months are incidents nobody is cleaning up while people live next to them. · caveat: null completion dates bias toward fast closures.
- **Where release calls concentrate.** Which states and ZIPs generate release calls over and over from a rotating cast of companies? — USCG NRC incidents (fed_uscg_nrc_incidents). *Harm:* a ZIP with hundreds of releases from rotating companies is a sacrifice zone with no single villain to sue. · caveat: the ZIP/state on file is the responsible party's address, not necessarily the spill location — resolve that first or the story inverts.
- **Watersheds and aquifers nobody measures.** Which watersheds, basins, and named aquifers have zero or near-zero monitoring stations — and where did stream gauges go dark? — USGS water APIs plus WQP monitoring stations (fed_usgs_water, fed_wqp_monitoring_stations). *Harm:* unmonitored watersheds are where contamination goes undetected until people are sick; a dead gauge is a lost flood warning. · caveat: the WQP extract is only 5,818 stations and may itself be partial — absence here may not mean absence in reality.
- **Who runs water monitoring.** How much of the water monitoring network is federal versus state versus volunteer groups? — WQP monitoring stations (fed_wqp_monitoring_stations). *Harm:* volunteer-dependent monitoring vanishes exactly where budgets are tightest. · caveat: extract may not represent the full national portal.
- **Basins in sustained decline.** Which river basins show streamflow in sustained decline against their historical median? — USGS water APIs (fed_usgs_water). *Harm:* declining basins are communities heading toward water restrictions and dry wells. · caveat: must filter parameter codes to discharge; datetime not timestamp-cast.
- **Contamination versus thresholds by basin.** For a chosen contaminant, which basins' measured distributions sit above the regulatory threshold? — USGS water APIs (fed_usgs_water). *Harm:* basins above the threshold are people drinking or swimming in it. · caveat: units differ by parameter and site and thresholds must come from outside — land a parameter-threshold reference table; unit normalization mandatory.
- **Watersheds that cross state lines.** Which subbasins span multiple states — water where no single regulator is in charge? — USGS watershed boundary dataset (FED_USGS_WBD_HUC8). *Harm:* pollution flows across the jurisdiction line; enforcement stops at it. · caveat: states field is a delimited string needing splitting.
- **Who kills land defenders, and over what.** How many land and environmental defenders are killed or attacked each year, tied to which industries, and who pulls the trigger? — Global Witness land and environmental defenders (intl_global_witness_defenders). *Harm:* land defenders murdered for opposing extraction — the count is the direct human cost. · caveat: 232 rows is far below Global Witness published totals — likely partial extract; trend shape may be distorted.
- **Indigenous defenders overrepresented.** Is the indigenous share of murdered defenders far above the indigenous share of population, region by region? — Global Witness defenders (intl_global_witness_defenders). *Harm:* indigenous communities absorb lethal violence far above their population share. · caveat: requires an external population denominator not on the platform — land a population-by-indigenous-status reference; indigenous status may be sparsely coded; partial extract.
- **Gendered patterns of attacks on defenders.** Do women defenders face different attack forms — threats and disappearances invisible in killing counts? — Global Witness defenders (intl_global_witness_defenders). *Harm:* different attack patterns hide in headline killing counts. · medium · caveat: tiny n once split three ways; gender may be largely blank.
- **Who filled the atmosphere versus who emits now.** How does cumulative historical CO2 responsibility by country compare with today's annual ranking? — OWID annual CO2 emissions (xc_owid_co2). *Harm:* countries suffering the worst climate damage contributed almost nothing to the stock. · caveat: entity column mixes countries with aggregates — filter on valid ISO codes.
- **The pledge-versus-path gap.** Which countries actually bent their emissions curve down after pledging, and which only talked? — OWID annual CO2 emissions (xc_owid_co2). *Harm:* populations of pledge-and-never-cut countries face the warming their governments promised to prevent. · caveat: the pledge side is external context not on the platform — land a pledges/targets reference table.
- **Small emitters, big exposure.** Do the countries least responsible for emissions sit in the most climate-exposed positions? — OWID annual CO2 emissions (xc_owid_co2). *Harm:* the core climate-injustice shape: least responsible, most exposed. · medium · caveat: a vulnerability measure is not on the platform — land a climate-vulnerability index source; effectively a two-source idea.
- **The warming baseline.** What does the global temperature anomaly series look like — the line every local harm story is measured against? — OWID global temperature anomaly (xc_owid_temp_anomaly). *Harm:* the single reference line for every local climate-harm story. · medium · caveat: entity mix unverified — may hold only one global series.
- **Certainty grew as warming grew.** Did the uncertainty band around global temperature narrow exactly as the warming signal grew? — OWID temperature anomaly bounds (xc_owid_temp_anomaly). *Harm:* undercuts the "too uncertain to act" delay argument used to justify decades of inaction. · caveat: band width must be derived; bounds may be null early.
- **Invaded places.** Which jurisdictions — especially islands — have the highest share of introduced species, where an ecosystem people depend on has already been replaced? — ITIS jurisdiction origin flags, native vs introduced (fed_itis_jurisdiction). *Harm:* island communities lose food, fisheries, and cultural species first when invasives take over. · caveat: the ratio is sensitive to how completely natives were catalogued — unequal effort can fake the signal.
- **Drinking-water enforcement: fifty rulebooks and a stopwatch.** For every drinking-water violation, how many days pass to the first enforcement action and how long do violations persist — ranked identically across all state primacy agencies, which regulators are statistical outliers in looking away? — EPA SDWA violations/enforcement, 15.4M rows, with the systems registry for state assignment (FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT, FED_EPA_SDWA_SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS). *Harm:* identical federal law, wildly unequal protection depending on the state you drink in — every extra month of lag is a month a community drinks water known to be out of compliance. · caveat: completeness unverified.

### energy (70)
- **Who controls generation vs who owns it.** For every utility, is the operator of its plants the same entity that owns them — who do ratepayers actually hold responsible? — EIA-860 utility schedule (FED_EIA860_1_UTILITY). *Harm:* when operator and owner differ, ratepayers can't tell who to blame for an outage or a leak. · medium · caveat: single 2024 snapshot; role-flag coding unverified.
- **Where public power survives.** Which states are still served by municipal and cooperative utilities versus investor-owned ones? — EIA-860 utility schedule (FED_EIA860_1_UTILITY). *Harm:* investor-owned utilities answer to shareholders on rate decisions that hit household bills. · medium · caveat: entity-type categories unverified; single-year snapshot.
- **Generation outside rate regulation.** How much generation sits outside traditional rate regulation, by state and sector? — EIA-860 plant schedule (FED_EIA860_2_PLANT). *Harm:* unregulated generation means no rate case where a household can contest what it is charged. · medium · caveat: status coding unverified.
- **Single-pipeline grid dependency.** Which gas pipelines single-handedly supply many power plants? — EIA-860 plant schedule (FED_EIA860_2_PLANT). *Harm:* one pipeline failure freezing a state's generation is exactly how people die in a cold snap. · caveat: pipeline names are free text — normalize before building the network; only three pipeline slots per plant, truncating multi-pipeline plants.
- **Who balances the grid, and is control consolidating.** Which balancing authorities control each region, where are the grid islands with no rescue path? — EIA-860 plant schedule plus EIA-861 balancing authority table (FED_EIA860_2_PLANT, FED_EIA_861_BALANCING_AUTHORITY). *Harm:* a region split across many operators — or an island with no interconnection — has nobody accountable when the lights go out. · medium · caveat: BA table is reference-grade (189 rows); consolidation could reflect reporting changes.
- **The retirement cliff.** How much generating capacity is scheduled to retire, when, by fuel and state — and is replacement lined up? — EIA-860 generator schedule (FED_EIA860_3_1_GENERATOR). *Harm:* retirement without replacement is the setup for the blackouts that kill people in heat waves. · caveat: planned dates are utility intentions, not commitments; 2024 snapshot only.
- **America's aging generator fleet.** Which states run on generators built in the 1960s, weighted by capacity? — EIA-860 generator schedule (FED_EIA860_3_1_GENERATOR). *Harm:* old, brittle generation fails first in extreme weather, on the people who cannot leave. · caveat: repowered units may still carry their original operating year.
- **Phantom firm capacity.** How much promised capacity evaporates exactly when it is needed — winter derates and dual-fuel switches to oil? — EIA-860 generator plus multifuel schedules (FED_EIA860_3_1_GENERATOR, FED_EIA860_3_5_MULTIFUEL). *Harm:* capacity that vanishes in a cold snap is how a grid promises power it cannot deliver when people freeze. · caveat: derates are reported, not measured; switch-capacity columns may be null for most units.
- **Turbine vendor concentration.** How few manufacturers stand behind the installed wind fleet? — EIA-860 wind schedule (FED_EIA860_3_2_WIND). *Harm:* one manufacturer's defect can ground a large share of clean capacity. · medium · caveat: manufacturer names are free text — normalize before ranking; 1,563 rows, 2024 snapshot.
- **Where and when renewables actually got built.** Which counties got the wind and solar buildout, and which regions got nothing? — EIA-860 wind and solar schedules (FED_EIA860_3_2_WIND, FED_EIA860_3_3_SOLAR). *Harm:* host counties absorb the land use while passed-over regions keep the older dirty plants. · medium · caveat: no coordinates in these schedules; county text needs a FIPS crosswalk; snapshot only holds generators still listed in 2024, so early years undercount.
- **Taller turbines in worse wind.** Did wind machines get taller as the good sites ran out — more burden per unit of power? — EIA-860 wind schedule (FED_EIA860_3_2_WIND). *Harm:* taller turbines in marginal wind mean more visual and noise burden per megawatt. · medium · caveat: height/speed casts and wind-class coding unverified.
- **First-generation wind reaching end of life.** How much early wind capacity is hitting end of life, and who pays for decommissioning? — EIA-860 wind schedule (FED_EIA860_3_2_WIND). *Harm:* decommissioning costs land on host landowners when the developer is long gone. · medium · caveat: status coding unverified; no retirement fields in this schedule.
- **Who gets net metering.** Where is rooftop/net-metered solar normal and where has it been effectively blocked? — EIA-860 solar schedule plus EIA-861 net metering (FED_EIA860_3_3_SOLAR, FED_EIA861_NET_METERING). *Harm:* in territories with near-zero installations, households are denied the one way to escape a rising bill. · caveat: per-capita rates need the customer denominator from the sales table.
- **Cheap solar hardware regions.** Which regions get the cheaper, lower-yield fixed-tilt solar hardware versus tracking systems? — EIA-860 solar schedule (FED_EIA860_3_3_SOLAR). *Harm:* cheaper fixed hardware means less generation per acre of land taken from a community. · medium · caveat: tracking flags' mutual exclusivity unverified.
- **DC overbuild by operator.** Which operators systematically overbuild solar panels relative to what they can deliver to the grid? — EIA-860 solar schedule (FED_EIA860_3_3_SOLAR). *Harm:* overbuilt, clipped DC is land and money burned that ratepayers ultimately fund. · wild · caveat: DC capacity column may be sparsely reported.
- **Who gets battery backup.** Which regions have grid-scale battery storage with a backup-power use case, and which take the blackouts? — EIA-860 storage schedule (FED_EIA860_3_4_ENERGY_STORAGE). *Harm:* regions without storage take the blackouts when the grid is stressed. · caveat: use-case flags may be multi-select with heavy blanks; no coordinates.
- **Storage for markets or for people.** Is grid storage built for arbitrage and frequency trading or for backup and peak shaving? — EIA-860 storage schedule (FED_EIA860_3_4_ENERGY_STORAGE). *Harm:* if ratepayer-funded storage trades rather than keeps lights on, the public funds an asset that never protects them. · caveat: use cases are non-exclusive; discharge rate may be null on older units.
- **Batteries propping up fossil plants.** Where do batteries directly support existing fossil units rather than renewables? — EIA-860 storage schedule (FED_EIA860_3_4_ENERGY_STORAGE). *Harm:* storage marketed as clean may be extending the life of the plant polluting the neighborhood. · wild · caveat: direct-support ID columns likely sparse; only three support slots.
- **Who really owns the grid.** How concentrated is ownership of generating capacity once joint-ownership slices are rolled up? — EIA-860 owner schedule (FED_EIA860_4_OWNER). *Harm:* concentrated hidden ownership means a handful of firms set terms in markets that look competitive. · caveat: owner names are free text with no ID — normalize names (or build an LEI crosswalk) before rollup; the same firm appears under many spellings.
- **Ownership fragmentation: nobody to blame.** Which jointly-owned generators are split across so many owners that no single responsible party exists? — EIA-860 owner schedule (FED_EIA860_4_OWNER). *Harm:* when a plant has a dozen part-owners, nobody is the responsible party a harmed neighbor can name. · medium · caveat: whether ownership shares sum to 100 is unverified.
- **Who got smart meters — and who is still invisible.** Which households got advanced meters, and which utilities wired up big customers first? — EIA-861 advanced meters (FED_EIA861_ADVANCED_METERS). *Harm:* without an advanced meter a household can't access time-of-use savings and outages go undetected longer. · caveat: territory overlaps may double count; zeros may mean no such customers.
- **Billed for smart meters customers can't use.** How big is the gap between installed smart meters and meters that actually give customers daily access to their own data? — EIA-861 advanced meters (FED_EIA861_ADVANCED_METERS). *Harm:* a customer billed for a smart meter that never shows them their usage cannot fight a wrong bill. · caveat: digital-access columns may be sparsely reported, exaggerating the gap.
- **The seven delivery-only companies.** Who do the delivery-only companies serve, and do households pay a higher per-unit delivery rate than industry? — EIA-861 delivery companies (FED_EIA861_DELIVERY_COMPANIES). *Harm:* households paying a higher delivery charge than factories are quietly cross-subsidizing them. · medium · caveat: only 7 rows — a callout, not a pattern.
- **Does demand response deliver what ratepayers pay for.** Do demand-response programs deliver the peak savings they promise? — EIA-861 demand response (FED_EIA861_DEMAND_RESPONSE). *Harm:* planners count phantom megawatts as reliability; the shortfall shows up as a rolling blackout. · caveat: potential vs actual may be defined differently by filer.
- **Who bears the curtailment.** When the grid is stressed, is it households or industry that gets curtailed? — EIA-861 demand response (FED_EIA861_DEMAND_RESPONSE). *Harm:* if households absorb the curtailment while industry is exempt, health risk lands on the people with least choice. · caveat: enrollment counts don't measure how often anyone was actually curtailed.
- **Utility-controlled water heaters.** How many home water heaters can the utility switch off remotely, and is that growing? — EIA-861 demand response (FED_EIA861_DEMAND_RESPONSE). *Harm:* a household can lose hot water on a cold morning because of a grid decision it never agreed to. · wild · caveat: field may be very sparsely reported.
- **Voltage optimization: the upgrade that stalled.** Which utilities have invested in circuit voltage optimization, and is adoption spreading or stalled? — EIA-861 distribution systems (FED_EIA861_DISTRIBUTION_SYSTEMS). *Harm:* un-optimized circuits waste energy customers pay for on every bill. · medium · caveat: genuinely thin source (five columns); zero may mean not reported.
- **Who gets access to cheaper rate designs.** Which customer classes and states get time-of-use and real-time pricing — is the cheapest rate design effectively industrial-only? — EIA-861 dynamic pricing (FED_EIA861_DYNAMIC_PRICING). *Harm:* households locked out of time-of-use rates pay peak prices they had no way to avoid. · caveat: enrollment counts lack a denominator; sparse reporting can fake exclusion.
- **Punitive peak pricing aimed at households.** Which utilities chose penalty-style critical-peak pricing over reward-style rebates for residential customers? — EIA-861 dynamic pricing (FED_EIA861_DYNAMIC_PRICING). *Harm:* critical peak pricing on a heat-wave day is a bill shock aimed at people who cannot turn off the air conditioner. · caveat: fields may be participant counts or Y/N flags; interpretation unverified.
