- **Efficiency dollars: savings or overhead.** Do ratepayer-funded efficiency programs buy real energy savings, or does the budget go mostly to administration? — EIA-861 energy efficiency (FED_EIA861_ENERGY_EFFICIENCY). *Harm:* efficiency money consumed by overhead never reaches a household's insulation or furnace. · caveat: incremental vs life-cycle columns must not be mixed; all-other-costs definition varies by filer.
- **Who got the retrofits.** Do efficiency incentive dollars — funded by every bill — flow to households or to commercial and industrial customers? — EIA-861 energy efficiency (FED_EIA861_ENERGY_EFFICIENCY). *Harm:* if households fund the surcharge but industry collects the retrofits, the transfer runs upward. · caveat: captures who received incentives, not who paid the surcharge.
- **Short-lived savings claims.** Are utilities claiming long measure lives to justify long-lived surcharges on equipment that dies in five years? — EIA-861 energy efficiency (FED_EIA861_ENERGY_EFFICIENCY). *Harm:* long-life claims justify surcharges that outlive the equipment. · wild · caveat: self-reported and possibly sparse.
- **The utilities that report almost nothing.** Which utilities file the fewest schedules or slide onto the short form, and how many people live behind that reporting blind spot? — EIA-861 frame, short form, and service territory tables (FED_EIA861_FRAME, FED_EIA861_SHORT_FORM, FED_EIA861_SERVICE_TERRITORY). *Harm:* utilities that report nothing cannot be held to account for outages, rates, or emissions by anyone. · caveat: a blank flag may mean not-required rather than declined-to-file; short-form eligibility is size-based.
- **Tiny unwatched utilities charging the most.** Which small short-form utilities charge far above the norm with no regulator watching? — EIA-861 short form (FED_EIA861_SHORT_FORM). *Harm:* customers of a tiny high-priced utility have no oversight and no way to leave. · caveat: small denominators make ratios noisy — needs a minimum customer threshold.
- **Unrecovered costs, tomorrow's rate hike.** Which utilities report unrecovered costs that will land in future rates? — EIA-861 short form flags (FED_EIA861_SHORT_FORM). *Harm:* unrecovered costs become tomorrow's rate increase for the same customers. · wild · caveat: flag columns are unlabeled form-line numbers — decode against the EIA form before publishing.
- **Local utilities swallowed by holding companies.** Where did local utilities disappear into distant holding companies, and when? — EIA-861 mergers (FED_EIA861_MERGERS). *Harm:* when the local utility becomes a line item in a distant holding company, the customer loses the nearest place to complain. · medium · caveat: only 4 rows landed — a snapshot year, not the full merger history.
- **Tariffs that quietly stopped paying rooftop solar.** Where do rooftop systems exist but export almost nothing per installed megawatt — fingerprints of tariff redesigns that turned against homeowners? — EIA-861 net metering (FED_EIA861_NET_METERING). *Harm:* a tariff that stops paying for exports strands households who invested in panels. · caveat: sell-back accounting rules changed over time and vary by state.
- **The battery pairing divide.** Which territories' solar homes have batteries (and ride out blackouts) and which go dark? — EIA-861 net metering (FED_EIA861_NET_METERING). *Harm:* a solar home without a battery still goes dark in a blackout — a split that follows income. · caveat: paired-battery columns are newer, null in earlier years.
- **Does virtual net metering reach small subscribers.** Does community-solar virtual net metering actually reach small subscribers, or only large ones? — EIA-861 net metering (FED_EIA861_NET_METERING). *Harm:* community solar sold as access for renters is worthless if only large subscribers can use it. · wild · caveat: virtual columns likely sparse outside a handful of states.
- **Private backup replacing the public grid.** Where has private backup-only generation grown large? — EIA-861 non-net-metering distributed (FED_EIA861_NON_NET_METERING_DISTRIBUTED). *Harm:* the receipt that the public grid failed — everyone who couldn't afford a generator just sat in the dark. · caveat: undercounts unregistered home generators.
- **Utility-captured distributed generation.** Where does the utility itself own the behind-the-meter assets, capturing the distributed market instead of customers? — EIA-861 non-net-metering distributed (FED_EIA861_NON_NET_METERING_DISTRIBUTED). *Harm:* customers pay for utility-owned assets in rates and keep none of the value. · caveat: utility-owned column may be null for many filers, inflating shares.
- **Line losses customers pay for.** Whose grid leaks the most power that customers are still billed for? — EIA-861 operational data (FED_EIA861_OPERATIONAL_DATA). *Harm:* line losses are recovered in rates — a leaky grid is a direct charge on every household on it. · caveat: loss accounting includes unbilled and theft in some filings.
- **Utilities earning from trading, not serving.** Which utilities make their money mostly from wholesale trading rather than retail service? — EIA-861 operational data (FED_EIA861_OPERATIONAL_DATA). *Harm:* a utility earning from trading has little reason to care about the retail customer paying its fixed costs. · caveat: revenue components may not sum to totals across filers.
- **Thin reserve margins.** Where is the margin between peak demand and available supply thinnest? — EIA-861 operational data (FED_EIA861_OPERATIONAL_DATA). *Harm:* a thin margin is the number that becomes a rolling blackout on the hottest afternoon. · caveat: peak demand and annual energy are different units; a true reserve margin needs capacity data not present here.
- **Power given away free.** Who gets free power off the system, quietly funded by paying customers? — EIA-861 operational data (FED_EIA861_OPERATIONAL_DATA). *Harm:* free power to institutions and the utility itself is funded by everyone else's bills. · wild · caveat: small, inconsistently reported categories; may be mostly street lighting.
- **Who sits in the dark longest — and is it getting worse.** Which utilities and states leave customers without power most often and longest, and where has reliability measurably worsened? — EIA-861 reliability (FED_EIA861_RELIABILITY). *Harm:* every outage minute is a real household without heat, refrigeration, or a working medical device. · caveat: state averages must be customer-weighted; year coverage of the mart unverified.
- **The major-event-day loophole.** How much outage time gets excused away by excluding "major event days" — exactly the storm hours when people died at home? — EIA-861 reliability (FED_EIA861_RELIABILITY). *Harm:* the excluded hours vanish from the headline reliability number. · caveat: MED exclusion is a legitimate IEEE standard; ranking must control for storm exposure.
- **Self-measured outage numbers.** Which utilities count their outages by hand rather than automatically? — EIA-861 reliability (FED_EIA861_RELIABILITY). *Harm:* hand-counted outage data lets a utility understate how badly it serves customers with no way to check. · caveat: flag semantics unverified; non-IEEE methods aren't comparable.
- **Households pay more than factories.** How wide is the residential-to-industrial price gap per utility, and who runs the widest ones? — EIA-861 sales to ultimate customers (FED_EIA861_SALES_ULT_CUST). *Harm:* a large gap is a transfer from families to large customers, decided in rate cases most people never see. · caveat: cost-to-serve genuinely differs by class — needs framing.
- **Did deregulation deliver cheaper power.** Do households on unbundled/choice service actually pay less than bundled customers in the same state? — EIA-861 sales to ultimate customers (FED_EIA861_SALES_ULT_CUST). *Harm:* households told supplier choice would save money can be shown whether it did. · caveat: service_type/part segmentation will double count if not filtered.
- **Price by ownership type.** Did investor-owned utility customers' prices diverge from co-op and municipal customers' over the years? — EIA-861 sales to ultimate customers (FED_EIA861_SALES_ULT_CUST). *Harm:* which kind of utility you live under can decide what you pay for the same electricity. · caveat: ownership cohorts aren't stable through mergers.
- **The energy burden map.** Where do high prices meet high forced consumption — the states where electricity costs crush low-income households hardest? — EIA-861 sales to ultimate customers (FED_EIA861_SALES_ULT_CUST). *Harm:* high consumption plus high price is where the energy burden crushes households. · caveat: customer counts are meters, not people; averages aren't tariffs.
- **Does community solar actually save subscribers money.** Do community-solar subscribers pay less per kilowatt-hour than the standard rate — or more? — EIA-861 community solar sales (FED_EIA861_SALES_ULT_CUST_CS). *Harm:* community solar marketed as savings for renters is a scam if subscribers pay more than the standard rate. · caveat: facility revenue may be allocated, not metered; rate comparison needs the main sales table.
- **Community solar wearing a corporate label.** Which "community" solar projects are dominated by commercial subscribers? — EIA-861 community solar sales (FED_EIA861_SALES_ULT_CUST_CS). *Harm:* a community program dominated by commercial subscribers took a subsidy meant for households. · caveat: customer counts may be blank for some facilities.
- **Is community solar real and scaling.** In which states does community solar actually exist, and is the model growing at all? — EIA-861 community solar sales (FED_EIA861_SALES_ULT_CUST_CS). *Harm:* a flat curve means a promised access route to clean power never opened for renters. · medium · caveat: 674 rows; a few states dominate; year coverage unknown.
- **The utility map of America.** Which counties are one-utility monopolies with literally no alternative, and which utilities sprawl across hundreds of rural counties? — EIA-861 service territory (FED_EIA861_SERVICE_TERRITORY). *Harm:* in a single-utility county a household has no alternative when service or price is bad. · caveat: county names are text without FIPS — needs a name-to-FIPS crosswalk; matching will fail on duplicates across states.
- **Quiet territory transfers.** Which counties changed utility hands across the years with no public process? — EIA-861 service territory (FED_EIA861_SERVICE_TERRITORY). *Harm:* a county handed to a new operator can see service standards change overnight. · wild · caveat: requires multiple data years in the mart — unconfirmed.
- **Vertically integrated utilities.** Which utilities control generation, transmission, distribution, and retail at once? — EIA-861 utility data (FED_EIA861_UTILITY_DATA). *Harm:* a utility that sells to itself passes the price to customers. · caveat: activity flags are self-declared Y/N.
- **Market seams and no-market regions.** Which customers live outside any RTO/ISO market — with no independent monitor watching what their utility charges? — EIA-861 utility data (FED_EIA861_UTILITY_DATA). *Harm:* non-market customers have no independent market monitor. · caveat: utilities can belong to multiple RTOs; flags overlap.
- **Reliability-regime shopping.** Which utilities straddle multiple NERC reliability regimes — and can shop between standards? — EIA-861 utility data (FED_EIA861_UTILITY_DATA). *Harm:* customers on the weaker side of a straddle pay for the weaker standard. · wild · caveat: region flags and the single region text column may contradict.
- **Pipeline incidents: where people got hurt.** Where have significant gas pipeline incidents happened since 2010, and where were people burned or killed? — PHMSA flagged pipeline incidents (FED_PHMSA_FLAGGED_INCIDENTS). *Harm:* every marked dot is a person burned or killed by a pipeline running past their town. · caveat: 2,039 rows, gas transmission + gathering only — not all pipelines.
- **Operators who keep having pipeline incidents.** Which pipeline operators rack up incident after incident, with people hurt, and no visible consequence? — PHMSA flagged pipeline incidents (FED_PHMSA_FLAGGED_INCIDENTS). *Harm:* a repeat operator with casualties and no consequence is a regulatory failure with a body count. · caveat: no penalty column here — absence of consequence must be joined from elsewhere, not asserted.
- **Operator response red flags.** Which operators kept lines running after large releases, and which report incidents slowest? — PHMSA flagged pipeline incidents (FED_PHMSA_FLAGGED_INCIDENTS). *Harm:* running a line after a big release risks the next town; late reporting delays every warning. · medium · caveat: shutdown indicator semantics unclear; timezone handling could fake lag.
- **Coal's last holdouts.** Which countries are still running (or growing) coal-heavy grids while the rest transition? — Ember yearly/monthly electricity data (intl_ember_elec). *Harm:* people downwind of coal plants in never-transitioned countries bear the health cost of the global lag. · caveat: category/variable taxonomy unverified; aggregates must be filtered from country rows.
- **Demand outrunning clean build.** In which countries is electricity demand growing faster than clean generation? — Ember electricity data (intl_ember_elec). *Harm:* populations in these countries get locked into decades more fossil combustion. · caveat: variable names for demand vs clean generation unverified.
- **Do rich-country blocs actually lead the transition.** Are the G7/OECD blocs that set climate policy actually the cleanest grids, or just the loudest? — Ember electricity data plus OWID fossil share (intl_ember_elec, xc_owid_fossil_share). *Harm:* if only wealthy countries can decarbonize, the burden lands on people who cannot afford it. · medium · caveat: wealth/region context needs a sibling OWID table; aggregate rows must be filtered.
- **Import-dependent grids.** Which populations depend on a neighbor's grid for their electricity? — Ember electricity data (intl_ember_elec). *Harm:* import-dependent populations take blackouts and price shocks decided elsewhere. · wild · caveat: import variable presence unverified.
- **Which countries cut fossil share — and which reversed.** Which countries actually reduced the fossil share of their energy over the last decade, and which went backwards? — OWID fossil fuel share (xc_owid_fossil_share). *Harm:* reversal countries are re-locking their populations into fossil dependence. · caveat: missing endpoint years silently drop countries.
- **Critical minerals the country cannot supply.** For which minerals is the US near-totally import-reliant, and from where? — USGS mineral resources (fed_usgs_minerals). *Harm:* supply shocks in high-reliance minerals hit manufacturing jobs and consumer prices. · medium · caveat: import reliance populated only on commodity-summary rows; grain must be split from site records.
- **Quiet maps lighting up — induced earthquakes.** Which historically quiet regions (Oklahoma, west Texas, Ohio) began shaking in the 2010s, against the long-run baseline of quake counts by magnitude band? — USGS Earthquake Catalog M2.5+ (fed_usgs_earthquakes). *Harm:* people in newly seismic regions live in houses never engineered for shaking and carry no earthquake insurance. · caveat: the time column may be raw text needing parsing; rising counts partly reflect better detection.

### courts-and-justice (118)
- **Impunity for defender killings.** How rarely does anyone face prosecution for killing a land or environmental defender? — Global Witness defenders notes fields (intl_global_witness_defenders). *Harm:* killings with no prosecution teach the next community that opposing a mine is free to punish. · wild · caveat: accountability lives only in free-text notes — needs text classification, which is not a stored field; partial extract.
- **Who reports crime and who absorbs it.** Which victims — by race, income, offense — never report crime to police at all, quietly absorbing it with no investigation or services? — BJS crime victimization survey extract (fed_bjs_data). *Harm:* Victims who never report get no investigation, no services, and no place in official crime counts. · caveat: only ~1,000 rows in the mart; survey weights must be applied; completeness unverified.
- **Hurt and unhelped.** What share of injured victims get no medical treatment, and how rarely do victim services actually reach anyone — broken by income, age, offense, locality? — BJS victimization survey extract (fed_bjs_data). *Harm:* Poor victims are hurt and then go untreated; a victim-services system reaching a tiny fraction is a promise on paper only. · caveat: small extract; treatment/services coding may collapse categories; completeness unverified.
- **Who armed violence finds.** Which people — by sex, age, race — end up on the receiving end of which weapon categories, and with what injury severity? — BJS victimization survey extract (fed_bjs_data). *Harm:* Shows which people are on the receiving end of armed violence. · medium · caveat: 1,000-row extract may not be representative without weights.
- **Offenses that never get solved.** Which offenses essentially never get cleared, in which states, and where has the clearance rate collapsed fastest over the modern series? — FBI crime data explorer state estimates (fed_fbi_cde). *Harm:* Victims of never-cleared offenses get no resolution at all; a growing pool of victims with no case outcome. · caveat: monthly clearance/offense ratios are approximate; reporting-agency participation shifts distort comparisons; completeness unverified.
- **Four decades of state crime trajectories.** How have state-level offense rates diverged since 1985 — which states broke from the national story, and when? — FBI crime data explorer (fed_fbi_cde). *Harm:* State divergence shows where policy choices actually changed who gets victimized. · caveat: participation changes over four decades can create artefact breaks.
- **The seasonality of violence.** How strong is the summer peak in violent offending, and is it intensifying year over year? — FBI crime data explorer (fed_fbi_cde). *Harm:* Predictable seasonal peaks are a staffing and prevention question nobody funds for. · medium · caveat: mixing offense categories washes out the pattern unless faceted.
- **Gun-check surge months.** When do firearm background checks spike by state and month since 1998 — which national events drove guns into homes fastest? — FBI background checks (fed_fbi_nics_checks). *Harm:* Surge months are when guns enter homes fastest, ahead of any policy response. · caveat: checks are not sales; no population column for true per-capita rates.
- **What's inside the gun-check totals.** How much of the headline background-check total is permit rechecks rather than actual transfers, and how has the handgun vs long-gun mix shifted per state? — FBI background checks (fed_fbi_nics_checks). *Harm:* Miscounting rechecks as sales distorts every public argument about gun availability; handgun-dominant markets carry different injury patterns. · caveat: some states report permits in bulk (artificial cliffs); multiple-gun checks muddy the mix.
- **Pawned guns as a distress signal.** Do rising prepawn vs redemption gun checks track acute household financial distress by state and time? — FBI background checks (fed_fbi_nics_checks). *Harm:* Pawning a firearm is a marker of acute household financial distress. · wild · caveat: only some states report pawn categories; zeros are non-reporting, not zero activity.
- **The voluntary minority: private-sale checks.** In how few states do private gun transfers go through the background-check system at all? — FBI background checks (fed_fbi_nics_checks). *Harm:* Untracked private transfers are the gap through which prohibited buyers get armed. · caveat: column populated only where state law requires it; zeros mean no law, not no sales.
- **Is the registry actually tracking anyone.** What share of sex-offender registrants are flagged non-compliant by county, and are the highest-risk tiers the least tracked? — Missouri sex offender registry (state_mo_sex_offender_registry). *Harm:* Counties where the registry has stopped tracking people offer the public a false sense of safety; if the top tier is least tracked, the tier system is theater. · caveat: compliance flag derived from a Y string (blanks may misread); tier vocabulary unverified; one state only.
- **The aging lifetime registry.** How much of the registry is now elderly and lifetime-listed — people in their eighties still on the list? — Missouri sex offender registry (state_mo_sex_offender_registry). *Harm:* Lifetime registration of the very old raises whether the list still protects anyone. · medium · caveat: date-of-birth is an ISO timestamp string; parse failures and placeholder dates likely.
- **Where registrants are pushed to live.** Which few addresses — boarding houses, encampments — host large clusters of registrants because housing bans exclude them from everywhere else? — Missouri sex offender registry (state_mo_sex_offender_registry). *Harm:* Housing bans concentrate people into a few addresses, harming both them and the neighborhood. · caveat: homeless and institutional placeholder addresses must be handled or the result is nonsense; ethically aggregate-only.
- **Two centuries of who judges.** How has the demographic composition of the federal bench (race, gender, birth state, era) changed — or failed to — from 1789 to today? — FJC judges plus CourtListener judge database (fed_fjc_judges, fed_courtlistener_judges). *Harm:* Litigants have faced a bench that looked nothing like them for almost the entire history of the country. · caveat: multi-appointment wide columns need unpivoting; CourtListener birth-country fields are broken numeric casts.
- **Does the ABA rating gate anything.** Do poorly ABA-rated nominees get confirmed anyway, and does the pattern differ by appointing party? — FJC judges (fed_fjc_judges). *Harm:* Poorly rated judges seated anyway decide cases affecting people for life. · caveat: ayes/nays is a combined text field requiring parsing.
- **The confirmation pipeline slowdown.** How have days from nomination to hearing to confirmation stretched over time, and where do nominations stall? — FJC judges and service records plus CourtListener positions (fed_fjc_judges, fed_fjc_service, fed_courtlistener_positions). *Harm:* Vacant benches mean litigants — including people in jail awaiting trial — wait years for a hearing. · caveat: older records have sparse hearing dates; wide appointment layout needs unpivoting.
- **The law school pipeline.** How few institutions supply the entire federal bench? — FJC judges (fed_fjc_judges). *Harm:* A bench drawn from a handful of schools brings a narrow set of life experiences to every ruling. · medium · caveat: school names are free text with historical spelling variation.
- **Seats that stay empty.** Which judicial seats have sat vacant longest between one judge's exit and the next commission? — FJC judges / service records (fed_fjc_judges, fed_fjc_service). *Harm:* Long vacancies concentrate caseloads and push defendants into longer pretrial detention. · caveat: requires the unpivoted service table; seat-id continuity across eras unverified.
- **Presidents' bench footprints.** Which presidents reshaped the courts most — judgeships filled per term, normalized by term length? — FJC judicial service (fed_fjc_service). *Harm:* One president's appointment run can set the legal environment for a generation. · caveat: recess appointments and reappointments may double-count without care.
- **Strategically timed retirements.** Do judges time senior status and retirement to presidential party turnover so their own party picks the replacement? — FJC judicial service (fed_fjc_service). *Harm:* Strategically timed retirements let a judge choose the politics of their own replacement. · caveat: fix: needs a tiny external president-party-by-date reference table before the timing read is trustworthy.
- **The revolving door before the bench.** Which firms and agencies feed the federal bench — what did judges do before appointment? — CourtListener positions (fed_courtlistener_positions). *Harm:* A bench drawn from corporate defense firms decides the cases of the people those firms fight. · caveat: organization names are free text; pre-bench positions may be incompletely recorded.
- **How judges exit.** How do judges leave the bench — retirement, elevation, resignation, and the rare disciplinary exits — over time? — CourtListener positions (fed_courtlistener_positions). *Harm:* How judges exit is the only visible accountability the judiciary has. · medium · caveat: termination-reason coding unverified and likely coarse.
- **Appointer lineage.** What do the chains of who-appointed-whom show about how durable one administration's imprint on the law is? — CourtListener positions (fed_courtlistener_positions). *Harm:* Tracing who put whom on the bench shows how durable one administration's imprint on the law is. · medium · caveat: appointer-id population unverified; only applies to appointed positions.
- **The circuit ideology lottery.** How much does judicial ideology vary within and between circuits — which appellate courts are uniform, which are split, and who are the outliers writing binding precedent? — Judicial Common Space appellate scores (xc_jcs_coa). *Harm:* Which circuit hears your case decides your rights — a lottery by geography. · caveat: only 705 rows, lifetime-score snapshot, no time axis and no case outcomes attached.
- **The court versus the country.** When has the Supreme Court's median (and each circuit's) sat far from the elected branches on one common ideology scale — the counter-majoritarian years? — Judicial Common Space institution medians (xc_jcs_medians). *Harm:* When the court sits far from the elected branches, rights get decided against the electorate's position with no way to reverse it. · caveat: 102 rows; circuit medians are 13 wide columns needing unpivoting; median columns untyped text; cross-institution comparability is the JCS premise but still an assumption.
- **The court's moving center.** How has each justice's ideology moved by term since 1937 — who held the median, which replacements shocked the court most, and who drifted over their tenure? — Judicial Common Space SCOTUS scores plus Supreme Court Database vote directions (xc_jcs_scotus, fed_scdb). *Harm:* A single replacement or a single justice's drift can flip settled rights for hundreds of millions without any election. · caveat: JCS score column untyped; seat changes must be inferred; SCDB direction codes need the codebook.
- **Bench longevity.** How long do the same individuals hold power on the federal bench — the tenure spans of a life-appointed institution? — CourtListener judges plus FJC service dates (fed_courtlistener_judges, fed_fjc_service). *Harm:* Decades-long tenure means a single person's views govern a whole region's litigants for a generation. · medium · caveat: CourtListener mart lacks appointment/retirement dates — tenure inferred from birth/death unless FJC service is used.
- **Outside income on the bench.** Which judges report outside income far beyond their peers — the long right tail of reported receipts? — CourtListener judges with follow-the-money totals (fed_courtlistener_judges). *Harm:* Judges with large outside income have financial relationships that can quietly shape rulings affecting ordinary litigants. · caveat: the received-total column is untyped and possibly sparse.
- **Judges amending their disclosures.** How often do judges have to file amended financial disclosures — the honor system correcting itself only after scrutiny? — CourtListener financial disclosures (fed_courtlistener_financial_disclosures). *Harm:* Amendments often follow journalism finding an omission — the pattern shows the honor system failing. · caveat: amendment flag coding unverified; year column is a cast.
- **The hidden share of judicial wealth.** How much of the judicial financial record is redacted, never machine-extracted, or only inferred — and are the largest holdings the ones most often hidden? — CourtListener disclosures and investments (fed_courtlistener_financial_disclosures, fed_courtlistener_investments). *Harm:* Redacted or unreadable disclosures mean litigants cannot check whether their judge has a stake in the case. · caveat: redaction/extraction flag semantics unverified; value codes are bands, not amounts; the round 500,000 investment row count looks like a load cap.
- **What judges own most.** Which companies appear most often in judicial investment disclosures — the widely-held conflicts most likely to go unnoticed? — CourtListener investments (fed_courtlistener_investments). *Harm:* Widely held stocks are the recusal conflicts most likely to go unnoticed in litigation. · caveat: description is free text needing heavy normalization; row count looks load-capped at 500k.
- **Judicial trading against the calendar.** Does judges' disclosed trading cluster around market events — or docket events? — CourtListener investments (fed_courtlistener_investments). *Harm:* A judge trading a company's stock while its case is on the docket is the conflict litigants fear. · caveat: transaction date is derived from raw text; population and precision unverified.
- **The religion field as artifact.** What did the bench's own reference data think was worth recording about judges — and what does the recorded religion field say about which biases can ever be tested? — CourtListener judges (fed_courtlistener_judges). *Harm:* What the registry records about judges shapes which biases anyone can ever test for. · wild · caveat: likely mostly null; provenance unclear; ethically sensitive framing.
- **What people sue over.** Which kinds of harm do people bring to federal court, and when did each wave of suits crest? — CourtListener dockets (fed_courtlistener_dockets). *Harm:* The mix of suits is a running record of what is being done to people and who bothers to sue. · caveat: catalog gives no mart row count while the model comment says 71.7M rows — grain and completeness unverified; nature-of-suit inconsistently populated across courts.
- **How long civil justice takes.** How many days from filing to termination does a civil case take, by district and suit type — where does a plaintiff wait years? — FJC civil case database plus CourtListener dockets (fed_fjc_idb_civil, fed_courtlistener_dockets). *Harm:* A plaintiff waiting five years for a wage or injury judgment is often bankrupt before the ruling lands. · caveat: date fields may be text; open cases must not be silently dropped; FJC's own date-use quality flags apply.
- **Dockets that go dark.** Where and when do dockets get flagged blocked or hidden from the public record, by court? — CourtListener dockets (fed_courtlistener_dockets). *Harm:* A sealed or blocked docket is a harm the public is not allowed to see. · caveat: "blocked" may mean search-engine blocking rather than sealing — semantics must be checked first.
- **Single-judge divisions and caseload imbalance.** Which judges draw a striking share of one case type — the single-judge divisions that let filers pick their outcome? — CourtListener dockets (fed_courtlistener_dockets). *Harm:* Single-judge divisions let filers pick their outcome, and the losing side is usually the individual. · caveat: assigned-judge string is free text with heavy variation; judge-id population unverified.
- **Districts falling behind.** Which federal districts terminate fewer cases than they take in, year after year — where is justice simply delayed indefinitely? — FJC civil filings/terminations, with US Courts caseload stats as corroboration (fed_fjc_idb_civil, fed_uscourts_stats). *Harm:* A district that falls further behind every year is a place where people wait years for a decision that changes their life. · caveat: the US Courts mart is a 50-row table index, not the caseload series — compute from the case database directly.
- **Argument-to-decision lag at the Supreme Court.** Which cases does the Court sit on longest between argument and decision? — Oyez Project (fed_oyez). *Harm:* Cases held longest are usually the ones where rights hang unresolved for the people who brought them. · medium · caveat: only 25 rows in the mart — a sample, unusable until re-pulled.
- **The elite Supreme Court bar.** How small is the group of advocates who argue most Supreme Court cases — the repeat players well-resourced parties can hire? — Oyez Project (fed_oyez). *Harm:* An elite repeat-player bar means well-resourced parties get better representation before the highest court. · caveat: advocate names are likely a nested list; 25-row mart is far too thin today.
- **Who wins before the Court.** Do businesses beat individuals and governments beat everyone at the Supreme Court, by party type and issue area since 1946? — Supreme Court Database (fed_scdb). *Harm:* If individuals lose systematically against government and business, the Court is not a neutral forum for ordinary people. · caveat: party codes are a large taxonomy needing collapsing; vote-grain rows must be deduped to case grain.
- **When the Court strikes down laws.** In which eras did the Court declare the most federal and state laws unconstitutional? — Supreme Court Database (fed_scdb). *Harm:* Every struck-down statute is a protection legislators built for people that the Court removed. · caveat: declaration codes distinguish types that must not be collapsed.
- **Issue areas that vanished.** Which categories of grievance did the Court stop agreeing to hear entirely? — Supreme Court Database (fed_scdb). *Harm:* An issue area the Court abandons is a class of harm with no national remedy left. · caveat: vote-grain rows need dedup first; issue codes need the codebook.
- **Precedent reversal bursts.** When did the Court rewrite settled law in clusters, and in which issue areas? — Supreme Court Database (fed_scdb). *Harm:* Clustered precedent reversals mean people planned their lives around rules that were then removed. · caveat: precedent-alteration is coder-declared and undercounts silent overrulings.
- **The real blocs.** Which justices actually vote together in split decisions, per natural court — the stable coalitions behind the outcomes? — Supreme Court Database (fed_scdb). *Harm:* Stable blocs mean outcomes on rights cases are determined by composition, not argument. · medium · caveat: pairwise agreement across 83k vote rows; natural-court boundaries must be respected.
- **Pro se appeals almost never win.** How close to zero is the success rate of appeals filed without a lawyer, by circuit? — FJC appellate case database (fed_fjc_idb_appellate). *Harm:* Prisoners and poor litigants appealing without a lawyer lose almost automatically, whatever the merits. · caveat: outcome/disposition are numeric codes; pro se flags need codebook mapping.
- **Poverty ends the appeal early.** Are fee-waived appeals disposed of procedurally far more often than paid ones — does poverty end the case before its merits? — FJC appellate case database (fed_fjc_idb_appellate). *Harm:* If fee-waived appeals die procedurally, poverty ends the case before the merits are ever heard. · caveat: fee-status codes unverified; procedural terminations may reflect a genuinely different case mix.
- **Deciding invisibly: unpublished opinions.** Which appeals courts decide the largest share of cases in unpublished opinions that create no precedent? — FJC appellate case database (fed_fjc_idb_appellate). *Harm:* An unpublished decision creates no precedent, so the same wrong is done to the next person. · caveat: publication-status coding unverified; judgment date may be text.
- **How long an appeal takes.** How many days from docket to judgment, by circuit and appeal type — where does an appeal take years? — FJC appellate case database (fed_fjc_idb_appellate). *Harm:* A detained or terminated person waiting years on appeal serves the harm before the ruling arrives. · caveat: date fields may be text; en banc and consolidated cases distort the tail.
- **Panel draw and reversal.** Which three-judge panel combinations overturn lower courts and which rubber-stamp them? — FJC appellate judge codes (fed_fjc_idb_appellate). *Harm:* Panel draw decides whether a wrongful conviction or denied benefit gets corrected. · wild · caveat: fix: judge codes are FJC-internal/anonymized and may be blank in public files — run a code-population check first, and naming needs a crosswalk that may not exist; three-judge combinations produce very sparse cells.
- **The government's home-court advantage.** Does the United States win far more often as appellant than as appellee, by agency and suit type? — FJC appellate case database (fed_fjc_idb_appellate). *Harm:* If the government wins far more often as appellant than as appellee, the playing field is not level. · caveat: agency codes need a lookup; unbalanced case mixes could explain the gap.
- **No lawyer, no chance: civil court.** Do pro se and fee-waived civil plaintiffs lose identical claims that represented plaintiffs win — dismissed on procedure, not merits? — FJC civil case database, CourtListener dockets for enrichment (fed_fjc_idb_civil). *Harm:* People who cannot afford a lawyer lose civil cases they would otherwise win, on identical claims. · caveat: pro se / in forma pauperis are coded values needing the FJC codebook; amount-received may be zero-filled rather than null.
- **Pennies on the dollar.** Which claim types systematically settle or judge out at a small fraction of the amount demanded? — FJC civil case database (fed_fjc_idb_civil). *Harm:* Injury and civil-rights plaintiffs who recover a fraction of their claim absorb the cost of the harm themselves. · caveat: amounts are stored in coded thousand-dollar buckets with sentinel values — needs the codebook; unpopulated for most cases.
- **Are civil-rights suits dying.** Where have civil-rights filings collapsed, and what share of those still filed are terminated before any judgment on the merits? — FJC civil case database (fed_fjc_idb_civil). *Harm:* A circuit where civil-rights filings collapsed is usually one where people learned they would lose; if plaintiffs never reach a jury, the courthouse door is closed in practice. · caveat: nature-of-suit codes must be mapped to the civil-rights family; per-capita needs external population.
- **Judge disposition fingerprints.** Which trial judges dismiss far more of the same case type than their bench colleagues in the same district? — FJC civil judge codes (fed_fjc_idb_civil). *Harm:* Drawing a dismissal-prone judge means an identical claim dies before it is ever heard. · wild · caveat: fix: filing/terminating judge are FJC-internal codes that may be masked or blank in public releases — check population before building; case mix varies even within a district.
- **The vanishing trial.** How close to zero has the share of civil cases reaching trial fallen, by decade and district? — FJC civil case database (fed_fjc_idb_civil). *Harm:* A system where nothing goes to trial resolves harm in private settlements nobody can audit. · caveat: trial date fields may be sparsely populated.
- **Class actions stripped.** How many cases filed as class actions are no longer class actions by termination — decertification removing the only tool small victims have? — FJC civil case database (fed_fjc_idb_civil). *Harm:* Decertification strips the only mechanism that lets many small victims sue at all. · caveat: the class-action flags may not mean formal certification.
- **Pro se bankruptcy: filing without relief.** Do people who file bankruptcy without a lawyer actually get their debts discharged, compared with represented filers, by chapter? — FJC bankruptcy case database (fed_fjc_idb_bankruptcy). *Harm:* People too poor to hire a bankruptcy lawyer are the ones who fail to get the debt relief they filed for — walking out still owing everything. · caveat: disposition codes need mapping; original-vs-current pro se flag variants must be chosen carefully; snapshot years must be deduped.
- **The Chapter 13 trap.** In which districts are debtors steered into Chapter 13 rather than Chapter 7, and how many Chapter 13 filers end up dismissed or converted with years of payments and nothing discharged? — FJC bankruptcy database, US Courts chapter tables as corroboration (fed_fjc_idb_bankruptcy, fed_uscourts_stats). *Harm:* A dismissed Chapter 13 means years of payments made and no debt discharged; being steered into it by local practice rather than finances is real harm. · caveat: chapter codes numeric; snapshot dedup required; district geography needs a crosswalk; US Courts mart is a 50-row index.
- **How much relief bankruptcy delivers.** How much debt actually gets discharged versus survives bankruptcy — the student loans, taxes, and support people still owe after losing everything? — FJC bankruptcy case database (fed_fjc_idb_bankruptcy). *Harm:* Non-dischargeable debt is what people still owe after losing everything; cases far below full relief are people who went through bankruptcy and came out still buried. · caveat: financial fields may be coded buckets or largely null; reporting inconsistent across chapters.
- **Bankruptcy geography.** Which ZIP codes and neighborhoods produce the most bankruptcy filings per capita — where household finance collapses most often? — FJC bankruptcy case database (fed_fjc_idb_bankruptcy). *Harm:* Concentrated bankruptcy ZIPs are the neighborhoods where medical bills and predatory lending land hardest. · caveat: debtor ZIP may be truncated to 3 digits for privacy; per-capita needs external population.
- **How deep the hole at filing.** How negative is the monthly income-minus-expenses margin when households finally file — how long were they insolvent before the court saw them? — FJC bankruptcy case database (fed_fjc_idb_bankruptcy). *Harm:* The gap between what people earn and owe each month is the mechanism that produces bankruptcy. · medium · caveat: means-test fields exist only for post-2005 filings — null on most of the historical file.
- **Filings through the law change and the crash.** How did the 2005 bankruptcy law and the 2008 crash redirect millions of households between chapters of relief? — FJC bankruptcy case database (fed_fjc_idb_bankruptcy). *Harm:* Legal changes redirected millions of households into harsher forms of relief. · medium · caveat: coverage window not verified from metadata.
- **The debt treadmill.** How often do the same households file bankruptcy again — proof the first filing fixed nothing? — FJC bankruptcy prior-filing flag (fed_fjc_idb_bankruptcy). *Harm:* A second or third filing means the first one did not fix anything for that household. · caveat: the prior-filing flag is self-reported at filing.
- **Small businesses that never reorganize.** How often do small-business Chapter 11 cases convert to liquidation instead of surviving? — FJC bankruptcy case database (fed_fjc_idb_bankruptcy). *Harm:* When a small business converts to liquidation, its workers and local suppliers lose too. · medium · caveat: small-business flag definition changed with statute over time.
- **Sentence by geography.** How much longer or shorter is the sentence for the same federal offense depending on the district where charges were filed? — FJC criminal case database (fed_fjc_idb_criminal). *Harm:* Two people with the same offense serve years more or less based purely on geography. · caveat: prison-total uses coded sentinel values (life, probation-only) that must be handled separately; offense codes need the codebook.
- **The trial penalty.** How much longer do defendants who insisted on a trial serve than those who pleaded to the same offense? — FJC criminal case database (fed_fjc_idb_criminal). *Harm:* Defendants who exercise their jury right serve dramatically longer — which is how the system buys guilty pleas. · caveat: disposition codes must be mapped plea-vs-trial; count-column semantics need the codebook.
- **Guilt negotiated, not proven.** How close to total is the federal plea rate, by offense category and decade — how rare is a trial? — FJC criminal case database (fed_fjc_idb_criminal). *Harm:* A plea rate near total means guilt is negotiated, not proven — and innocent defendants take deals. · caveat: disposition codes require the codebook.
- **Fines on top of prison.** How large are the financial penalties stacked on defendants who are also serving prison time? — FJC criminal case database (fed_fjc_idb_criminal). *Harm:* A large fine on top of prison follows a person for life and blocks reentry, housing, and employment. · caveat: fine total may be coded in buckets; severity codes need mapping.
- **Who buys their way out.** Which offense classes end in fines while others end in years of prison — the two-tier system in one comparison? — FJC criminal case database (fed_fjc_idb_criminal). *Harm:* White-collar offenses paying fines while drug offenses serve years is the two-tier system in one chart. · caveat: fine amounts likely zero for most defendants; log scaling needed.
- **Warrants that never close.** How long do fugitive spans stay open, and for which offenses — years-open warrants for minor charges? — FJC criminal case database (fed_fjc_idb_criminal). *Harm:* Long-open warrants for minor offenses trap people out of jobs and housing for years without any trial. · medium · caveat: fugitive dates sparsely populated; date fields may be text.
- **Charge stacking and the bargain-down.** How do charges filed compare with charges of conviction — does stacking five counts at filing produce the plea, and what gets bargained away? — FJC criminal filing/terminating offense codes (fed_fjc_idb_criminal). *Harm:* Stacked charges are the lever prosecutors use to make a plea the only rational choice — this makes the leverage visible. · caveat: repeated offense blocks may be sparsely used; correlation is suggestive, not causal; multi-count cases complicate the flow.
- **Counsel type and sentence.** Do defendants with appointed counsel get longer sentences than those with retained counsel for matched offenses? — FJC criminal case database (fed_fjc_idb_criminal). *Harm:* If appointed counsel correlates with longer sentences for the same offense, poverty adds years. · caveat: counsel codes unverified; offense-severity matching is imperfect.
- **Time from charge to sentence.** How long do defendants wait between charge and sentence, by district — the pretrial period served before any conviction? — FJC criminal case database (fed_fjc_idb_criminal). *Harm:* Long pretrial periods mean detention without conviction for defendants who cannot make bail. · medium · caveat: pretrial detention status is not in the model; fugitive status is only a weak proxy.
- **The second sentence: supervision.** How many months of supervised release and probation get added on top of prison, by offense? — FJC criminal case database (fed_fjc_idb_criminal). *Harm:* Years of supervision after release is a second sentence that quietly returns people to prison on technicalities. · medium · caveat: supervised-release units may be months or a coded value.
- **Mass harm's few courtrooms.** Which mass injuries currently hold the most plaintiffs in multidistrict litigation, and in which small set of districts does national product litigation land? — JPML pending MDLs plus CourtListener/FJC MDL fields (fed_jpml_pending_mdls, fed_courtlistener_dockets, fed_fjc_idb_civil). *Harm:* Each pending action is a person injured by the same product waiting on one consolidated ruling; a few courthouses' local norms govern nationwide compensation. · caveat: JPML mart is a 162-row snapshot with no time axis; closed mega-MDLs are missing; MDL docket formats may differ across systems.
- **The MDL judges.** How few individual judges control mass-tort outcomes for millions of injured people? — JPML pending MDLs (fed_jpml_pending_mdls). *Harm:* One judge's rulings on evidence or settlement decide compensation for hundreds of thousands of injured people. · caveat: judge names are free text; only pending MDLs in scope.
- **Stuck mass torts.** Which MDLs have resolved most of their claims and which are stuck — thousands still waiting? — JPML pending MDLs (fed_jpml_pending_mdls). *Harm:* An MDL with high total and low resolution is thousands of injured people still waiting. · medium · caveat: pending-vs-total definitions may differ across MDL types; single snapshot.
- **Federal prisons in fifty rows.** What does the federal prison system publish about itself — population, staffing ratios, facility mix — and which of its own metrics have been frozen for years? — BOP inmate statistics (fed_bop_statistics). *Harm:* Population-to-staff ratios are the mechanism behind lockdowns, missed medical care, and violence inside; frozen published metrics mean conditions are not actually being measured. · medium · caveat: only 50 summary rows — no facility-level detail; may be a single snapshot with no time axis.
- **Europe's rights violators, right by right.** Which states does the European Court of Human Rights find in violation most, of which Convention articles, and when did the docket surge against whom? — ECHR case-law database (intl_hudoc). *Harm:* Each violation judgment is a person whose government was formally found to have abused them; Article 3 and 5 clusters are torture and unlawful detention findings against named states. · caveat: 2,000-row mart is likely a capped page pull with recency bias; articles/violation are packed multi-value strings.
- **Attention rationing at the ECHR.** Does the Court's importance-level flag predict outcome — attention reserved for cases it plans to uphold? — ECHR case-law database (intl_hudoc). *Harm:* Low-importance-flagged cases are real people whose claims get less judicial attention. · medium · caveat: importance is a Court-assigned code; 2,000-row sample.
- **Police killings: where, and by which departments.** Where do police killings cluster nationally, and which agencies kill repeatedly, year after year, with what share of victims unarmed? — Mapping Police Violence (xc_mapping_police_violence). *Harm:* Every point is a named person killed; departments that kill year after year with the same profile are institutions, not accidents. · caveat: county column is a broken numeric cast; agency names are free text — the ORI identifier is the real join key and its population is unverified.
- **Charges almost never filed.** Across a decade of police killings, how flat is the line of officers criminally charged? — Mapping Police Violence (xc_mapping_police_violence). *Harm:* A decade of killings with almost no charges is the accountability gap stated numerically. · caveat: charges field is free text needing classification; dispositions lag by years for recent cases.
- **Which neighborhoods absorb lethal force.** Do police killings concentrate in poorer, Blacker census tracts at rates the national average hides? — Mapping Police Violence with ACS tract fields (xc_mapping_police_violence). *Harm:* Poor and Black neighborhoods absorb police killings at rates the national average hides completely. · caveat: tract demographics are a fixed 2019 ACS snapshot applied to all years; income field untyped.
- **Does the prosecutor decide accountability.** Does whether an officer faces charges depend on the elected prosecutor's party and identity rather than on what happened? — Mapping Police Violence prosecutor fields (xc_mapping_police_violence). *Harm:* Whether an officer faces charges may depend on the elected prosecutor rather than on what happened. · caveat: prosecutor fields are volunteer-coded and likely sparse; small cells will be noisy.
- **Do body cameras change anything.** Does the presence of body-camera footage change official dispositions or charging outcomes at all? — Mapping Police Violence (xc_mapping_police_violence). *Harm:* If footage does not change outcomes, the cameras funded as a reform are doing nothing for victims' families. · caveat: body-camera field is sourced from WaPo shootings only, biasing coverage.
- **Officers who kill again.** How many named officers appear in more than one killing — kept armed after a prior one? — Mapping Police Violence officer names (xc_mapping_police_violence). *Harm:* An officer allowed to remain armed after a prior killing is a foreseeable risk to the next person. · wild · caveat: fix: officer names are free text and frequently withheld — needs careful same-person resolution before any claim, and extreme care on misidentification; field likely mostly blank.
- **Two justice systems in one county.** In which counties is the Black jail incarceration rate a multiple of the white rate — and how extreme does the ratio get? — Vera incarceration trends (xc_vera_incarceration_trends). *Harm:* A county where Black residents are jailed at ten times the white rate is running two different justice systems. · caveat: rate fields null for many county-years; small-population counties produce unstable ratios.
- **The rural jail boom.** Why did jail populations rise in rural counties while urban rates fell? — Vera incarceration trends (xc_vera_incarceration_trends). *Harm:* Rural jail growth means people locked up far from family, lawyers, and services. · caveat: urbanicity is a fixed classification applied across all years; jail reporting coverage varies by year.
- **Beds for rent.** Which local jails hold significant populations for ICE, the Marshals, and BOP — running as federal detention for revenue? — Vera federal-hold columns (xc_vera_incarceration_trends). *Harm:* Counties paid per federal detainee have a cash incentive to keep beds full of immigrants and pretrial defendants. · caveat: federal-hold columns may be null for most counties and years; contracted-in definitions vary.
- **Jails above rated capacity.** Which jails hold more people than they are rated for, year after year? — Vera incarceration trends (xc_vera_incarceration_trends). *Harm:* Overcrowded jails are where deaths, assaults, and denied medical care happen. · caveat: rated capacity is sparsely reported; capacity definitions differ by state.
- **Jailed without conviction.** What share of each state's jail population is held pretrial — locked up unconvicted, mostly for inability to pay bail? — Vera incarceration trends (xc_vera_incarceration_trends). *Harm:* Pretrial detention is people who have not been convicted losing jobs and housing because they cannot pay bail. · caveat: pretrial columns have significant missingness across counties and years.
- **The fastest-growing jail population: women.** How fast are female jail and prison rates growing, and where? — Vera incarceration trends (xc_vera_incarceration_trends). *Harm:* Incarcerating mothers at rising rates puts children into foster care as a second-order harm. · caveat: female prison coverage varies; prison data is state-attributed to counties by Vera's method.
- **Churn counties.** Which counties cycle thousands through short jail holds rather than holding few people long — destroying jobs without convictions? — Vera admissions columns (xc_vera_incarceration_trends). *Harm:* High-churn counties arrest huge numbers for short holds, which destroys jobs without any conviction. · wild · caveat: admissions reporting is the weakest column family in Vera's file; many counties never report it.
- **Countries that halved their killings.** Which countries genuinely reduced homicide rates — proof that lethal violence is a policy outcome, not fate — and how far apart do world regions sit? — OWID homicide rates (xc_owid_homicide). *Harm:* Whole regions live with an order-of-magnitude higher chance of being killed; large declines prove it is changeable. · caveat: coverage patchy — gaps are missing data, not zero homicide; differing first/last years make comparisons uneven.
- **Gun dealer density and where guns enter the market.** Where do federal firearms licensees concentrate relative to population, and which states host the manufacturers and importers where guns enter circulation? — ATF Federal Firearms Licensees, 77,514 licensees (fed_atf_ffl). *Harm:* dealer density is one of the strongest correlates of local gun-trace volume — it maps onto who gets shot. · caveat: current snapshot only, no time axis; per-capita reads need an external population denominator; license-type codes need the ATF codebook.
- **Kitchen-table gun dealers.** How many licensees operate from residential premises — the segment hardest for ATF to inspect and a known diversion channel? — ATF FFL premise vs mail address comparison (fed_atf_ffl). *Harm:* residential dealers are the hardest to inspect and a known diversion channel. · caveat: address-text detection is heuristic and premise/mail matching does not prove residency — validate the residential heuristic against a labeled sample before trusting.
- **Operators holding many gun licenses.** Which operators hold multiple FFLs across districts, letting inventory move between entities in ways a single-license inspection never sees? — ATF FFL license/business name grouping (fed_atf_ffl). *Harm:* multi-license operators can move inventory between entities invisibly. · wild · caveat: name matching on a snapshot merges distinct people with common names — entity-resolve names before claiming one operator holds many licenses.
- **The WRA record of who was taken.** Who was incarcerated in the WWII relocation camps — from which counties, at what ages, with what citizenship — and were families split across camps? — NARA WRA records, Japanese American relocation (fed_nara_wra_aad). *Harm:* most people imprisoned as security risks were US citizens, children, and the elderly — the record proves the targeting. · caveat: only 38 rows landed against a series of over a hundred thousand people — a probe load; needs a full reland before any claim.
- **Where police kill, and whether a camera was on.** Where do fatal police shootings happen, and has body-camera presence actually risen since 2015 — or stalled far below full coverage? — Washington Post Fatal Force (xc_wapo_fatal_force). *Harm:* without footage, the only account of a killing is the officer's. · caveat: covers shootings only, excludes other in-custody deaths; the field records camera presence, not whether footage was released or retained; coordinates often block-level.
- **Killed younger, by race.** Are some racial groups killed by police markedly younger — more years of life lost, concentrated in specific communities? — WaPo Fatal Force age/race fields (xc_wapo_fatal_force). *Harm:* being killed younger means more years of life lost, concentrated in specific communities. · caveat: race is partly imputed — the race_source field must be shown alongside.
- **Unarmed and fleeing.** How many people were unarmed and fleeing when police killed them — the clearest avoidable deaths? — WaPo Fatal Force armed-with x flee status x threat type (xc_wapo_fatal_force). *Harm:* unarmed people shot while running away are the clearest case of avoidable death. · caveat: armed-with and threat-type are department-reported and may be self-serving.
- **Crisis calls that end in death.** In which states is a rising share of fatal police shootings mental-illness-related — crisis response left to armed police? — WaPo Fatal Force mental-illness flag by state over time (xc_wapo_fatal_force). *Harm:* people in psychiatric crisis are dying because the responder sent was armed. · caveat: the flag depends on after-the-fact reporting and is likely undercounted.
- **Justice depends on the district.** Run identical metrics — time to disposition, dismissal rates, judgment patterns — across all 94 federal district courts and rank the outlier districts and case types. — FJC Integrated Database, civil 10.9M cases, plus criminal 6.3M, bankruptcy 7M, appellate 1M (fed_fjc_idb_civil et al.). *Harm:* litigants whose odds and wait times are set by geography, not merits. · caveat: completeness unverified.
- **Census of the federal bench.** Who sits on the bench — age, gender, religion, birthplace — how has that mix shifted era by era, and who is still deciding cases into their 80s and 90s under life tenure? — CourtListener judge biographies, 16,191 people (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_JUDGES). *Harm:* an unrepresentative, aging bench with no fitness check decides the rights of people it does not resemble. · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; completeness vs publisher unverified.
- **What judges did before the robe.** What careers feed the bench — prosecutors, public defenders, corporate law firms, academia, government — and how has the mix changed over time and by court? — CourtListener judicial positions: position type, sector, pre-bench jobs (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_POSITIONS). *Harm:* a bench drawn overwhelmingly from prosecution and corporate practice tilts the courtroom before a case is even heard. · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; completeness of pre-bench position records unverified.
- **Disclosure filing compliance.** Which judges have missing disclosure years, chronic amendments, or failed extractions — filing gaps and amendment spikes as a compliance signal? — CourtListener annual financial disclosure filings, 66,287 rows (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_FINANCIAL_DISCLOSURES). *Harm:* disclosure is the only public window into judicial conflicts; a judge who files late, amends after press attention, or skips years closes that window. · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; one duplicate ID deduped at mart build; many filings are OCR-extracted with varying quality.
- **What the judiciary owns.** What assets do federal judges hold — most common holdings, individual stocks vs funds, transaction churn, value bands — across 1.9M reported investment line items? — CourtListener disclosure investments (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_INVESTMENTS). *Harm:* heavy individual-stock ownership on the bench is the raw fuel of recusal violations — litigants can face a judge with a personal stake. · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; header row count was wrong (500K) until re-verified at 1.9M; values are letter-coded ranges, not dollars; some line items OCR-inferred.
- **Gifts to judges.** Who gives gifts to federal judges, what are they worth — and is the striking smallness of the table (2,025 rows across the whole judiciary) itself the under-reporting story? — CourtListener disclosed gifts (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_DISCLOSURE_GIFTS). *Harm:* undisclosed largesse to judges — the Thomas/Crow pattern — erodes the promise that both sides stand equal in court. · medium · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; absence of gifts cannot be read as absence of giving — reporting rules exempt "personal hospitality".
- **Who pays for judges' travel.** Which organizations reimburse judges for trips — who pays, to where, for what stated purpose — and which sponsors host the most judges? — CourtListener disclosed reimbursements, 33,472 rows (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_DISCLOSURE_REIMBURSEMENTS). *Harm:* privately funded judicial junkets are a documented influence channel — the seminar circuit shapes how judges see the issues they rule on. · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; sponsor names free text; completeness vs publisher unverified.
- **Judges in debt.** Which judges report personal debts, to which creditors, in what value bands — and are bench-wide creditor concentrations visible? — CourtListener disclosed liabilities, 18,775 rows (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_DISCLOSURE_DEBTS). *Harm:* a judge indebted to an institution that litigates in federal court has a conflict of obligation, not stake. · medium · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; creditor names free text; value bands only.
- **Judicial moonlighting.** What outside income (teaching, books, speeches) and outside positions (boards, trusteeships) do sitting judges hold, from which institutions, and how much? — CourtListener outside income (15,302 rows with dollar amounts) and outside positions (37,050 rows) (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_DISCLOSURE_NON_INVESTMENT_INCOME, JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_DISCLOSURE_POSITIONS). *Harm:* an institution paying a sitting judge a salary-sized side income holds quiet leverage no litigant can see. · medium · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; spousal income table is source-type only and heavily redacted.
- **How long federal justice takes.** Case volume and duration (filing to termination) by court, year, and nature of suit across 71.7M dockets — where is the backlog worst, which case types stall, and how concentrated is multidistrict litigation? — CourtListener federal dockets (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_DOCKETS). *Harm:* justice delayed is the most universal courtroom harm — plaintiffs die, businesses fold, defendants sit in limbo while dockets age. · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; docket coverage is scraped/PACER-derived and uneven across courts and eras; date population per court must be checked before duration claims.
- **Who actually wins in federal civil court.** Dispositions, judgment amounts, demanded-vs-received money, class-action outcomes, and the pro se penalty across 10.3M linked federal civil cases — by suit type, district, and county. — FJC civil-case outcomes linked to CourtListener dockets (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_FJC_IDB_CL_LINKED). *Harm:* the single richest who-gets-hurt table in the family — who wins, who loses, and how much less you get without a lawyer. · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; FJC judgment amounts are known-noisy (sentinel/rounded values) — profile amount_received before ranking on it.
- **The appeal waiting room.** How long does an appeal actually take — lower-court judgment to notice of appeal to receipt at the appeals court — by originating court and over time? — CourtListener originating-court records for appealed cases, 973,419 rows (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_ORIGINATING_COURT_INFO). *Harm:* appellate delay means wrongly decided cases stay wrong for years — for prisoners and deportees, the delay is the punishment. · medium · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; date-field population unverified.
- **The shape of published law.** Decision output over time, the precedential vs unpublished split by court and era, and which decisions are most cited — is more and more law being made in opinions that cannot be cited? — CourtListener opinion clusters, 10.1M decisions (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_OPINION_CLUSTERS). *Harm:* the growth of unpublished decisions means ordinary litigants — disproportionately pro se and immigration appellants — get rulings that bind them but constrain no one else. · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; citation_count is publisher-computed and the citation-network load retry is still pending.
- **The Supreme Court's direction.** For the Supreme Court subset carrying political-science coding, how has decision direction (liberal/conservative) and vote closeness moved across decades? — CourtListener opinion clusters, SCDB fields (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_OPINION_CLUSTERS). *Harm:* the Court's drift decides abortion, voting, unions, environment — the most concentrated policy lever in the dataset. · medium · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; SCDB fields populated only for the SCOTUS subset, population rate unverified.

### immigration (32)
- **Border encounters month by month.** How do nationwide border encounter totals move month to month across the fiscal year? — CBP nationwide encounters (fed_cbp_encounters). *Harm:* Encounter spikes are the months detention capacity is most overwhelmed and people are held worst. · medium · caveat: only 9 rows — a single published summary table, not record-level data.
- **Nationality mix of enforcement.** How does the nationality composition of border enforcement shift with policy changes — is enforcement following migration or targeting nationalities? — DHS statistics office enforcement tables (fed_dhs_ohss). *Harm:* Sharp shifts in which nationalities get enforced against reveal policy targeting rather than changing migration. · caveat: country columns are wide and populated only on some sheets; multi-sheet compilation means mixed grain in one table.
- **Border versus interior enforcement.** When did enforcement move away from the border line and into neighborhoods, workplaces, and courthouses? — DHS enforcement tables (fed_dhs_ohss). *Harm:* Interior enforcement hits settled families rather than new arrivals. · caveat: border/interior columns may populate on only a subset of sheets; encounter-type taxonomy unverified.
- **Families in the enforcement machine.** Which enforcement actions fall most on family units versus single adults, month by month? — DHS enforcement tables (fed_dhs_ohss). *Harm:* Family-unit enforcement means children inside the detention and removal process. · caveat: family-status field may be null on most sheets; overlapping count columns may be differently defined.
- **The criminality label under the numbers.** How often does the public "criminal alien" framing match the data — what share of encounters carry any criminality tag, by sector? — DHS enforcement tables (fed_dhs_ohss). *Harm:* Labelling people with no criminal history as criminal enforcement justifies harsher treatment for everyone in the pipeline. · caveat: criminality categories are agency-defined and may collapse immigration violations into "criminal"; sheet coverage uneven.
- **Front door narrowing, back door widening.** How do lawful permanent resident admissions compare to removals year over year — when do removals outpace admissions? — DHS yearbook of immigration statistics (fed_dhs_yearbook). *Harm:* Every year removals outpace admissions is a year more families are split than joined. · caveat: only 27 rows in the mart — almost certainly a table index, not the full yearbook series.
- **Visa classes quietly throttled.** Which visa classes have quietly become much harder to win, by admission count and year-over-year change? — DHS yearbook (fed_dhs_yearbook). *Harm:* A throttled visa class means specific families waiting years longer to reunite. · medium · caveat: 27-row mart; country fields are broken numeric casts on name columns.
- **Denial rates by law firm.** Which high-volume immigration law firms have the worst client outcomes — big case volume, high denial rates? — foreign labor certification disclosures (fed_dol_oflc). *Harm:* Workers who paid a high-volume firm and got denied lose their status and their money at once. · caveat: law-firm names are free text with heavy variation; case-status value set unverified.
- **What floods the immigration-court docket.** How has the composition of the immigration-court docket shifted with each administration — which case types flood in when? — EOIR immigration court cases (fed_eoir_case_data). *Harm:* A docket flooded with one case type means judges spend minutes per person on life-or-death claims. · caveat: immigration court table is a husk: 12.6M rows, one real column — blocked until the mart is widened/reloaded.
- **The asylum judge lottery.** How wildly do asylum grant rates vary between judges sitting in the same court? — EOIR immigration court cases (fed_eoir_case_data). *Harm:* Two people with identical claims get opposite outcomes based purely on the judge assigned. · caveat: judge/decision/court columns not exposed in the husk table — blocked until reloaded; a classic, proven finding elsewhere.
- **Which local jails feed deportation.** Which detention facilities and local jails generate the most ICE detainers, and in which regions? — ICE detainers (fed_ice_detainers). *Harm:* A county jail issuing thousands of detainers is a local government choosing to act as an immigration arm. · caveat: facility geography is city/state text only — mapping needs geocoding; 609k person-level rows; completeness unverified.
- **Enforcement without a conviction.** What share of ICE detainers and arrests hit people with no criminal conviction at all — the sharpest test of the "worst first" claim? — ICE detainers plus ICE enforcement statistics (fed_ice_detainers, fed_ice_statistics). *Harm:* People arrested with no criminal record are detained purely for immigration status while being publicly framed as criminals. · caveat: blank charge fields must be shown as their own category, never dropped; the statistics mart is only 221 aggregate rows.
- **The threat label versus the sentence.** Does ICE's assigned threat level actually track what a court imposed as a sentence, or is it discretion dressed as fact? — ICE detainers (fed_ice_detainers). *Harm:* If the threat label does not track the sentence, the label is a discretionary judgment dressed as a fact. · caveat: three separate sentence-unit columns must be reconciled; sentence may be blank on most rows.
- **Who gets detained: nationality and generation.** Which nationalities and birth cohorts does the detainer system concentrate on, and does that match any plausible baseline? — ICE detainers (fed_ice_detainers). *Harm:* Disproportionate targeting by nationality is discrimination the aggregate numbers can prove. · caveat: no population denominator by nationality in the table — disproportionality claims need an outside baseline.
- **Detainers lifted — including against citizens.** How often are detainers withdrawn and on what grounds — including the count lifted because the person turned out to be a US citizen? — ICE detainers (fed_ice_detainers). *Harm:* A detainer lifted for citizenship means the agency held a US citizen — the count of those is the story. · caveat: lift reason likely blank on most rows; the code vocabulary is undocumented in the model.
- **From jails into neighborhoods.** How has the mix of apprehension methods — jail transfers, at-large arrests, border encounters — shifted as policy changed? — ICE detainers (fed_ice_detainers). *Harm:* When at-large arrests rise, enforcement moves from jails into neighborhoods and schools. · caveat: method vocabulary changes across administrations; the same label may not mean the same thing across years.
- **The detention map.** Where is every immigration detention facility, of what type, run by whom — and how much of the network is contracted county jails rather than federal sites? — ICE detention facility codes and facility list (fed_ice_detention_facility_codes, fed_ice_detention_facility_list). *Harm:* People held in contracted county jails fall outside federal detention standards and oversight; regions dominated by private beds have a financial incentive to keep people detained. · caveat: type taxonomy meanings unverified; no capacity or population figures in either table; the list has one published duplicate name+city pair.
- **Detention far from lawyers.** Which detention facilities sit deliberately remote from any metropolitan area or immigration court, cutting detainees off from counsel and family? — ICE facility coordinates and list (fed_ice_detention_facility_codes, fed_ice_detention_facility_list). *Harm:* Remote detention placement is how people lose access to counsel and lose their cases. · caveat: fix: needs an external city/metro/court location reference to compute distances — a small static crosswalk makes it trustworthy; coordinates may be missing for some facilities.
- **How long people are held, by facility.** How does detention stay length vary by facility — where do stays run months longer than the system average? — ICE detention stints (fed_ice_detention_stints). *Harm:* Months of extra detention at one facility is months of a person's life taken by an operational choice. · caveat: two book-in/book-out pairs exist at stay and stint level — picking the wrong pair changes the answer; duplicate-drop flags must be applied first.
- **Freedom priced out of reach.** How large is the gap between bond set and bond actually posted — how many people stay locked up purely because they cannot pay? — ICE detention stints (fed_ice_detention_stints). *Harm:* Bond set above what a person can pay converts a release decision into indefinite detention by wealth. · caveat: multiple bond columns plus a duplicate-likely-bond flag signal known data-quality problems in exactly this field.
- **Detention length by race and nationality.** Do identical case categories produce different detention lengths by race, ethnicity, and citizenship country? — ICE detention stints (fed_ice_detention_stints). *Harm:* Same case category, longer detention for one group, is discrimination measurable in days of a person's life. · caveat: race/ethnicity are agency-assigned, not self-reported; reliability unknown and must be stated.
- **Where you're held decides how you leave.** Do some facilities release almost entirely by removal while others release on bond or supervision, for comparable case mixes? — ICE detention stints (fed_ice_detention_stints). *Harm:* Where you are detained determines whether you go home or get deported — which should not be true. · caveat: two release-reason columns may disagree; facility case mixes must be controlled for.
- **The detention transfer network.** What are the routes along which detainees are transferred between facilities — moving people far from lawyers and family mid-case? — ICE detention stints linked across stints by person hash (fed_ice_detention_stints). *Harm:* Transferring someone across the country severs them from counsel and family right when they need both. · caveat: fix: relies on the anonymized person hash being a stable real link — run a collision/stability check (distinct hashes vs stint counts, demographic consistency within hash) before trusting the graph; instability breaks the whole graph.
- **Enforcement intensity by region.** Which ICE areas of responsibility arrest and remove hardest, and when? — ICE enforcement statistics (fed_ice_statistics). *Harm:* Living in a high-intensity region means a routine traffic stop can end in removal. · caveat: only 221 rows; region is a name needing a state mapping.
- **Monitors instead of — or on top of — detention.** Did electronic monitoring (alternatives to detention) replace detention or simply add surveillance on top of it? — ICE enforcement statistics (fed_ice_statistics). *Harm:* Ankle monitors on people who would otherwise be free is surveillance sold as mercy. · caveat: monitoring-type column may be null outside one metric family; 221 rows.
- **Deportation without a judge.** How has the mix of removal authorities shifted between expedited removal and full immigration-court process? — ICE enforcement statistics (fed_ice_statistics). *Harm:* Expedited removal means deportation without ever seeing a judge. · caveat: citizenship-country column is a broken numeric cast — nationality cuts unavailable.
