- **Which applications quietly became unwinnable.** Which immigration form types show rising denial rates by fiscal year? — USCIS data (fed_uscis_data). *Harm:* A form's rising denial rate is thousands of specific people losing status, work permits, or family reunification. · caveat: approvals/denials/receipts are raw text in the mart; category granularity varies by report; completeness unverified.
- **The backlog mountain and processing creep.** Which application categories drifted from months to years of processing, and how fast is the pending backlog accumulating relative to adjudication? — USCIS data (fed_uscis_data). *Harm:* Every unit in the backlog is a person in limbo — a lapsed work permit is a family losing its income while waiting. · caveat: processing-time and pending columns are untyped text; taxonomy stability across reports unverified.
- **The field office lottery.** Do identical applications get approved at different rates depending on which USCIS field office handles them? — USCIS data (fed_uscis_data). *Harm:* Where you happen to live changes whether your identical application is approved. · caveat: office field may populate on only a minority of report types; office-to-state mapping needed.
- **Requests for evidence as soft denial.** Do heavy request-for-evidence volumes function as an informal rejection channel that exhausts applicants out of valid claims? — USCIS data (fed_uscis_data). *Harm:* An RFE avalanche exhausts applicants into abandoning valid claims without ever being formally denied. · wild · caveat: RFE counts may populate on very few rows; the causal read is a hypothesis, not a measurement.
- **Where the world's refugees come from.** Which countries produce the world's refugees, decade by decade — which displacement crises persist for generations? — OWID refugee population by origin (xc_owid_refugees). *Harm:* Decades-long refugee populations are generations of people born and raised with no country. · caveat: aggregate country-year data only; OWID entity list mixes countries with regions and must be filtered.
- **The fastest displacements on record.** Which year-over-year refugee increases were the sharpest — the years millions had days to leave home? — OWID refugee population by origin (xc_owid_refugees). *Harm:* The steepest slopes are the years millions of people had days to leave home. · caveat: reporting-methodology changes can create artificial jumps indistinguishable from real crises.

### sanctions-and-enforcement (30)
- **Repeat FTC respondents.** Which companies get sued by the FTC repeatedly — firms treating enforcement as a cost of doing business? — FTC enforcement actions (fed_ftc_datasets). *Harm:* A company sued repeatedly for the same consumer harm keeps harming consumers between cases. · caveat: respondent is free text with name variation; EIN column likely mostly blank; ~1,200 rows may be a partial scrape.
- **What the FTC chases and drops.** Which consumer harms did the FTC pursue in each era, which did it abandon, and how has the consumer-protection vs antitrust balance shifted? — FTC enforcement actions (fed_ftc_datasets). *Harm:* Topics the FTC stops enforcing are harms consumers absorb with no recourse. · caveat: topic taxonomy may be inconsistent; partial scrape may bias the mix.
- **FTC cases that never close.** What share of FTC actions are still pending years after filing — conduct continuing while the case sits? — FTC enforcement actions (fed_ftc_datasets). *Harm:* An action pending for years means the conduct continues while the case sits. · medium · caveat: no resolution-date column — duration inferred from filing date and current status only.
- **Forty years of multistate settlements.** How have the size, structure, and era patterns of state-AG multistate settlements changed since 1980, including under different presidential administrations? — NAAG multistate settlements (fed_naag_multistate_settlements). *Harm:* Enforcement droughts are years consumers were harmed with no one bringing a case. · caveat: amount fields are likely text with currency formatting; date formats unverified; administration labeling inconsistent.
- **Who actually gets restitution.** What sliver of each settlement actually reaches harmed consumers versus state budget lines and fees? — NAAG multistate settlements (fed_naag_multistate_settlements). *Harm:* When restitution is a sliver of the settlement, the injured consumers subsidized a state budget line. · caveat: restitution column likely null for many rows and text-formatted; definitions vary across decades.
- **Party lines in consumer enforcement.** Which industries draw bipartisan AG action and which split on party lines — and whose consumers got no relief because their AG sat out? — NAAG multistate settlements (fed_naag_multistate_settlements). *Harm:* Consumers in states whose AG sat out an industry-wide settlement got no relief at all. · caveat: party-count fields may be text lists; industry taxonomy inconsistent over 40 years.
- **Repeat settlement defendants.** Which corporations appear in multistate settlements again and again across different issue areas and decades? — NAAG multistate settlements (fed_naag_multistate_settlements). *Harm:* A company settling repeatedly across industries and decades has priced the penalty into the business model. · caveat: defendants is a free-text list needing splitting and name normalization.
- **Monitors: teeth or theater.** Do settlements with corporate-monitor provisions differ in size or repeat-offense behavior from those without? — NAAG multistate settlements (fed_naag_multistate_settlements). *Harm:* Settlements without ongoing monitoring let the same conduct resume the day the check clears. · wild · caveat: monitor-provision population unverified; provision types are free text.
- **The indefinitely banned.** Who gets suspended from the federal mortgage system, for how long, and where do the banned individuals and companies cluster? — FHFA suspended counterparties (fed_fhfa_suspended_counterparties). *Harm:* Being banned from the federal mortgage system is the consequence — who receives it versus who does not is the question. · medium · caveat: only 222 rows; end-date column is the word "Indefinite" on most rows and nulls after casting; state counts will be single digits.
- **Repeat names across suspension orders.** Do the same individuals and companies appear across multiple suspension orders under related names — enforcement chasing shells rather than people? — FHFA suspended counterparties (fed_fhfa_suspended_counterparties). *Harm:* Repeat actors banned under multiple names show enforcement chasing shells rather than people. · wild · caveat: fix: name-only clustering inside a tiny table — a company-registry crosswalk (state registration or EIN) would make it trustworthy; 222 rows may yield almost no clusters.
- **The shape of every sanctions regime.** How do the US, EU, UK, and UN sanctions regimes compare in size, programme mix, entity types targeted, and growth timing relative to world events? — consolidated screening list, OFAC SDN, EU/UK/UN lists, OpenSanctions schema mix (fed_consolidated_screening_list, fed_ofac_sdn, intl_eu_sanctions, xc_uk_sanctions_list, xc_un_consolidated_sanctions_list, intl_opensanctions). *Harm:* Regime size and timing show where pressure is actually applied, which crises get named but not enforced, and whether states act during harm or after it is politically safe. · caveat: OFAC mart has no designation date; EU/UK marts are one row per name-variant and must be deduplicated by entity id before any count; the screening list has ~96 published duplicate entry ids.
- **Designations without end or review.** How many designations have run for decades with no end date and no review — no realistic route off the list? — screening-list start/end dates plus UN listed-on vs last-reviewed dates (fed_consolidated_screening_list, xc_un_consolidated_sanctions_list). *Harm:* Permanent designation with no review traps people and companies with no route to challenge it. · caveat: null end dates mean active, not missing — must be distinguished; UN last-updated field is a raw JSON blob whose date cast likely nulls out.
- **Which countries' citizens bear the watchlists.** Where does export-denial and watchlisting land hardest by country, normalized by population — where does an ordinary citizen face routine banking refusal? — screening-list addresses/nationalities plus OpenSanctions countries (fed_consolidated_screening_list, intl_opensanctions_default). *Harm:* Citizens of over-listed countries face routine banking refusal and remittance blocks with no individual wrongdoing. · caveat: country fields are packed multi-value strings needing splitting; population normalization is external.
- **The sanctioned fleet.** How much shipping capacity is under sanction, registered where, of what type, and concentrated in whose hands — the handful of operators behind most of the fleet? — OFAC SDN vessel fields, screening-list vessel entries, UK ship fields (fed_ofac_sdn, fed_consolidated_screening_list, xc_uk_sanctions_list). *Harm:* Sanctioned tankers still sail; targeting hulls instead of owners will never work when a few operators control dozens of vessels. · caveat: tonnage fields likely text; the OFAC IMO number is described as derived — needs a distinct-value check before being trusted (platform-wide masked-ID trap); listed owner is often not the true one.
- **Names good enough to freeze the wrong person.** How much identifying detail does each listing regime actually publish — alias depth, birth dates, addresses, documents — and which sources publish names with nothing else, guaranteeing false matches? — alias and remarks fields across the screening list, OFAC, EU, UK, and OpenSanctions (fed_consolidated_screening_list, fed_ofac_sdn, intl_eu_sanctions, xc_uk_sanctions_list, intl_opensanctions_default). *Harm:* A name-only listing guarantees false matches — and the person wrongly matched loses their bank account with no appeal; thin detail also lets the real target evade. · caveat: fill checks must use distinct-value counts, not null counts — packed empty strings read as populated; alias counts also reflect transliteration, not evasion.
- **Does sanctioning punch up or down.** Do sanctions regimes name the ministers and financiers who order and fund abuses, or the soldiers, clerks, and young operatives beneath them — by recorded role, title, and birth-year profile? — EU function/gender fields, UN designation text, OpenSanctions birth dates (intl_eu_sanctions, xc_un_consolidated_sanctions_list, intl_opensanctions). *Harm:* If sanctions hit soldiers and clerks but not the ministers who ordered them, the regime punishes downward and the money that funds violence is untouched. · medium · caveat: role fields are free text with low fill; birth dates often partial years that null out on casting.
- **Addresses behind the designations.** Which buildings host multiple sanctioned entities — the corporate service providers that keep sanctioned money moving? — EU sanctions address fields (intl_eu_sanctions). *Harm:* Shared registered addresses expose the corporate service providers that keep sanctioned money moving. · caveat: the address-country column is wrapped in a numeric cast and will null out — a modelling bug; address fields sparse.
- **Reasons given or merely asserted.** Which UK designations come with a substantive statement of reasons and which are merely asserted — unchallengeable by the person destroyed? — UK sanctions statement-of-reasons text (xc_uk_sanctions_list). *Harm:* A designation with no stated reason cannot be challenged by the person it destroys. · caveat: text length is a crude proxy for explanatory quality; fill rate unverified.
- **UN listings no police force acts on.** What share of UN designations carry an Interpol notice — a name on a list versus a name someone will actually stop? — UN consolidated list Interpol-link fields (xc_un_consolidated_sanctions_list). *Harm:* A UN designation with no Interpol notice is a name on a list that no police force will ever act on. · medium · caveat: the has-interpol-link derivation looks malformed in the staging model and may not evaluate as intended; 1,011 rows.
- **The watchlist is mostly not sanctions.** How much of the global 1.28M-entry screening universe is politically-exposed-person listings rather than sanctions — people flagged with no offence alleged? — OpenSanctions default collection (intl_opensanctions_default). *Harm:* Being flagged as politically exposed can freeze an ordinary person's bank account with no offence alleged — the composition shows how large that population is. · caveat: datasets field is a packed multi-value string across 443 sources needing classification; no ownership edges in the flat export.
- **Quiet churn on the watchlists.** How many targets are added, revised, and quietly dropped each month — delistings nobody announces or defends? — OpenSanctions first-seen/last-seen dates (intl_opensanctions_default). *Harm:* Targets quietly dropped from watchlists with no announcement are people harmed by a listing nobody now defends. · caveat: first/last-seen reflect OpenSanctions crawl history, not the issuing authority's decision dates.
- **Crypto wallets on the lists.** How fast did wallet-level designations grow, and how wide is the net they sweep — anyone who ever transacted with an address? — OpenSanctions crypto entity types (intl_opensanctions_default). *Harm:* Wallet-level designations sweep in anyone who ever transacted with an address, including people with no knowledge of it. · medium · caveat: crypto entity types may be a tiny slice or absent from the flat export.
- **Perfect laws, zero enforcement.** Which countries score high on technical anti-money-laundering compliance but near zero on effectiveness — excellent laws that do nothing? — FATF assessment ratings (intl_fatf_ratings). *Harm:* A country with perfect laws and zero enforcement is the safest place in the world to launder money. · caveat: only 200 rows — far too few for full coverage; country column is a broken numeric cast that may destroy names; ratings need a defensible ordinal mapping.
- **The stale AML report card.** What does the global AML compliance grid look like country by recommendation, and which countries have not been assessed in over a decade? — FATF ratings (intl_fatf_ratings). *Harm:* A country last assessed twelve years ago has an unexamined financial system everyone still treats as vetted. · medium · caveat: 200-row sample; country cast bug; evaluation-year fill unverified.
- **Targets only one jurisdiction names.** Which targets does every jurisdiction agree on versus names only one country lists — free to trade everywhere else? — OpenSanctions dataset-overlap counts (intl_opensanctions). *Harm:* Targets named by only one country can trade freely everywhere else — which is how sanctions regimes leak. · caveat: dataset field is a packed multi-value string; the countries column is a broken numeric cast.
- **Who actually debars, and for how long.** Which agencies use federal debarment and which never do, how inconsistent are exclusion lengths for the same conduct, and where do the debarred cluster geographically? — federal contractor exclusions (fed_sam_exclusions). *Harm:* Agencies that never debar keep sending public money to contractors who already failed the people they served; wildly inconsistent penalties mean the punishment depends on who caught you. · caveat: 2,940 rows in the mart against a described ~9k source — landed slice may be partial; null termination date means indefinite, not missing.
- **Debarment stops at the corporate shell.** Does enforcement reach individuals, or only companies whose executives simply start a new one? — exclusions individual/entity split (fed_sam_exclusions). *Harm:* When only companies are debarred, the executives who made the decisions simply start a new company. · caveat: the individual-vs-entity derivation relies on last-name-null — a fragile heuristic.
- **Debarment recidivists.** Which entities and individuals cycle through the exclusion list repeatedly — excluded, reinstated, excluded again — showing debarment failing as a deterrent? — exclusion spells per entity (fed_sam_exclusions). *Harm:* An entity debarred twice kept winning public money in between — the gap between spells is the finding. · medium · caveat: mart is a partial slice (2,940 of ~9k); UEI fill must be checked before spell-linking on it.
- **Vessels going dark.** Where do vessels switch off their transponders while underway — the specific waters where blackouts begin? — NOAA nationwide AIS positions, 58M rows, 2024 (fed_noaa_ais). *Harm:* transponder blackouts are the cover for illegal fishing, sanctions evasion, and dumping — all of which land on coastal communities. · caveat: gaps also come from receiver coverage holes; 2024 only; imo_number is ~56% blank/placeholder — use mmsi, never imo.
- **Ship-to-ship transfer signals.** Do reported draft changes away from any port reveal at-sea cargo transfers — how sanctioned and untaxed cargo enters the supply chain? — NOAA AIS draft readings per vessel over voyages (fed_noaa_ais). *Harm:* ship-to-ship transfers at sea are how sanctioned and untaxed cargo enters the supply chain. · wild · caveat: draft is manually entered by crew and notoriously stale or wrong.

### money-in-politics (92)
- **Twenty-four years of NYC money.** Stack all five NYC campaign-finance cycles (2001–2025) into one panel: how did donor geography, small-dollar share, and bundling shift — and did the matching-funds programme actually broaden who funds city politics? — NYC CFB contributions, five cycles (ST_NYC_CFB_CAMPAIGN_2001…2025). *Harm:* Watching one city's money move over 24 years shows whether reform broadened who funds politics or not. · caveat: column layouts differ across cycles and need harmonizing; donor identity across cycles is name+ZIP only; 2025 cycle incomplete. *(Vintages of one source family — one source under the counting convention; moved from tier 4 on consistency review.)*
- **Pop-up political vehicles.** How many political money vehicles — 527 groups, FEC committees, big ad advertisers — appear from nowhere in the weeks before a vote, spend, and dissolve before anyone can trace them? — IRS 527 registry, FEC committee masters, Google political ads weekly spend (irs527_8871_orgs, fed_fec_bulk_committees, fed_fec_bulk, fed_google_polads_advertiser_weekly_spend). *Harm:* Groups spun up weeks before a vote spend big with no track record to check, and are gone before scrutiny arrives. · caveat: established-date parsing over text is a known platform trap; first-observed week in the ad archive is an artifact of the archive, not entity formation.
- **Groups that claim disclosure exemptions.** How many 527 registrations claim exemption from periodic or annual reporting — the legal on-ramp to spending without disclosure — and is it trending up? — IRS 527 registry (irs527_8871_orgs). *Harm:* Claiming exemption is the legal on-ramp to spending without disclosure. · caveat: indicator encoding unverified; blanks may not mean no.
- **One mailbox, many committees.** Which single addresses host dozens of nominally separate political committees — where is the shared-office political industry? — IRS 527 registry addresses plus FEC committee master addresses (irs527_8871_orgs, FED_FEC_COMMITTEES, fed_fec_bulk). *Harm:* One consultant office fronting dozens of grassroots-sounding groups misleads every voter who reads the name. · caveat: fix: normalize address strings and split suite lines before clustering, and rule out compliance-firm and PO-box benign explanations; the multi-cycle FEC committee mart has unnamed positional columns.
- **Boilerplate purposes.** How vague are 527 groups' stated purposes, and how often does the name promise something the purpose text never says? — IRS 527 registry purpose text (irs527_8871_orgs). *Harm:* Vague boilerplate purpose statements are how the real backer stays invisible. · medium · caveat: purpose is long free text; grouping requires a judgment-call keyword scheme.
- **The scale of 527 money.** How much undisclosed-donor political money moves through 527 organizations each reporting period and each cycle? — IRS 527 periodic reports (irs527_8872_reports). *Harm:* The raw scale of undisclosed-donor political money moving each cycle. · caveat: totals are report-level; amendments may double count without dedup on form id.
- **Late and burst money.** How much political money — 527 spending, independent expenditures, digital ad buys, late contributions — lands in the final days before a vote, after the last chance for scrutiny or fact-checking? — IRS 527 reports, FEC independent expenditures, Google ads weekly spend, NYC 2021 contributions (irs527_8872_reports, FED_FEC_INDEPENDENT_EXPENDITURES, fed_google_polads_advertiser_weekly_spend, st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2021_contributions). *Harm:* Money landing after the last disclosure deadline shapes votes with no time for rebuttal. · caveat: IE date fields are untyped text; election-day alignment needs an external calendar; ad cycle labels may not map to voting dates.
- **Warehoused political cash.** Which political organizations raise heavily and never spend — whose donor money sits parked indefinitely with no accountability for its eventual use? — IRS 527 reports plus FEC PAC/party summary (irs527_8872_reports, FED_FEC_PAC_SUMMARY). *Harm:* Cash parked in a political shell is money whose purpose no voter ever learns. · caveat: amended reports could inflate totals; the PAC summary mart has 27 unnamed positional columns blocking it until decoded.
- **Dead groups that rise again.** Which 527 groups file a final report and then re-emerge under the same EIN — resetting their public record? — IRS 527 reports final-report flag (irs527_8872_reports). *Harm:* Declaring the group dead and re-emerging is how a donor network resets its record. · wild · caveat: final-report flag encoding unverified; EIN reuse across successor groups is assumed.
- **The operator class.** Which individuals run many nominally separate political vehicles at once — the officers, treasurers, and responsible signers who appear on dozens of committees and filings, sometimes as the entire board? — IRS 527 directors/officers, FEC committee treasurer fields, California lobbying filings (irs527_directors_officers, FED_FEC_COMMITTEES, ca_lobby_chg_log, ca_lobby_cover2). *Harm:* A handful of operators steer dozens of separate-looking political groups, and a one-person board means no internal check on the money. · caveat: fix: person names are free text with no person id — build name normalization (or a person spine) before trusting the network; common names merge, spelling variants split; the multi-cycle FEC committee mart has unnamed columns.
- **Local names, out-of-state control.** How much local-sounding political and lobbying activity is actually run and funded from another state — officers, parent entities, firms, and clients based far from the place they influence? — IRS 527 officers and related entities, California firm locations, Texas out-of-state clients (irs527_directors_officers, irs527_related_entities, ca_lobby_cover, tx_lobby_individual_reporting). *Harm:* Local-sounding groups run from another state are astroturf by definition — influence with no local accountability. · medium · caveat: officer/client addresses may simply repeat a registered agent or the organization address, collapsing the comparison.
- **527s playing in many states.** Which 527 organizations hold election-authority registrations in many states — national operations wearing separate local faces? — IRS 527 election authority IDs joined within family to the registry (irs527_eain, irs527_8871_orgs). *Harm:* Multi-state operations concentrate influence while looking like separate local efforts. · medium · caveat: only 17,853 rows; coverage may be partial and state-issued fill rate unverified.
- **The declared affiliation web.** Which separate-looking political committees declare themselves related — and what kinds of ties do they admit to? — IRS 527 related entities (irs527_related_entities). *Harm:* Declared affiliations reveal which separate-looking committees are actually one machine — and set the floor for what regulators could already check. · caveat: fix: node identity is name-only — normalize names or wire EINs before treating clusters as one machine; relationship vocabulary is free text; blanks likely common.
- **Which foreign interests buy the most US voice.** Which foreign governments and principals maintain the deepest standing paid representation in the US, and how much moves through it? — foreign-agent registrations (fed_fara_bulk, fed_fara). *Harm:* Standing foreign representation is a permanent lobbying presence that ordinary constituents cannot match. · caveat: the fed_fara mart is a 30-row token sample, not the real corpus; the bulk mart mixes four record shapes and country fields are free text; completeness unverified.
- **Foreign influence timed to events.** Do new foreign-agent registrations surge right after invasions, sanctions, and scandals — and are the engagements short-lived contracts timed to specific votes or crises? — foreign-agent registration/termination dates (fed_fara_bulk, fed_fara). *Harm:* A surge of paid US representation right after a crisis shows who is buying reputation management during it. · caveat: event overlay is external context; registration-date cast reliability unverified; termination dates null for active registrations.
- **Firms serving rival governments.** Which lobbying and PR firms represent rival foreign governments simultaneously — selling access rather than advocacy? — foreign-agent registrant-principal pairs (fed_fara_bulk). *Harm:* A firm representing rival governments at once is selling access, not advocacy. · caveat: fix: registrant and principal names need entity resolution before the bipartite network is trustworthy; the four record shapes may not all carry both sides of the pair.
- **Nobody stays on the foreign account.** Which firms cycle staff so rapidly through foreign accounts that individual accountability never attaches to anyone? — foreign-agent short-form registrations (fed_fara_bulk). *Harm:* Rapid staff churn on a foreign account keeps accountability from ever attaching to a person. · medium · caveat: short-form fields may be null on most rows since the mart mixes record types.
- **The influence industry's street address.** How physically concentrated is the influence industry — the few blocks near the Capitol and the state capitols where the access business lives? — foreign-agent registrant addresses plus California filer addresses (fed_fara_bulk, ca_lobby_chg_log). *Harm:* Concentration a few blocks from power shows influence is a proximity business closed to everyone else. · medium · caveat: address fields sparse across record shapes; ZIP formatting unverified.
- **The corporate parents behind PACs.** Which corporations and unions sponsor the most political committees — who is actually behind the PAC names on the filings? — FEC committee master connected-organization field (fed_fec_bulk). *Harm:* The PAC name on a filing is rarely the company writing the cheque; the connected org is who actually wants the vote. · caveat: connected-organization fill rate unverified and likely blank for many committee types.
- **Where committee infrastructure is thin.** Which states have dense super-PAC and party infrastructure and which have almost none — where are races nobody is watching? — FEC committee master (fed_fec_bulk). *Harm:* States with thin committee infrastructure have races nobody is watching, where local harm goes unchallenged. · medium · caveat: committee state reflects mailing address, not where money is spent.
- **Who reports often enough to watch.** Which committees file monthly versus quarterly — who can spend through an entire primary before anyone sees a number? — FEC committee master filing-frequency field (fed_fec_bulk). *Harm:* Quarterly filers can spend through an entire primary before the public sees a number. · caveat: frequency codes need decoding; some frequencies are legally mandated rather than chosen.
- **Identity churn in political archives.** How much political history is lost to renaming — committee names reused under new IDs, ad-archive advertiser and creative IDs re-keyed — breaking every link back to the record? — FEC committee name/id pairs plus Google ads id remaps (fed_fec_bulk_committees, fed_google_polads_advertiser_id_mapping, fed_google_polads_creative_id_mapping). *Harm:* An entity that changes name or id sheds its spending history, and the public loses the paper trail. · caveat: remap tables carry ids only, no names or dates; committee-name normalization produces false positives from legitimate re-registrations.
- **Candidates running many money vehicles.** Which candidates operate the most committees at once — including leadership PACs and joint vehicles — fragmenting the money trail so no single filing shows the true total, and which committees are shared between candidates as off-ballot alliances? — FEC candidate-committee linkages plus leadership PAC sponsors (fed_fec_bulk_linkages, FED_FEC_CAND_CMTE_LINKAGE, FED_FEC_LEADERSHIP_PAC). *Harm:* Money split across many committees is money a voter cannot trace back to the candidate who benefits. · caveat: joint-fundraising and leadership designations legitimately multiply counts; the leadership PAC mart carries ids only (no names); one linkage mart has undecoded positional columns.
- **Does money buy vote share.** How tightly do campaign receipts predict general-election vote share, and who are the exceptions who won cheap or lost rich? — FEC all-candidate financial summary (fed_fec_bulk_summary). *Harm:* If money reliably predicts the winner, the vote ratifies a fundraising race most people cannot enter. · caveat: general-election percentage only exists for candidates who reached the general; dollar columns are untyped text needing casts.
- **The self-funding entry ticket.** Which campaigns are bankrolled by the candidate's own money and loans — where is personal wealth the price of admission to running? — FEC candidate financial summary (fed_fec_bulk_summary). *Harm:* When personal wealth is the entry ticket, the pool of people who can run shrinks to the already rich. · caveat: dollar columns untyped; loan repayments not netted.
- **People-funded versus organisation-funded.** Which candidates are funded mostly by individuals and which mostly by committees and party organs — who owes their seat to people and who to organisations? — FEC candidate financial summary plus NYC 2021 small-dollar shares (fed_fec_bulk_summary, st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2021_contributions). *Harm:* A candidate funded overwhelmingly by committees owes their seat to organisations, not constituents. · caveat: itemised vs unitemised individual money is not split in the federal summary, so small-donor is an approximation; threshold choices must be shown.
- **Campaigns that end in the red.** Which campaigns close the cycle owing more than they hold — and who never gets paid? — FEC candidate financial summary debt fields (fed_fec_bulk_summary). *Harm:* Campaign debt often means unpaid local vendors and staff who never get made whole. · medium · caveat: no creditor detail — who is owed is invisible here.
- **Refunds as a compliance tell.** Which campaigns had to give back unusual amounts of money — the visible residue of contributions that should never have been taken? — FEC refund fields plus NYC refund dates (fed_fec_bulk_summary, st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2009_contribution). *Harm:* High refunds usually mean money was taken that should not have been — illegal, over-limit, or disowned. · caveat: refunds also occur for routine over-limit corrections and need a baseline; NYC refund dates parsed permissively and mostly null.
- **Committees that switch candidates.** Which committees move from one candidate to another across cycles, carrying their donor lists and cash with them? — FEC multi-cycle candidate-committee linkage (FED_FEC_CAND_CMTE_LINKAGE). *Harm:* A committee that changes candidates transfers political power invisible on any ballot. · wild · caveat: blocked on positional-column decoding; requires a stable committee id across cycles, which the file may not preserve.
- **The real coalitions.** Cluster the PAC-to-candidate money network: which industries fund which blocs of legislators, regardless of party label? — FEC committee-to-candidate transactions (fed_fec_committee_to_candidate). *Harm:* The coalition map shows which industries own which blocs of legislators, whatever the party label says. · caveat: 866k rows require aggregation; transaction types mix contributions and independent expenditures and must be separated.
- **Money timed to the vote.** Do PAC contributions cluster in the days right before and after key legislative moments — the visible shape of purchased access? — FEC committee-to-candidate transaction dates (fed_fec_committee_to_candidate). *Harm:* Contributions clustering right before a vote are the clearest visible form of purchased access. · caveat: transaction date is untyped MMDDYYYY text needing parsing; the legislative calendar is external context.
- **Donors who fund both sides.** Which committees and donors fund opposing candidates in the same race — buying access to whoever wins? — FEC committee-to-candidate, Elections Canada contributions, NYC 2021 contributions (fed_fec_committee_to_candidate, intl_elections_canada_contributions, st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2021_contributions). *Harm:* A donor funding both sides is not buying an outcome, it is buying access whoever wins — which is worse. · caveat: fix: individual-donor versions ride name-only matching — needs donor identity resolution, and the FEC version needs the candidate master joined to know which candidates share a race; no contributor id exists in the Canadian or NYC files.
- **Races funded from far away.** Which races are funded predominantly from out of state or out of district — where are local voters the audience rather than the constituency? — FEC contributor geography plus NYC borough-grain donations (fed_fec_committee_to_candidate, st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2001_contribution). *Harm:* A race funded from three thousand miles away answers to people who do not live with the consequences. · caveat: PAC contributor state is usually a DC headquarters, blunting the federal signal; NYC borough coding unverified.
- **Attack-money saturation.** Which races are drowned in opposition spending rather than support — where do voters hear only attacks? — FEC independent expenditures support/oppose fields (FED_FEC_INDEPENDENT_EXPENDITURES). *Harm:* Voters in the most attack-saturated districts are the least informed about what candidates actually propose. · caveat: expenditure amount is untyped text needing casts; support/oppose coding assumed S/O.
- **One-patron races.** In which races does a single outside spender supply most of the money — where does the winner owe one unelected patron? — FEC independent expenditure spender fields (FED_FEC_INDEPENDENT_EXPENDITURES). *Harm:* When one outside group funds most of a race, the winner owes a single unelected patron. · caveat: fix: spender identity fragments across name variants — verify the spender id or normalize names before computing concentration; completeness unverified.
- **What the money bought.** What tactics does outside money buy — digital, mail, canvass, TV — and which voters get which treatment (or get written off)? — FEC independent expenditure purpose text (FED_FEC_INDEPENDENT_EXPENDITURES). *Harm:* The tactic mix reveals which voters are targeted with which message, and who is written off entirely. · medium · caveat: purpose is uncontrolled free text with heavy variation; clustering quality unknown.
- **The record, rewritten.** How often are disclosure filings amended after the public read them — what gets changed (lobbyists added and deleted, employers removed, spending restated), who rewrites most, and do corrections cluster at deadlines? — FEC independent-expenditure amendment chains plus California lobbying amendments and change log (FED_FEC_INDEPENDENT_EXPENDITURES, ca_lobby_amendments, ca_lobby_chg_log). *Harm:* Amendments after the fact are how a lobbying relationship or a spend number gets written out of the version the public already read. · caveat: amendment-chain fill rates unknown; heavy amendment may be routine for some form types; attribute codes may need a lookup not in the model.
- **Employer-bundled giving.** Which employers' staff collectively give the most — corporate political power routed through individuals to sidestep corporate-contribution rules? — FEC itemized individual contributions employer field plus NYC 2009 contributions (fed_fec_indiv_contributions, st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2009_contribution). *Harm:* Bundled employee giving is corporate political power routed through individuals. · caveat: fix: employer is uncontrolled free text with millions of spelling variants — normalization quality decides whether this works at all; federal file covers cycles 2024 and 2026 only; NYC 2009 column layout unread and may differ.
- **The donor-class map.** Which few ZIP codes and neighbourhoods fund politics while most supply nothing — the geography of who gets heard, federally, in Canada, and in NYC? — FEC contributions by ZIP, Elections Canada by postal code, NYC 2013/2025 by zip (fed_fec_indiv_contributions, intl_elections_canada_contributions, st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2013_contribution, st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2025_contributions). *Harm:* A few affluent ZIPs supply most political money while most supply none — a geography of who gets heard. · caveat: population normalization needs an external denominator; ZIP formats vary (5 vs 9 digit); Canadian privacy thresholds may drop small donors; 2025 cycle incomplete.
- **'Retired' as the top donor occupation.** How much political money is attributed to occupations that hide the real source ('retired', 'not employed', blank) — and what does the occupation mix of each candidate's funders actually reveal? — FEC contributions occupation field plus NYC 2025 occupations (fed_fec_indiv_contributions, st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2025_contributions). *Harm:* When the top donor occupations are 'retired' and 'not employed', the disclosure law that names donors has quietly stopped working. · caveat: occupation is self-reported free text, often blank or self-serving; the pattern is real but explaining it requires care.
- **Conduit money.** How much money reaches committees through earmarking conduits — where the committee a donor thinks they gave to is not the one that spends it? — FEC contributions conduit/other-id fields (fed_fec_indiv_contributions). *Harm:* Conduits mean the committee a donor thinks they gave to is not the committee that spends the money. · caveat: other-id fill rate and meaning unverified; conduit semantics differ by transaction type.
- **The maxed-out cohort.** How small is the cohort of donors who hit the legal maximum, and how many committees does each of them max out to in a cycle? — FEC itemized individual contributions (fed_fec_indiv_contributions). *Harm:* A small cohort maxing out to dozens of committees is how legal contribution limits are made meaningless. · caveat: fix: donor identity across name spellings is unresolved — needs donor entity resolution before cohort counts are real; contribution limits change by year and committee type.
- **Recurring-donation rhythms.** Does contribution volume pulse on paydays and billing cycles — the fingerprint of automated recurring-withdrawal programmes that have drained small and elderly donors? — FEC contributions daily timing (fed_fec_indiv_contributions). *Harm:* Recurring-donation rhythms expose the automated withdrawal programmes that have drained small donors, especially elderly ones. · wild · caveat: no recurring-donation flag exists; the rhythm is inferred from timing alone.
- **PACs that are fundraising businesses.** Which PACs raise heavily and pass almost nothing to candidates — donors funding an overhead machine, not a campaign? — FEC PAC/party summary (FED_FEC_PAC_SUMMARY). *Harm:* Donors who think they are funding a candidate are often funding a fundraising business. · caveat: blocked on unnamed positional columns; the low-pass-through pattern also fits legitimate issue advocacy.
- **Senators most active in the market.** Which senators trade most, in what volume, in the markets they regulate? — Senate stock-trade disclosures (fed_senate_stock_watcher). *Harm:* A legislator trading heavily in industries they oversee holds an information advantage no constituent has. · caveat: coverage ends Dec 2020; amounts are bands, so totals are estimates; 546 exact-duplicate rows kept as landed; name-only source; journalism-use-only by law.
- **Selling before the crash.** Who sold ahead of the early-2020 market crash the public did not see coming? — Senate stock-trade timeline (fed_senate_stock_watcher). *Harm:* Selling ahead of a crash the public did not see coming is the one case where insider advantage is undeniable. · caveat: no disclosure date in this source, so the trading-to-telling gap cannot be measured; coverage ends Dec 2020; journalism-use-only.
- **The spouse's portfolio.** How much congressional trading runs through spouses, children, and joint accounts rather than the member's own name? — Senate stock-trade owner field (fed_senate_stock_watcher). *Harm:* Routing trades through a spouse keeps the household benefit while blunting the accountability. · medium · caveat: owner field values unverified and may be sparsely populated; coverage ends Dec 2020.
- **Lobbyists writing checks to their targets.** Which officials receive campaign contributions directly from the registered lobbyists who lobby them? — California lobbyist contributions (ca_lobby_contributions). *Harm:* A lobbyist writing checks to the official they are lobbying is the plainest conflict there is. · caveat: only 6,505 rows — may be a lightly-used disclosure form, a thin slice of the real money.
- **Influence money on the legislative clock.** Does influence spending pulse with the legislative calendar — lobbyist giving near deadlines, employer spend spiking five-fold in a bill's quarter, firms staffing up before sessions, retainers ending right after passage, meals crescendoing in session weeks? — California lobbying timing tables plus Texas cover-sheet and meal dates (ca_lobby_contributions, ca_lobby_employer, ca_lobby_firm_lobbyist, ca_lobby_employer_firms, tx_lobby_cover, tx_lobby_food_beverage). *Harm:* Money surging exactly when bills move shows the transaction, not coincidence — and the bill is where the harm lives. · caveat: wide-format quarter columns with undocumented calendar mapping; session calendars are external context; several link tables are thin.
- **The biggest lobbying shops by paperwork.** Which firms file the most lobbying disclosures and represent the most filers across two decades of California records? — California lobbying cover pages (ca_lobby_cover). *Harm:* The handful of firms that file most are the firms that shape most of what passes. · caveat: 525k rows mix four form types with different meanings; firm names free text, firm ids blank on older filings.
- **Which issues draw the heaviest paid pressure.** Which policy areas attract the most lobbying money and attention — federally and in Texas and California — and which public interests have no paid voice at all? — Senate lobbying filings issue fields, Texas subject matter, California activity text (fed_senate_lda_filings, tx_lobby_subject_matter, ca_lobby_cover). *Harm:* The issues with the most money aimed at them are the issues where the public interest is most outgunned. · caveat: Senate lobbying filings only ~9% of 1.98M loaded — totals unsafe until reloaded; issue fields are delimited or free text; TX subject codes may have changed meaning across decades.
- **Disclosure that arrives late.** Who habitually files lobbying disclosures late — so the public learns who lobbied only after the vote? — California cover-page dates plus Texas due/filed dates (ca_lobby_cover, tx_lobby_cover). *Harm:* Late disclosure means the public learns who lobbied after the vote is already over. · caveat: date columns may be text; statutory deadlines differ by form type and are not in the data.
- **Who signs and how deep.** Who actually signs lobbying disclosures (chief executives or junior clerks), and how many associated parties do filings really list — how seriously is disclosure treated? — California cover page 2 titles and line items (ca_lobby_cover2). *Harm:* Whether a chief executive or a junior clerk signs tells you how seriously the disclosure is treated. · medium · caveat: title is uncontrolled free text; line-item semantics undocumented and may be a sequence number.
- **Clients with armies of lobbyists.** Which clients and employers field the most individual lobbyists — who can put thirty bodies in a hallway that no citizen group can match? — California employer-lobbyist links plus Texas entity reporting (ca_lobby_emp_lobbyist, tx_lobby_individual_reporting). *Harm:* A client fielding thirty lobbyists outguns every citizen group in the building. · caveat: fix: client names are free text with variant spellings — verify the on-behalf id fill rate or normalize names before counting rosters; CA link table is only ~1,500 rows and may cover a narrow session window; in-house lobbyists may register through a different form.
- **Lobbyists who change shirts.** Which individual lobbyists move between firms and employers — carrying relationships and client knowledge across nominally separate operations, and across administrations? — California employer/firm-lobbyist links plus Senate lobbying name lists (ca_lobby_emp_lobbyist, ca_lobby_firm_lobbyist, fed_senate_lda_filings). *Harm:* The same handful of people carry influence across firms and administrations regardless of who won the election. · caveat: fix: lobbyist id stability across sessions is unverified (classic id trap) and federal names are packed free text — build person-level resolution first; Senate lobbying filings only ~9% loaded.
- **Who spends most on lobbying access.** Which organizations are the biggest buyers of state-level lobbying access, in California and Texas? — California employer session totals plus Texas expenditure totals (ca_lobby_employer, tx_lobby_cover). *Harm:* The organizations spending most on access shape laws that touch people who cannot buy a lobbyist. · caveat: CA employer table is only 1,730 rows and amounts may be text; TX filers may hold several idents so totals must sum on the id, not the name.
- **Blanketing the capitol.** Which employers retain many lobbying firms at once — and which firms serve competing employers simultaneously? — California employer-firm links (ca_lobby_employer_firms). *Harm:* Hiring six firms buys access through six separate relationships that all point one way; a firm on both sides of an issue is a conflict the public never sees. · caveat: only 524 rows — may be a thin slice of actual retainer relationships; labeling interests as competing requires outside judgment.
- **The influence market's structure.** How concentrated is the lobbying industry — do ten of 256 California firms take most of the money, which firms live off single windfall quarters, and who are the gatekeepers? — California lobbying firms (ca_lobby_firm). *Harm:* If a handful of firms capture most of the money, influence in the largest state has a handful of gatekeepers; windfall quarters mark the moments a firm was paid to kill or pass something specific. · caveat: 256 rows suggests one session snapshot rather than full history; amounts may be text; wide-format quarters have undocumented calendar mapping.
- **The price of one relationship.** What does a specific firm-client lobbying engagement cost per period, and what does the firm claim it was doing for the money? — California firm-employer filings (ca_lobby_firm_employer). *Harm:* The billing curve of a firm-client pair is the price tag on a specific legislative outcome; vague activity text on a six-figure engagement is disclosure that discloses nothing. · caveat: only 170 rows — extremely thin, possibly partially loaded; verify completeness before drawing any conclusion.
- **Money-vehicle types over time.** Which committee types and designations proliferated when — does the mix of money vehicles track how money routes around each new rule? — FEC leadership PAC sponsor linkages by year (FED_FEC_LEADERSHIP_PAC). *Harm:* Shifts in vehicle type track how money routes around each new rule. · medium · caveat: election-year fields may be text; two year columns exist and their difference is undocumented.
- **Advertisers with nothing behind the name.** Which political advertisers declare no promoter, no regulatory id, and no public identifier — entities buying persuasion that cannot be traced to anyone? — Google political ads advertiser declared stats and public-id fields (fed_google_polads_advertiser_declared_stats, fed_google_polads_advertiser_stats). *Harm:* Voters shown a political ad by an entity with no declared promoter cannot know who is talking to them. · caveat: declared-stats table is only 469 rows; declaration requirements differ by region so blanks may be lawful; the public-ids column is a packed list.
- **Claimed scope versus actual reach.** Which advertisers declare narrow local scope while running ads elsewhere — spend crossing jurisdictions that never approved it? — Google political ads declared scope vs region (fed_google_polads_advertiser_declared_stats). *Harm:* Scope mismatches are how ad spend crosses jurisdictions that never approved it. · medium · caveat: tiny table; scope values may be a short controlled list.
- **Where political ad money lands.** Where in the world does political ad spend concentrate — by country and subdivision, absolutely and per capita — which democracies are being advertised at hardest? — Google political ads geo spend tables (fed_google_polads_geo_spend, fed_google_polads_advertiser_geo_spend). *Harm:* Small countries saturated with political ads are the most vulnerable to influence operations. · caveat: advertiser-geo table sits at exactly 500,000 rows suggesting a load cap; multi-currency columns need normalizing; per-capita needs an external population source.
- **Places saturated by few voices.** Which places hear their political debate from a handful of ad buyers — subdivisions where one advertiser supplies the argument and calls it the debate? — Google political ads advertiser geo spend (fed_google_polads_advertiser_geo_spend). *Harm:* A district blanketed by one advertiser hears one argument and calls it the debate. · caveat: likely 500k row cap; subdivision naming inconsistent across countries; currency conversion needed.
- **The biggest ad operations.** Who are the biggest political ad buyers worldwide, and which entities operate across many elections at once — campaigns versus standing persuasion operations? — Google political ads advertiser stats (fed_google_polads_advertiser_stats). *Harm:* An entity working many elections at once is running an operation, not a campaign. · caveat: dollar-only ranking undercounts non-US buyers; the elections field is a packed list needing parsing.
- **Who ads target — and exclude.** Which demographics are singled out by political ad targeting, which geographies are deliberately excluded from hearing a message, and where do mass-produced creative variants and premium placements point to micro-targeted persuasion? — Google political ads creative stats targeting fields plus advertiser creative counts (fed_google_polads_creative_stats, fed_google_polads_advertiser_stats). *Harm:* Ads aimed at one narrow demographic mean that group hears claims nobody else can rebut; excluding a region is a decision about who is allowed to hear the message. · caveat: targeting fields are packed strings; impressions are bucketed ranges; the 500k row count suggests a load cap.
- **Buying in foreign currency.** Which advertisers buy political ads in currencies far from their apparent home — a lead on foreign influence? — Google political ads weekly spend currency columns (fed_google_polads_advertiser_weekly_spend). *Harm:* Buying political ads in a foreign currency is a signal worth chasing on foreign influence. · wild · caveat: currency of purchase does not prove nationality of the buyer.
- **Ads that live for a day.** Which political ads ran briefly and vanished — messages designed to land before anyone could challenge them? — Google political ads creative serve timestamps (fed_google_polads_creative_stats). *Harm:* Ads that ran for a day and vanished are the ones nobody had time to challenge. · caveat: timestamp fields may be text; possible 500k row cap.
- **Platform-subsidized political ads.** How much political messaging is funded by the platform's own ad grants — free credit putting a thumb on the scale? — Google political ads ad-grants flag (fed_google_polads_creative_stats). *Harm:* Free platform credit flowing into political messaging is the platform putting a thumb on the scale. · wild · caveat: flag may be almost entirely false; an unnamed trailing column in the model suggests a parsing issue.
- **The most-lobbied doors.** Which agencies and committees are named most often as lobbying contacts — whose rulemaking is saturated with paid pressure the affected public cannot match? — Senate lobbying filings government-entities field (fed_senate_lda_filings). *Harm:* An agency saturated with lobbying contact is one whose rulemaking the affected public cannot match. · caveat: Senate lobbying filings only ~9% of 1.98M loaded — rankings unsafe until reloaded; the entities field is a delimited list with naming drift.
- **Foreign-backed domestic lobbying.** How much domestic lobbying lists a foreign entity behind it, on which issues, and is it growing? — Senate lobbying filings foreign-entity flag (fed_senate_lda_filings). *Harm:* Foreign money shaping domestic rules is influence the affected public has no vote over. · caveat: Senate lobbying filings only ~9% loaded; the foreign-entity field's semantics (Y/N vs free text) unverified.
- **Terminate and re-register.** Which lobbying clients formally terminate and quietly re-register — making sustained influence look like occasional engagement? — Senate lobbying filings termination dates (fed_senate_lda_filings). *Harm:* Termination-and-restart is how sustained influence gets to look like occasional engagement in the public record. · wild · caveat: Senate lobbying filings only ~9% loaded; termination-date casts may fail widely; needs a stable client id across cycles.
- **The pile-up at the legal max.** What does the distribution of contribution amounts look like against the legal annual maximum — who can afford to give the cap every single year, and who gives once and stops? — Elections Canada contributions (intl_elections_canada_contributions). *Harm:* The pile-up at the legal cap shows who can afford maximum influence every year while everyone else gives once. · caveat: amounts parsed with try_to_number over text; installment lines legitimately repeat and inflate naive per-donor sums.
- **The between-election funding void.** Does political giving detonate around campaigns and flatline between them — leaving the period when policy is actually made unfunded and unscrutinized? — Elections Canada contributions timeline (intl_elections_canada_contributions). *Harm:* Between-election silence is when policy actually gets made, and it is the period nobody is funding scrutiny of. · medium · caveat: date parsing over untyped text may drop older rows; electoral-event field population unverified.
- **In-kind influence nobody counts.** Which political entities are funded largely in goods and services rather than money — support that never shows up in headline fundraising numbers? — Elections Canada non-monetary contribution fields (intl_elections_canada_contributions). *Harm:* In-kind support is real influence that never shows up in the numbers voters see. · caveat: non-monetary amounts may be mostly zero or null; in-kind valuation methods vary by filer.
- **Who bankrolled the city cycle.** Who funded each NYC municipal cycle, candidate by candidate and office by office — the plain money picture before any argument about what winners later did? — NYC campaign contributions by cycle (st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2001_contribution and siblings). *Harm:* Establishes who was bankrolled before any argument about what they did in office. · medium · caveat: dates parsed permissively; 248 near-duplicate key collisions in 2001 resolved by hash tiebreak may be genuine double entries.
- **The bundler network.** Who are the intermediaries who bundle other people's checks to city candidates — the fixers who convert many small legal donations into one large unregulated relationship? — NYC intermediary fields, 2001 and 2025 cycles (st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2001_contribution, st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2025_contributions). *Harm:* Bundlers broker political access no contribution limit constrains, and they are almost never named in coverage. · caveat: fix: intermediary names are free text and likely null on most rows — measure fill rate and normalize names before sizing the network; 2001-era intermediary reporting may be inconsistent; the 2025 cycle is incomplete.
- **Does matching money work.** How much does NYC's public matching programme actually amplify small local gifts — and for whom? — NYC 2009 contributions match amounts (st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2009_contribution). *Harm:* Public matching is the only counterweight small donors have; its actual reach is testable here. · caveat: match amount may be zero for ineligible donations and the eligibility rules are not in the data.
- **Landlord money in a tenant city.** Which NYC candidates are funded by real-estate-connected donors — in a city where housing cost is the defining harm? — NYC 2013 contributions occupation/employer fields (st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2013_contribution). *Harm:* In a city defined by housing costs, which candidates landlords and developers fund is directly a tenants' issue. · caveat: fix: the real-estate classification rides free-text occupation/employer — publish the keyword scheme and normalize employers first; the classification is a judgment call that must be shown.
- **How donors pay.** Do cash and money-order gifts cluster differently from checks and cards — what does payment method say about who is participating and how? — NYC 2013 contributions payment-method field (st_nyc_cfb_campaign_2013_contribution). *Harm:* Payment method is a proxy for donor circumstance; the pattern shows who participates and how. · medium · caveat: payment-method coding unverified and may be sparsely populated.
- **The awards loophole.** Who receives lobbyist-funded awards and mementos in Texas, is the category growing as others get restricted, and which filers report only awards? — Texas lobby awards schedule (tx_lobby_awards). *Harm:* Awards are a socially acceptable wrapper for the same paid access; spending migrating into a lightly watched category is how disclosure gets routed around. · medium · caveat: only 1,589 rows — rankings may hinge on a few filings.
- **Three decades of Texas access spending.** What is the running price of access to Texas lawmakers — total lobby expenditure by category (food, entertainment, transport, gifts, events, media) from 1993 forward? — Texas lobby cover sheets (tx_lobby_cover). *Harm:* The running price of access to lawmakers, paid by industries whose bills affect residents. · caveat: paper-era totals from 1993 may not be comparable to electronic filings from 2005 on.
- **Disclosure that discloses nothing.** How much of the Texas lobby record is zero-filled reports and bracket-only amounts — a disclosure regime that legally hides the real numbers? — Texas cover sheets plus food/beverage range reporting (tx_lobby_cover, tx_lobby_food_beverage). *Harm:* A disclosure regime that mostly collects zeros and brackets is not disclosing anything. · caveat: zero-vs-null distinction may be a loader artifact; range codes need a lookup that may not be in the mart.
- **Lobbying the rule-writers.** Which Texas state agencies are lobbied directly on rulemaking dockets — influence aimed at the branch with no vote and no hearing — and is it growing? — Texas lobby dockets schedule (tx_lobby_dockets). *Harm:* Agency lobbying shapes rules that never get a legislative vote or public hearing. · medium · caveat: only 1,207 rows and free-text agency names; likely under-reported rather than genuinely rare.
- **The officials most courted.** Which Texas officials are the most frequent recipients of lobbyist-paid meals and gifts, what were the gifts, and is reported gift-giving declining or just better hidden? — Texas entertainment, food/beverage, and gifts schedules (tx_lobby_entertainment, tx_lobby_food_beverage, tx_lobby_gifts). *Harm:* Repeat dinner guests and gift recipients are the officials with the most industry face time. · caveat: fix: recipient names are free text (sometimes organizations, not people) — normalize and resolve before ranking named officials; thin tables (2,836 and 4,084 rows); exact amounts often null in favor of ranges; a reporting decline cannot be separated from a rule change without external context.
- **The rooms where policy is made.** Which restaurants and venues host the most lobbyist-paid meals and entertainment — naming the physical rooms where informal access happens? — Texas food/beverage and entertainment venue fields (tx_lobby_food_beverage, tx_lobby_entertainment). *Harm:* Naming the rooms makes the informal access channel visible to the public. · caveat: venue names unstandardized; address/city fields likely sparse.
- **Card-routed spending.** Does credit-card-flagged lobby spending obscure who ultimately paid for the favor? — Texas entertainment credit-card flag (tx_lobby_entertainment). *Harm:* Card-routed spend can obscure who ultimately paid for the favor. · wild · caveat: flag meaning unverified; may be routine bookkeeping with no signal.
- **Lobby-funded events.** Which interests fund which officials' events in Texas, what kinds of events are the preferred vehicle, and where does the named beneficiary differ from the named recipient — the pass-throughs? — Texas events schedule (tx_lobby_events). *Harm:* Event sponsorship funnels money to officials with almost no public visibility; when the person entertained is not the person benefiting, the pass-through is the story. · caveat: 3,107 rows; beneficiary names are free text and often blank; event-kind codes need a lookup not visible in the mart.
- **Where lobbyists fly officials.** Where does lobbyist-funded travel take Texas officials — the flight routes, the resorts and lodges, the stated purposes, and the private-plane rides that are the highest-value gift of all? — Texas transportation schedule (tx_lobby_transportation). *Harm:* Paid travel to resorts is access money that never looks like a payment, and a private jet ride is a gift no citizen can match. · caveat: city and lodging strings unstandardized; dates may be text; vague free-text purposes make grouping subjective.
- **Everything-lobbyists.** Which lobbyists and firms register across every subject area — selling access itself rather than expertise? — Texas subject matter breadth per filer (tx_lobby_subject_matter). *Harm:* Firms lobbying on everything are selling access itself, not expertise. · medium · caveat: filers register broad subject lists defensively, which inflates breadth.
- **Issues with no opposing lobby.** Which policy areas are dominated by a single interest with no paid counterweight — where the public has no voice at all? — Texas subject matter filer counts (tx_lobby_subject_matter). *Harm:* One-sided issue areas are where the public has no paid voice at all. · wild · caveat: which side a filer is on is not in the data, so dominance is inferred.
- **Campaign money already stamped on the judge record.** Which judges (mostly state-elected) carry a total-campaign-money-received figure on their biography row, how big, and how does the money map across states and court types? — CourtListener judge biographies, FollowTheMoney totals baked onto the judge row (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_JUDGES: ftm_total_received). *Harm:* elected judges raising money from lawyers and parties who then appear before them is the bluntest money-to-robe pipe in American courts. · medium · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; aggregate totals only, no donor-level detail; field population unverified.

### politics-and-government (91)
- **The safety net, district by district.** How many safety-net clinic sites and weekly hours sit in each congressional district — tied to the representative who votes on their funding? — HRSA UDS delivery sites with district and representative fields (fed_hrsa_uds_service_delivery_sites). *Harm:* ties safety-net coverage directly to the members of Congress who vote on it. · caveat: representative names are as-of-ingest and go stale each election.
- **When the polluter is the government.** How many Superfund sites and toxic-release facilities are federal — government-caused contamination where the route to redress is narrowest? — Superfund federal-facility flag plus TRI federal agency fields (fed_epa_superfund_site_boundaries, FED_EPA_TRI_FACILITY). *Harm:* when the polluter is the government, the path to redress is much narrower — and least covered. · caveat: federal-facility flags sparsely populated in both sources.
- **Does government contamination linger longer.** Do federal-facility Superfund sites sit in proposed/unresolved status longer than private ones? — Superfund site boundaries federal flag, status and record dates (fed_epa_superfund_site_boundaries). *Harm:* when the polluter is the government, the cleanup may also be the slowest. · medium · caveat: status dates reflect GIS maintenance in part; small n.
- **Provisional ballots thrown out.** Which jurisdictions reject the most provisional ballots — where do voters show up and still not get counted? — federal election administration survey (fed_eac_eavs). *Harm:* A rejected provisional ballot is a citizen who showed up and was not counted. · caveat: survey columns are opaque question codes needing the codebook; many jurisdictions leave items blank; completeness unverified.
- **Where election administration is thinnest.** Which jurisdictions have the fewest polling places and poll workers per registered voter — where do lines push working people out of voting? — federal election administration survey (fed_eac_eavs). *Harm:* Fewer polling places and thinner staffing mean hours-long lines and more errors for the voters served. · caveat: codebook needed to confirm which coded columns hold registration and polling-place counts; completeness unverified.
- **The mail-ballot attrition funnel.** How many mail ballots die at each stage from transmitted to returned to counted to rejected, per state? — federal election administration survey (fed_eac_eavs). *Harm:* Every step of the funnel is a place a mail voter's ballot silently dies. · caveat: column-to-question mapping needs the codebook; states define stages differently.
- **Election offices that report nothing.** Which election offices leave most of the federal survey blank — which parts of the machinery cannot be audited at all? — federal election administration survey (fed_eac_eavs). *Harm:* An election office that reports nothing cannot be audited by the public it serves. · caveat: blank versus not-applicable is not distinguishable without the codebook.
- **Jurisdictions going dark.** Did the election jurisdictions that stopped answering the federal survey show rising ballot rejection or thinning infrastructure in the cycles before they went dark? — federal election administration survey across waves (fed_eac_eavs). *Harm:* An office that goes dark right as its numbers worsen is removing itself from public audit at the worst moment. · medium · caveat: requires multiple survey waves in the table — verify wave coverage; blank-vs-not-applicable needs the codebook.
- **Districts with no real choice.** How many House districts have only one major-party candidate (on the ballot or even registered), where is it chronic, and is it growing? — MEDSL House returns plus FEC candidate masters (fed_medsl_house_returns, fed_fec_bulk_candidates, FED_FEC_CANDIDATES). *Harm:* Voters in uncontested districts have their representative chosen for them. · caveat: uncontested definition depends on minor-party/write-in treatment; the multi-cycle FEC candidate mart has unnamed positional columns (c1..c15) blocking it until decoded.
- **Safe seats and the disengagement spiral.** Do safe seats cluster with low turnout — does lack of competition itself depress participation, further insulating the incumbent? — MEDSL House returns (fed_medsl_house_returns). *Harm:* Safe seats depress turnout, which further insulates the incumbent from the people. · caveat: total votes is not a turnout rate without a registered-voter denominator this table lacks.
- **Third-party presence and the ballot squeeze.** Where is minor-party and write-in support real and sustained, and where have alternative candidacies disappeared from the ballot entirely? — MEDSL House returns plus FEC candidate master (fed_medsl_house_returns, fed_fec_bulk_candidates). *Harm:* Sustained third-party share signals voters who feel unrepresented by both majors; where third parties cannot even register, voters have exactly two options. · medium · caveat: party labels vary by state and year and need normalising; ballot-access law differences confound comparisons.
- **How states moved their electorates to mail.** Which states shifted their votes to mail and early modes, and when? — MEDSL House returns vote-mode fields (fed_medsl_house_returns). *Harm:* How a state lets people vote determines who can actually vote. · caveat: mode is only reported by some states and years; blanks are unreported, not zero.
- **Fifty years of state margins.** How have state-level presidential margins realigned across five decades — where did the map flip and when? — MEDSL presidential state returns (fed_medsl_president_returns). *Harm:* Realignment determines whose policy priorities get served for a generation. · caveat: two-party margin must be computed from candidate rows; strong third-party years complicate it.
- **Spoiler races.** In which state-years did third-party vote share exceed the winning margin — where did the electoral system misrepresent voter intent? — MEDSL presidential state returns (fed_medsl_president_returns). *Harm:* Races decided by less than the third-party vote are where the system misrepresented voter intent. · caveat: major/minor party classification needs a hand-built list.
- **Turnout growth versus flatline.** Which states expanded participation over decades and which flatlined despite population growth? — MEDSL presidential state returns (fed_medsl_president_returns). *Harm:* Flat participation over decades of population growth means fewer people getting a say. · medium · caveat: no population denominator in the table, so growth confounds population with turnout.
- **The special-election turnout penalty.** How much does participation collapse in special Senate elections versus regular ones in the same state? — MEDSL Senate returns 1976-2024 (fed_medsl_senate_returns). *Harm:* Specials decide six-year terms with a fraction of the electorate present. · caveat: special elections are rare, so per-state comparisons will be thin.
- **States that locked up.** Which states went from competitive Senate races to locked, and when did the contest die? — MEDSL Senate returns (fed_medsl_senate_returns). *Harm:* Locked states mean two senators chosen without a real contest. · caveat: staggered six-year classes make each state's series irregular.
- **Who holds the gavels.** How concentrated is committee power — who chairs what, and how lopsided is party control of each panel? — congressional committee membership (fed_congress_committee_membership). *Harm:* Committee chairs decide which harms get a hearing and which never reach the floor. · caveat: snapshot only — no date column, so this is a current-Congress still frame with no history.
- **Members stretched across too many committees.** Which members carry so many committee and subcommittee assignments that they cannot scrutinize any of them? — congressional committee membership (fed_congress_committee_membership). *Harm:* Members overloaded across many panels cannot scrutinize any of them properly. · medium · caveat: no date column; subcommittee flag semantics unverified.
- **Committees that are the same room.** Which committees share so many members they are effectively one bloc shaping several policy areas at once? — congressional committee membership (fed_congress_committee_membership). *Harm:* Overlapping membership means a single bloc can shape several policy areas at once. · wild · caveat: snapshot only; may include stale or duplicated assignments.
- **Does Congress look like the country.** How has the composition of Congress — gender, party, and age — tracked or diverged from the people it governs across two centuries? — congress-legislators reference (fed_congress_legislators). *Harm:* An institution that looks and ages nothing like its electorate legislates on futures it will not live in. · caveat: term dates and birthday are not date-cast in the model and need parsing; historical values may be partial.
- **Incumbency entrenchment and perennial candidates.** How entrenched is incumbency — how long do members hold seats, how fast do challengers vanish after one cycle, and who are the perennial repeat-runners who never win? — congress-legislators plus FEC candidate masters (fed_congress_legislators, fed_fec_bulk_candidates, FED_FEC_CANDIDATES). *Harm:* When challengers vanish and incumbents never do, constituents cannot dislodge a member who stops representing them. · caveat: incumbent-status codes need decoding; candidate-id stability across cycles assumed; the multi-cycle FEC mart has unnamed columns.
- **Delegation churn and political families.** Which states recycle the same members and families for generations, and which churn their delegations? — congress-legislators reference (fed_congress_legislators). *Harm:* Low-churn states concentrate power in a handful of political families for generations. · medium · caveat: requires clean term dates; district field is text and may include at-large codes.
- **Which industries staff which regulators.** Which industries supply the personnel of which federal agencies, and which agencies are most captured by the sector they police? — Revolving Door Project personnel map (fed_revolvingdoor_project). *Harm:* Regulators staffed by the industry they police do not protect the people that industry harms. · caveat: only 406 rows, snapshot grain, one administration; capture flags derived from free-text position matching.
- **Appointees with many industry ties.** Which appointees carry the widest webs of distinct industry connections into government? — Revolving Door Project (fed_revolvingdoor_project). *Harm:* Appointees with many industry ties have many conflicts across the areas they oversee. · caveat: derived sector counts over a messy wide layout; 406 rows.
- **The polarization fan and the vanishing middle.** How far have the parties' ideology medians diverged since 1789, and when did the moderate middle empty out? — Voteview member ideology (fed_voteview_members). *Harm:* A polarized Congress cannot pass the bills that address slow-moving harms. · caveat: ideology score is text-typed in the model and needs casting; party codes need a lookup.
- **The second dimension's return.** When did a second axis of division (historically race and region) open and close in congressional voting? — Voteview member ideology (fed_voteview_members). *Harm:* The second dimension historically tracked civil-rights splits — the axis on which people's rights were traded. · medium · caveat: dim2 is noisy in modern congresses; interpretation is contested.
- **Members who drift.** Which members moved ideologically between their first and last congress, and in which direction? — Voteview member ideology (fed_voteview_members). *Harm:* Members who drift after election are the ones constituents cannot hold to their pitch. · caveat: DW-NOMINATE constrains drift by construction, so movement may be understated.
- **Pattern-breaking votes.** Which members and which specific votes defy the ideology model — where are the remaining swing votes and conscience breaks? — Voteview members plus roll-call probability fields (fed_voteview_members, fed_voteview_rollcalls). *Harm:* Unpredictable members are the last remaining swing votes for anything that helps people. · wild · caveat: error counts and probabilities are model artifacts, not behavior; a roll-call vote-positions mart on the platform has a standing defect vs its canonical twin — confirm whether this table is affected before building claims.
- **How close are the votes.** Does Congress decide by landslide or by one vote — what is the distribution of margins, and is it changing? — Voteview roll-call metadata (fed_voteview_rollcall_meta). *Harm:* One-vote margins mean a single member's choice decided a policy affecting millions. · caveat: date field is untyped; use congress/session ordering if parsing fails.
- **Procedure crowding out substance.** What share of roll calls are procedural rather than substantive, and is the chamber increasingly voting on process instead of people's problems? — Voteview roll-call metadata (fed_voteview_rollcall_meta). *Harm:* A chamber voting mostly on procedure is a chamber not voting on people's problems. · caveat: requires classifying free-text vote questions; no stored procedural flag.
- **The voting volume decline.** Is Congress recording fewer and fewer votes per session over the long run? — Voteview roll-call metadata (fed_voteview_rollcall_meta). *Harm:* Fewer recorded votes means fewer moments a constituent can hold a member accountable. · medium · caveat: 3,364 rows suggests a subset of congresses, not the full 1789-present roll-call set.
- **The most-fought bills.** Which bills drew the most near-tied roll calls — where did Congress fight hardest? — Voteview roll-call metadata (fed_voteview_rollcall_meta). *Harm:* The most-contested bills are usually the ones redistributing something real. · medium · caveat: bill-number formatting may not join cleanly to the bill-status table.
- **Who skips the votes.** Which members miss the most votes per congress, leaving their districts unrepresented? — Voteview roll-call votes matrix (fed_voteview_rollcalls). *Harm:* A member who does not show up leaves their district unrepresented on every one of those votes. · caveat: cast-code semantics (absent vs not-in-office) can invert the chart; a roll-call vote-positions mart has a standing defect vs its canonical twin — verify before building claims.
