- **The factions party labels hide.** Which members actually vote together — what are the real voting blocs beneath the party labels? — Voteview roll-call votes matrix (fed_voteview_rollcalls). *Harm:* Hidden voting blocs are the real units deciding which harms get addressed. · caveat: 945k rows require pre-aggregation; roll-call positions mart standing-defect stamp applies.
- **Defectors and party unity.** Which members defect from their party line, how often, and on what? — Voteview roll-call votes matrix (fed_voteview_rollcalls). *Harm:* Defectors are the members whose constituents actually pull them off the party line. · caveat: party majority position requires joining the roll-call metadata sibling; standing-defect stamp applies.
- **The moment members back away.** When do members withdraw cosponsorships — the rare public act of backing off a bill — and what clusters around those moments? — congressional bill cosponsors (fed_govinfo_bill_cosponsors). *Harm:* Withdrawals mark the moment lobbying or backlash flipped a member off a bill. · caveat: withdrawal dates exist only for withdrawals, so n is small and may be very sparse.
- **Does bipartisanship exist on paper.** Do cross-party cosponsorship ties actually exist, and are they collapsing over time? — congressional bill cosponsors (fed_govinfo_bill_cosponsors). *Harm:* When cross-party ties collapse, bills that would help people stop moving entirely. · caveat: 367k rows require aggregation to member-pair counts before rendering.
- **Early signers versus safe signers.** Who commits to bills at introduction and who only signs late once it is safe? — congressional bill cosponsors (fed_govinfo_bill_cosponsors). *Harm:* Members who only sign safe bills late are not spending capital on their constituents. · medium · caveat: introduction date lives in the sibling bill-status table, so strictly this needs that second table.
- **Signature machines.** Which members cosponsor everything and which barely sign — and does volume correlate with anything actually passing? — congressional bill cosponsors (fed_govinfo_bill_cosponsors). *Harm:* High cosponsor counts with no passed bills is a member performing work rather than doing it. · medium · caveat: does not distinguish serious legislating from bulk signing.
- **The lawmaking funnel and its graveyard.** How tiny is the enacted slice of everything introduced, and which bill types and congresses have the biggest dead-on-arrival share (a single action, then nothing)? — congressional bill status (fed_govinfo_billstatus). *Harm:* Bills that never get a second action are issues the leadership decided nobody needed to hear about. · caveat: law fields are populated only for enacted bills — nulls mean not-enacted, not missing; action-count semantics unverified.
- **High-volume, zero-result sponsors.** Which members introduce bills constantly and never pass anything? — congressional bill status (fed_govinfo_billstatus). *Harm:* Members who introduce constantly and pass nothing are performing representation, not delivering it. · caveat: fair cross-congress comparison needs majority/minority status, which is not in this table.
- **Is lawmaking slowing down.** Is the time from introduction to enactment stretching over the decades? — congressional bill status (fed_govinfo_billstatus). *Harm:* Slower lawmaking means urgent harms wait longer for any legal response. · medium · caveat: latest-action date is not the enactment date for every bill; approximation only.
- **Does support predict passage.** Does broad cosponsorship actually predict a bill becoming law, or is public support decoration? — congressional bill status (fed_govinfo_billstatus). *Harm:* If cosponsorship does not predict passage, public support signals are theatre. · caveat: the latest-action-text column is number-cast in the model and will be nulled — avoid relying on it.
- **Candidates who don't live there.** How many candidates' mailing addresses sit outside the state or district they seek to represent? — FEC candidate master address fields (fed_fec_bulk_candidates). *Harm:* Candidates who do not live where they would govern are less accountable to the people they represent. · medium · caveat: mailing address is often a campaign office or PO box, so mismatches include false positives.
- **What vanished from public DOJ pages.** Which documents were linked on DOJ public listing pages at one capture and gone at the next — what did the public record quietly lose? — DOJ document-library manifest plus Wayback replays of the listing and deep pages (fed_doj_epstein_library, xc_wayback_replay_doj_listing, xc_wayback_replay_doj_deep_pages). *Harm:* Documents that vanish from a public library are documents the public was meant to see and now cannot. · caveat: absence at a later capture may mean pagination or a crawl gap rather than removal; needs multiple snapshots to diff at all.
- **Disclosure by news cycle.** Do document releases arrive in bursts around news events rather than on a legal schedule? — DOJ document-library manifest (fed_doj_epstein_library). *Harm:* Release timing reveals whether disclosure is driven by law or by news-cycle management. · medium · caveat: 777 links across 12 pages; snapshot cadence unverified.
- **Silent edits, relabels, and archive blind spots.** How often are public records pages silently edited or documents relabeled, and where are the archive coverage gaps in which changes could pass unobserved? — Wayback replays of DOJ pages plus the library manifest (xc_wayback_replay_doj_listing, xc_wayback_replay_doj_deep_pages, fed_doj_epstein_library). *Harm:* Silent edits to public records pages are undocumented changes to the public record; archive gaps are exactly where a change can be made unobserved. · caveat: digest changes can be boilerplate; whitespace noise creates false label variants; gaps reflect crawler behavior, not necessarily DOJ action.
- **Arms-race trajectories.** Which countries' military spending is accelerating, which rivalries are racing, and which single states dominate their region? — OWID military spending, SIPRI mirror (intl_owid_milspend). *Harm:* Money spent on arms is money not spent on the health and housing of the same population. · caveat: regional aggregate rows must be filtered out or they dominate; Taiwan presence flagged uncertain in source notes.
- **Guns versus everything else.** When a country's military spending rises, what happens to its social and health spending over the same window? — OWID military spending (intl_owid_milspend). *Harm:* When defense budgets rise and clinics close, the tradeoff has a body count. · medium · caveat: the social-spending side is not in this table — strictly this needs a second source to become answerable.
- **Who writes European law.** Which EU institutions author the rules that bind citizens, what stays in force for decades, and which texts are not published in every citizen's language? — EU law corpus probe (intl_eurlex_cellar). *Harm:* Rules written by unelected bodies still bind citizens who never voted on them; a citizen who cannot read a binding rule cannot contest it. · wild · caveat: only 53 rows — an API probe, not a corpus; country column is a broken numeric cast.
- **Europol's warning cadence.** How regularly do Europol threat assessments appear, in which languages, and how long are the gaps when the public flies blind? — EU organized-crime assessment register (intl_eu_socta_europol). *Harm:* Long gaps between assessments mean the public flies blind on organized crime; publics who cannot read the assessment are excluded from the debate about their own safety. · wild · caveat: only 26 rows and no substantive content columns — a document register, not data; two ideas is the honest ceiling.
- **A missile program's learning curve.** How did North Korea's test cadence, failure rate, range/apogee envelopes, and glide-vehicle entries evolve across four decades — and how much of that record rests on unconfirmed reporting? — CNS DPRK missile test database plus its flight-test mirror (intl_nti_cns_dprk_missile_tests, xc_nagix_dprk_missile_tests). *Harm:* A maturing program changes the threat calculus for civilians across the region; policy built on unverified test claims can escalate against a phantom. · medium · caveat: only 303 curated rows; outcome/apogee/distance are free text including "Unknown"; the mirror is derived, not primary.
- **Launch sites, bearings, landings.** Which facilities fire what, along which corridors, landing where — and which neighboring populations sit under the trajectories and impact zones? — CNS DPRK facility coordinates plus mirror bearings/landing points (intl_nti_cns_dprk_missile_tests, xc_nagix_dprk_missile_tests). *Harm:* Bearings point at the populations that live under the trajectory; fishing fleets and coastal communities sit inside impact zones. · medium · caveat: facility/missile fields in the mirror are slug codes needing a lookup that may not be landed; landing column may be nested text, not clean coordinates.
- **The arsenal curve.** How have estimated nuclear stockpiles moved since 1945, and in what sequence did each state join the club? — OWID estimated nuclear warhead stockpiles (xc_owid_nuclear_warheads). *Harm:* Every warhead on the curve is a standing threat to civilian populations; each new entrant widens the set of people living under nuclear risk. · medium · caveat: estimates, not counts; threshold states absent by construction; first non-zero year is not a first test date.
- **Sabotage arriving in Europe.** How has Russian activity against Europe shifted from information operations to physical sabotage of rail, water, and power — and which countries absorb it? — Leiden Russian operations dataset (intl_leiden_russian_ops_europe). *Harm:* Sabotage of rail, water, and power hits ordinary civilians, not the states being pressured. · medium · caveat: only 153 curated incidents — a research dataset with selection bias baked in; locations are free text.
- **Disposable agents.** Is the pattern shifting toward locally recruited proxies who go to prison while the sponsors never appear? — Leiden Russian operations dataset (intl_leiden_russian_ops_europe). *Harm:* Locally recruited proxies are the people who go to prison while the sponsors never appear. · caveat: the flag is a coder judgement in a 153-row curated set — not a census.
- **Who kills civilians, by name.** Which named armed actors — including governments — kill the most unarmed people, and which conflicts are fought mainly against civilians rather than combatants? — UCDP georeferenced event dataset (intl_ucdp_ged). *Harm:* Names the specific armed actors responsible for killing civilians; conflicts that kill mostly civilians are wars aimed at ordinary people. · caveat: best/low/high estimate spread is wide; actor ids change across versions; naming state actors needs careful framing.
- **Thirty-five years of violence, mapped.** Where has every organized-violence event since 1989 landed — the communities living inside a war? — UCDP georeferenced event dataset (intl_ucdp_ged). *Harm:* Every dot is people killed at a known place; the clusters are communities living inside a war. · caveat: location precision varies widely — some points are a country centroid, not a village.
- **The uncounted dead.** Where does the world's record of violent death rest on a single report, wide guesswork bands, or no count at all — the countries and regions that do not count their dead? — UCDP source counts and estimate spreads plus OWID homicide coverage gaps (intl_ucdp_ged, xc_owid_homicide). *Harm:* Under-sourced regions are where atrocities go unrecorded and therefore unpunished; countries that do not count homicides cannot be held to account for them. · caveat: low source counts may mean danger or censorship rather than less violence; estimate columns not numeric-cast in the model; extract gaps may reflect the extract.
- **Terrorism's actual burden.** Where do terrorism deaths actually concentrate — overwhelmingly outside the countries that dominate the terrorism debate? — OWID terrorism deaths (xc_owid_terrorism_deaths). *Harm:* The people killed by terrorism are mostly not the people whose governments frame the terrorism debate. · caveat: fatalities column not numeric-cast; definitions of terrorism vary by source.
- **Ecuador's captured public buyers.** Which Ecuadorian public buyers send most of their contract value to a single favored supplier? — Ecuador SERCOP procurement OCDS (intl_ec_sercop). *Harm:* captured procurement in health and school feeding means children and patients get whatever the favored vendor delivers. · caveat: OCDS records may be partial per contracting process; currency mixing needs handling.
- **The red flags of rigged procurement.** Where does the final contract price drift from what was tendered, how much value moves through direct and emergency awards, and which contracts are signed impossibly fast after publication? — Ecuador SERCOP tender/award/contract values, methods and dates (intl_ec_sercop). *Harm:* contracts signed days after publication were decided before the public ever saw them; emergency rules used routinely turn oversight off permanently. · caveat: values may mix currencies per row; method taxonomies change across 2015-present; date completeness varies by publisher stage.
- **Which countries are backsliding on freedom.** Which countries are losing freedom fastest, is the decline regionally contagious, and which flip from free to not-free status? — Freedom House Freedom in the World (intl_freedomhouse). *Harm:* populations in fast-declining countries are losing rights in real time. · caveat: the country-name column is number-cast and likely nulled — identity must come from the code column; status comparable only back to 2013.
- **Which freedom breaks first.** In backsliding countries, which pillar falls first — elections, media, or courts? — Freedom House sub-indicator scores A-G (intl_freedomhouse). *Harm:* knowing which pillar falls first tells defenders where to hold before the collapse. · caveat: sub-indicator letters need the codebook to mean anything.
- **Elections kept, liberties gutted.** Which countries maintain political-rights scores while civil-liberties scores collapse — the regimes hardest for outsiders to see? — Freedom House PR vs CL ratings by edition (intl_freedomhouse). *Harm:* countries holding elections while crushing speech escape the scrutiny reserved for open dictatorships. · caveat: ratings are ordinal 1-7 scales; treating them as continuous is a simplification.
- **Holes and lateness in official European statistics.** Where do official statistical series have missing, flagged, provisional, or chronically late observations — the gaps citizens cannot hold government to? — Italy ISTAT API and Eurostat SDMX API (intl_it_istat, intl_eurostat). *Harm:* gaps in official statistics are gaps in the evidence citizens can hold government to; decisions get made on provisional numbers later quietly revised. · medium · caveat: both loads are API samples, not full corpora — gap patterns may reflect the crawl, not the publisher; SDMX codes need legends.
- **Statistics that vanish in inconvenient years.** Which Egyptian official indicators quietly stop being published, and in which politically loaded years? — Egypt CAPMAS data portal (intl_eg_capmas). *Harm:* statistics that vanish in politically inconvenient years hide who is getting worse off. · caveat: 150-row sample — the gap pattern may reflect the crawl rather than real publication gaps; country column number-cast.
- **Blocs, drift, and isolation at the UN.** Which voting blocs formed and collapsed at the UN General Assembly over 70 years, which states drifted from which sponsors, and who is most isolated now? — UNGA voting data, Voeten dyads, 1.8M dyad-years (intl_voeten_unga_votes). *Harm:* voting blocs decide which populations get UN protection; isolation predicts sanctions whose cost lands on civilians. · caveat: dyadic grain requires dedup per country-year; Correlates-of-War codes need a crosswalk to be readable.
- **Corruption trajectories and collapses.** Which countries' corruption-perception scores cleaned up or rotted over time, which moved sharpest, and is corruption regionally contagious? — OWID Corruption Perceptions Index (xc_owid_cpi). *Harm:* corruption is a tax paid disproportionately by people who cannot afford to bribe. · caveat: CPI is a perceptions index, not measured corruption; methodology breaks make long-run comparison questionable.
- **Severe events nobody covers.** Which severe world events get near-zero media coverage or are known through a single outlet — the harms nobody will be held accountable for? — GDELT 2.0 global events (intl_gdelt). *Harm:* severe events with near-zero coverage are the ones most easily denied or disappeared. · medium · caveat: the landed table is a 1,015-row slice of one 15-minute file, not the real GDELT corpus — unusable until reloaded; severity scale is a proxy.
- **Who acts on whom.** Which states and organizations repeatedly act against which populations, in cooperation or conflict? — GDELT actor-pair events (intl_gdelt). *Harm:* maps which actors repeatedly coerce which populations. · medium · caveat: tiny sample slice; actor country-code columns are number-cast over alpha codes and will null out entirely.
- **How tiny the searchable federal archive is.** How little of the federal record is online-searchable at NARA, which record groups have nothing at all, and which decades are simply absent? — NARA Access to Archival Databases catalog (fed_nara_aad). *Harm:* records the public cannot search are records the public cannot use to hold anyone accountable. · medium · caveat: 18 rows — a catalog-of-datasets view only.
- **The tribal land base and its stale map.** How much tribal land remains by state, how long since the federal government last maintained each layer of the official tribal map, and is fragmentation (checkerboarding) even measurable? — BIA tribal geospatial portal, 102 rows (fed_bia_tribal_geo). *Harm:* stale official boundaries mean tribes get miscounted in every federal program keyed to geography; fragmented land is unfarmable, unfinanceable, unpoliceable. · medium · caveat: 102 rows is likely a layer catalog, not parcel geometry — fragmentation is unanswerable until real geometry lands.
- **Regions missing from national open-data portals.** Which provinces, states, and municipalities are absent or only coarsely covered in their national open-data portals (Argentina, Germany, Spain, France)? — country portal catalogs (intl_ar_datosgob, intl_de_govdata, intl_es_datosgob, intl_fr_data_gouv). *Harm:* provinces with no published data are provinces where no one can prove anything about local spending; national-only publication makes local harm invisible. · caveat: all are portal samples (1k-5k rows); Spain's mart is explicitly defective from a loader parse bug; spatial fields are packed strings.
- **Agencies that quietly stopped publishing.** Which government departments dumped data once and never updated it — publishing rhythm as an audit of whether transparency is alive or dead? — portal metadata dates by organisation (intl_ar_datosgob, intl_ca_open_canada, intl_gr_datagov). *Harm:* departments that stopped publishing are departments whose current conduct is unauditable. · caveat: portal samples only; metadata dates are often auto-touched by portal migrations; date fields untyped text.
- **Update promises versus reality.** Which agencies declare monthly or daily update frequencies and deliver yearly or nothing — and how long do agencies sit on data before releasing it? — portal frequency fields vs actual gaps (intl_ca_open_canada, intl_ch_opendataswiss, intl_fr_data_gouv, intl_br_dados_gov). *Harm:* an agency claiming daily updates and delivering none is publishing a false claim about its own transparency; a two-year lag means findings describe a world that moved on. · caveat: frequency vocabularies need decoding into intervals; all samples; Brazil is a 10-row stub.
- **Open-data theatre: PDFs posing as data.** How much of each country's open data is scanned PDFs and images rather than machine-readable files — compliance theatre that keeps numbers out of reach? — portal resource format mixes (intl_cl_datosgob, intl_gr_datagov). *Harm:* publishing a scanned PDF and calling it open data keeps the numbers out of everyone's reach. · caveat: format fields are packed multi-value strings; samples only.
- **Legally mandated datasets that are missing.** Which EU-mandated high-value datasets have Germany and Greece actually published, by state and theme — and which legal transparency duties go unmet? — portal high-value-dataset flags (intl_de_govdata, intl_gr_datagov). *Harm:* missing high-value datasets are a legal transparency duty being ignored, invisible to the public without this chart. · caveat: is_hvd fill rates unverified; 5,000-row samples of much larger portals.
- **The silent majority of agencies.** How concentrated is portal publishing in a few institutions, with hundreds of public bodies publishing nothing at all? — portal publisher concentration (intl_cl_datosgob, intl_gr_datagov). *Harm:* institutions publishing nothing are the ones whose conduct no citizen can examine. · caveat: samples with known duplicate dataset ids (Greece).
- **Licences that block reuse of public data.** How much of the public record carries restrictive, bespoke, or private-flagged terms that stop citizens republishing what their taxes produced? — portal license fields and private flags (intl_ar_datosgob, intl_de_govdata, intl_ch_opendataswiss). *Harm:* a restrictive licence on public data means journalists and citizens cannot legally republish it; a portal listing datasets it will not release is a catalogue of what the public is denied. · medium · caveat: licence strings are inconsistent free text; private-flag fill unverified.
- **Published but unread, advertised but unobtainable.** Which agencies publish heavily but are never read, which single datasets carry all the attention, and where do high views meet near-zero downloads or dead links? — portal usage metrics and maintainer reachability (intl_fr_data_gouv, intl_gh_datagovgh, intl_ch_opendataswiss). *Harm:* publication volume without readership is transparency that satisfies a rule while informing nobody; with no reachable maintainer, an error has nowhere to be reported. · medium · caveat: counts are untyped text; Ghana is a 10-row stub; confirming dead links needs live fetching.
- **Language exclusion in official portals.** How much of Canada's official data record exists in English only, cutting French-only speakers out of holding their government to account? — Canada portal English vs French completeness (intl_ca_open_canada). *Harm:* French-only speakers cut out of the data record are cut out of accountability. · medium · caveat: 500-row sample; blank-vs-placeholder French needs a distinct-value check, not a null check.
- **The DOJ Epstein library under the microscope.** Was the DOJ's Epstein document library quietly edited, shrunk, or restricted — attested content changes, shrinking listing pages, dead URLs, and public lockout windows? — Wayback CDX census of the DOJ Epstein library, 1.54M captures, Nov 2025 onward (xc_wayback_doj_epstein). *Harm:* quiet edits and removals from a government document library are the public record being changed without notice. · caveat: digest and byte-length changes can come from page furniture — a step down is a lead, not a proof; capture density varies, so absence of captures is not absence of the page.
- **Comment windows too short to use.** Which agencies routinely give the public the least time to comment on rules, against the baseline of who regulates at all? — Federal Register documents (fed_federal_register_documents). *Harm:* a 15-day comment window on a complex rule silences everyone without a paid lobbyist. · caveat: Federal Register is only ~9% loaded — agency-level claims unreliable until the full corpus lands; null close dates may be the interesting cases.
- **Effective before anyone can react.** Which long, complex rules take effect almost immediately on publication, giving affected people no time to comply or challenge? — Federal Register days-until-effective vs page length (fed_federal_register_documents). *Harm:* rules effective on publication give affected people no time to comply or challenge. · caveat: Federal Register ~9% loaded; effective dates null for notices — filter to rules.
- **How rules dodge scrutiny.** Which agencies avoid the significant-rule label that triggers extra review, and do unpopular rules cluster in dead news windows like Friday afternoons and holidays? — Federal Register significance flags and publication timing (fed_federal_register_documents). *Harm:* rules that dodge the significant label dodge cost-benefit review of who they hurt; burying a rule in a dead window avoids the people it affects. · medium · caveat: Federal Register ~9% loaded; significance-flag semantics unverified; fixed publication schedule may flatten day-of-week signals.
- **The legalization wave, and who stayed criminalized.** How did cannabis legalization spread state by state, and who kept getting arrested in late-adopting states for what was legal next door? — US state cannabis policy bundles (st_cannabis_policy_bundles). *Harm:* residents in late-adopting states kept getting arrested for what was legal next door. · caveat: approval and implementation columns must not be conflated; one text column is number-cast and likely nulled.
- **Approved but unimplemented.** Where did years pass between a cannabis law passing and taking effect — patients still unable to legally get medicine — and which states forced it by ballot over legislative refusal? — cannabis policy bundles, approval vs implementation years (st_cannabis_policy_bundles). *Harm:* a law approved but unimplemented means patients still cannot legally get medicine. · caveat: first-true-year per state must be derived; scale columns unexplained without the codebook.
- **Party-line breakers, ranked.** Defection rate from party-line voting per member per congress, run identically across every member and era — who actually crosses, on what topics, and is defection dying? — Voteview members and roll-calls (fed_voteview_members, fed_voteview_rollcalls). *Harm:* voters told their representative is independent when the roll-call record says otherwise. · medium · caveat: the roll-call vote-positions mart has a standing defect (disagrees with its canonical twin) — do not build claims on it until rebuilt.
- **How judges get their seats.** How long does nomination-to-confirmation take, how have vote margins and voice votes changed, and how common are recess appointments and failed nominations — by era, party control, and court level? — CourtListener judicial positions/appointments, 51,290 rows (JUSTICE.FED_COURTLISTENER_POSITIONS). *Harm:* a slowing, polarized confirmation pipeline leaves seats empty and cases waiting — real people's disputes stall for years. · caveat: CourtListener family is not in Ripple's entity map — internal IDs are publisher-verified only; vote-percent columns are ~100% null (checked 2026-08-11), raw yes/no tally population unverified.

### federal-money (44)
- **Where False Claims money leaks.** Which fraud types drain which federal agencies, and do some districts systematically settle cheap? — DOJ False Claims Act settlements (fed_doj_fca_settlements). *Harm:* Money stolen from Medicare or defense contracts is money not spent on the patients and troops it was for. · medium · caveat: only 12 rows in the mart — far below real DOJ volume; unusable until re-ingested.
- **The whistleblower's cut.** What portion of recovered fraud goes to the person who risked their job to report it? — DOJ False Claims Act settlements (fed_doj_fca_settlements). *Harm:* Whistleblowers who lose careers over reporting fraud recover a fraction of what they saved taxpayers. · medium · caveat: 12-row mart; relator share may be null for most cases.
- **The national debt: level, composition, rhythm.** What has total federal debt done across the full record — growth by fiscal year, the public vs intragovernmental split, and the predictable within-year borrowing rhythm? — Treasury debt outstanding and debt to the penny (fed_treasury_debt_outstanding, fed_treasury_debt_to_penny). *Harm:* the denominator behind every fiscal argument aimed at cutting programs people depend on; intragovernmental holdings are largely the trust funds benefits ride on. · medium · caveat: debt-outstanding table has only 237 rows (grain unstated); fiscal-year fields untyped; no per-capita or GDP denominator in-table.
- **Debt-ceiling standoffs in the daily data.** Where does the daily debt series flatline against a ceiling before jumping — the standoffs, made visible as plateaus? — Treasury debt to the penny (fed_treasury_debt_to_penny). *Harm:* debt-ceiling standoffs delay payments people are counting on. · caveat: identifying a plateau as a standoff requires external context not in the table.
- **The daily federal cash pulse.** What does daily money into the Treasury look like — which categories dominate, and where are the tax-deadline spikes and the quiet troughs when payments to those least able to wait get stalled? — Treasury Daily Treasury Statement deposits (fed_treasury_dts_deposits). *Harm:* the daily cash position determines whether benefit payments go out on time in a shutdown. · medium · caveat: row count is exactly 10,000 — the signature of a loader page cap; series likely truncated; FYTD amounts are cumulative and double-count if summed naively.
- **Accounting lines that appear and vanish.** Which Treasury transaction categories quietly appear or disappear over time — the accounting lines through which spending changes escape the public summary? — Treasury DTS deposit categories over months (fed_treasury_dts_deposits). *Harm:* accounting lines that quietly disappear are how spending changes escape the public summary. · wild · caveat: category renames will look like disappearances; the 10,000-row cap will manufacture false gaps at the edges.
- **Who funds the state.** How heavily does federal revenue lean on individual income and payroll taxes versus corporate taxes, how has the mix shifted, and where does the official category hierarchy stop splitting? — Treasury Monthly Treasury Statement receipts (fed_treasury_mts_receipts). *Harm:* the split between what workers pay and what corporations pay is the clearest picture of who funds the state. · caveat: rows mix parent and child classification levels — summing without respecting hierarchy double-counts; FYTD comparisons only valid at matched month positions.
- **Refunds clawing back the gross.** In which tax categories do refunds claw back most of the gross receipts — who does the tax code hand money back to? — Treasury MTS gross receipts vs refunds (fed_treasury_mts_receipts). *Harm:* large refund flows in one category next to none in another shows who the tax code favors. · caveat: refund amounts may be sign-flipped or zero-filled for most classifications.
- **Cost of federal borrowing by security type.** How has the average interest rate on each class of federal debt moved — bills vs notes vs savings bonds — and do small savers' instruments systematically earn less than institutions' paper? — Treasury average interest rates (fed_treasury_avg_interest_rates). *Harm:* rising debt service crowds out budget lines that fund public services; small savers may systematically earn less. · medium · caveat: security descriptions need careful grouping; no inflation series for real returns; ragged series start dates.
- **Set-aside designations that carry no money.** Across every socioeconomic contracting flag — veteran-owned, women-owned, HUBZone, tribal, minority-owned — which designations actually carry dollars and which are decorative? — USAspending bulk award archive flag columns (fed_usaspending_bulk). *Harm:* designations that carry no dollars are a promise of inclusion the government never kept. · caveat: explicitly a 50,000-row capped sample — shape only, never totals; parent USASpending corpus capped at exactly 20M rows.
- **Money banked far from where the work happens.** How often do recipient state and place-of-performance state diverge — money nominally spent in poor states actually banked in a few rich ones? — USAspending recipient vs place-of-performance states (fed_usaspending_bulk, fed_usaspending_contracts). *Harm:* a community hosting the work but not the payroll gets the disruption without the income. · caveat: 50k-row sample on one mart, single-year window on the other; place of performance is coarse for services; 20M-row cap on the full table.
- **Work started before the price was agreed.** How often do agencies book undefinitized contract actions — work begun before terms were set, locking in cost overruns on the public tab? — USAspending undefinitized-action flag (fed_usaspending_bulk). *Harm:* starting work before agreeing a price is how cost overruns get locked in. · medium · caveat: sample only; flag is code-based and may need decoding; USASpending 20M cap.
- **Foreign-owned federal vendors.** How much federal work — including defense — sits with vendors flagged foreign-owned, by agency and dollars? — USASpending curated prime contracts foreign-owned flag (fed_usaspending_contracts). *Harm:* accountability gets harder to enforce the further the owner sits from US courts. · medium · caveat: single-year window (FY2025); foreign_owned is self-reported; USASpending 20M cap.
- **The parent-company rollup: true contractor concentration.** When subsidiaries are collapsed into their parent UEI, how concentrated is federal contracting really — the conglomerates hidden behind hundreds of subsidiary names? — USASpending recipient vs parent UEI (fed_usaspending_contracts). *Harm:* subsidiary sprawl is how a handful of conglomerates look like a competitive market. · caveat: parent-UEI completeness unverified — blanks silently understate concentration; USASpending capped at exactly 20M rows and the entity spine reads a smaller copy.
- **Executive pay inside federal vendors.** How large is disclosed top-officer pay at vendors whose revenue is substantially federal, plotted against contract size? — USASpending highly-compensated-officer fields (fed_usaspending_contracts, FED_USASPENDING_CONTRACTS_FULL). *Harm:* public money paying outsized private executive salaries while the delivered service is thin. · medium · caveat: exec comp only reported above thresholds — coverage partial and self-reported; USASpending 20M cap.
- **Competition disappearing from federal contracts.** What share of contract dollars is awarded without full-and-open competition per agency since FY2007, and how big is the pile of large contracts where exactly one bid was received? — USASpending competition fields and offers-received (FED_USASPENDING_CONTRACTS_FULL). *Harm:* noncompetitive contracting means the public overpays and no one can point to the cheaper bid that lost. · caveat: number_of_offers_received is often 1 by reporting convention, not reality — verify before claiming capture; USASpending capped at exactly 20M rows.
- **Set-asides feeding giants.** How much small-business and disadvantaged set-aside money flows to subsidiaries of very large parents? — USASpending set-aside type vs recipient parent (FED_USASPENDING_CONTRACTS_FULL). *Harm:* set-asides exist to help genuinely small firms; capture by giants takes that ladder away. · caveat: parent UEI blank on many rows; parent-size rollup is an in-source aggregation; USASpending 20M cap.
- **Contracts that balloon past what was bought.** Which awards grew far beyond their base-and-exercised value — value creep absorbing budget appropriated for something else? — USASpending award value fields (FED_USASPENDING_CONTRACTS_FULL). *Harm:* ballooning contracts absorb budget that was appropriated for something people needed. · caveat: transaction grain repeats values — take the latest modification per award key; USASpending 20M cap.
- **Closed subcontractor rings.** Do the same firms subcontract to each other across awards in closed loops that keep new and local firms permanently outside? — USAspending sub-award network (fed_usaspending_subawards). *Harm:* closed contracting rings keep new and local firms permanently outside. · wild · caveat: 5,000-row API slice; prime identity may only exist inside the raw JSON blob — extract it and re-ingest the full FSRS corpus before trusting.
- **Obligated but never outlaid.** Which agencies and programs announce far more than they spend — obligations that never become outlays, and multi-year awards funded at a trickle? — USASpending obligation vs outlay fields (fed_us_usaspending_api, FED_USASPENDING_ASSISTANCE_FULL). *Harm:* announced-but-unspent money is a press release the intended recipients never see. · caveat: API mart is a 300-row sample; outlay fields repeat per transaction and must be deduped by award key; assistance table is 20M-row transaction grain.
- **The counties assistance never reaches.** Mapped by county of performance across FY2007-FY2026, which counties receive almost no federal assistance decade after decade? — USASpending federal assistance by county FIPS (FED_USASPENDING_ASSISTANCE_FULL). *Harm:* counties that never appear on the assistance map are the ones with the worst health and housing outcomes. · caveat: 20M-row transaction grain — modifications double-count without care; FIPS may be text with lost leading zeros.
- **Loans for the poor, grants for the rich.** By place, which communities get assistance as grants they keep versus loans they must repay? — USASpending assistance type and loan face value (FED_USASPENDING_ASSISTANCE_FULL). *Harm:* communities handed debt instead of grants carry a repayment burden richer places never take on. · caveat: loan face value and obligation are different scales — the ratio needs explicit definition; 20M-row grain.
- **COVID and IIJA money trails.** Did once-in-a-generation pandemic and infrastructure money actually reach the places that needed it most — traced from supplemental source through agency and program to place? — USASpending supplemental funding columns (FED_USASPENDING_ASSISTANCE_FULL). *Harm:* shows whether historic relief money reached the places that needed it most. · caveat: supplemental columns are award-level and may be mostly null; 20M-row aggregation is heavy.
- **The maze of federal accounts.** How many separate pots of money does each agency run, and how deep is the account tree before you reach an actual dollar — structural complexity as a barrier to tracing money? — USASpending TAS filter tree (fed_usaspending_tas_filter_tree). *Harm:* more accounts means more places money moves without a visible line item. · wild · caveat: only 92 rows and it is a UI filter tree, not spending data; ancestors array unparsed.
- **Serial winners of small-business research money.** Which firms have made a business out of winning SBIR/STTR awards for decades — including single-digit-employee firms holding multi-million-dollar awards? — SBIR/STTR awards (fed_sbir_sttr_awards). *Harm:* a program meant to seed new small businesses paying the same firms for thirty years is not reaching the entrepreneurs it was sold to. · caveat: employee counts self-reported at application time; verify UEI/DUNS fill rates (older awards predate the IDs) and normalize company names before lifetime counts.
- **Does the program reach the founders it was sold on.** What share of SBIR/STTR awards go to woman-owned, disadvantaged, and HUBZone firms per agency over time? — SBIR/STTR designation flags (fed_sbir_sttr_awards). *Harm:* the set-aside categories exist because these founders were shut out; the chart shows whether that ever changed. · caveat: flags are self-reported text and may be blank for most rows — blank would look like zero rather than unknown.
- **Where innovation money physically lands.** Which handful of metros capture most federal small-business research dollars, and which agencies grew or shrank the spend? — SBIR/STTR awards geography and agency timeline (fed_sbir_sttr_awards). *Harm:* federal innovation money concentrating in five metros is federal money not building jobs anywhere else. · caveat: company address is a mailing address; award_year text-cast; amounts missing for a share of records.
- **Phase one forever.** Which agencies actually graduate SBIR grantees from phase one to phase two, and which just fund studies forever? — SBIR/STTR phase fields (fed_sbir_sttr_awards). *Harm:* a program that funds phase one forever leaves small firms with sunk costs and no product. · caveat: phase linkage is not guaranteed in the data — a phase-1-to-phase-2 linking key (company + topic) must be built first.
- **Audit firms that never find problems.** Which single-audit firms disclose implausibly few material weaknesses relative to their audit volume — the rubber stamps? — Federal Audit Clearinghouse single audits (FED_FAC_SINGLE_AUDIT). *Harm:* rubber-stamp audits let grant money serving poor communities go unaccounted for. · caveat: boolean-looking columns are untyped (may be Y/N text); low finding rates can be genuine for small-client portfolios.
- **Going-concern clusters among federally funded organizations.** Where are the grantees flagged as going concerns — the clinics and housing nonprofits about to stop serving people — by state, entity type and dollars? — FAC going-concern flag (FED_FAC_SINGLE_AUDIT). *Harm:* a going-concern flag on a clinic or housing nonprofit means services are about to stop. · caveat: flag may be sparse; ZIP text includes ZIP+4 variants.
- **Repeat audit offenders who keep the low-risk label.** Which auditees keep disclosing material weaknesses year after year yet retain low-risk-auditee status — earning lighter future scrutiny after failing? — FAC cohort of findings vs low-risk status (FED_FAC_SINGLE_AUDIT). *Harm:* low-risk status means lighter scrutiny for the exact organizations that already failed. · caveat: requires stable auditee EIN across years — verify EIN stability and value shape first, EIN is the platform's documented masking trap.
- **Overloaded oversight agencies.** Which federal agencies nominally oversee the most single-audit money with the least attention? — FAC oversight/cognizant agency fields (FED_FAC_SINGLE_AUDIT). *Harm:* overloaded oversight agencies are why bad grantees keep drawing money. · medium · caveat: agency codes need a lookup; dollars column untyped.
- **Years-late single audits.** Which classes of grantee chronically file audits years after fiscal year end — misuse discovered long after the money and the harm are gone? — FAC fiscal-year-end vs acceptance dates (FED_FAC_SINGLE_AUDIT). *Harm:* years-late audits mean misuse is discovered long after the money is gone. · medium · caveat: date casts are try_to_date over text and may silently drop rows.
- **Single-audit red flags, mapped by state and agency.** What is the rate of adverse or qualified findings per auditee, compared identically across states and awarding agencies — whose grantees fail audits most, and which agencies keep funding them? — Federal Audit Clearinghouse single audits, 412k (FED_FAC_SINGLE_AUDIT). *Harm:* grant dollars repeatedly routed to entities that fail their audits, at the expense of the people the grants serve. · caveat: completeness unverified.
- **EITC money left unclaimed.** In which low-income ZIPs is EITC take-up lowest — households leaving thousands of owed refund dollars unclaimed? — IRS Statistics of Income by ZIP (fed_irs_soi). *Harm:* low take-up ZIPs are households leaving thousands of dollars of owed refund unclaimed. · caveat: most numeric columns left as untyped text in the mart; ZIP-level SOI suppresses small cells.
- **Agencies sitting on unobligated authority.** Which federal agencies hold budget authority they never obligate or outlay — appropriated help that never reaches anyone? — USAspending top-tier agency budget file (fed_usaspending_toptier_agencies). *Harm:* unobligated authority is appropriated help that never reaches anyone. · medium · caveat: 111 rows, single fiscal-quarter snapshot; mid-year figures naturally look under-obligated.
- **Grant design that shuts out small applicants.** Which agencies post grants with windows too short for unstaffed community groups, advertise big ceilings while planning few awards, or write eligibility that structurally excludes nonprofits and tribes? — Grants.gov opportunity search (fed_grants_gov). *Harm:* short windows and exclusionary eligibility lock out the communities a program claims to serve. · medium · caveat: only a 100-row live-search snapshot, not a historical corpus; ceiling/floor fields untyped.
- **Promised versus delivered foreign aid.** In which countries is US aid announced repeatedly but never disbursed? — ForeignAssistance.gov (fed_foreignassistance). *Harm:* announced aid that never disburses leaves people relying on services that were never funded. · caveat: amount fields untyped; obligations and disbursements legitimately lag across fiscal years.
- **Clinics or weapons — the character of aid.** Which countries get health and food aid versus mostly security assistance, and where is the aid relationship run by defense rather than development agencies? — ForeignAssistance.gov sector mix and managing agency (fed_foreignassistance). *Harm:* security-heavy aid mixes often mean the population sees weapons before it sees clinics. · caveat: sector taxonomies and agency naming changed over the years — not fully comparable across the span.
- **Aid whiplash.** Which countries have their aid cut off abruptly, shuttering clinics and schools mid-year? — ForeignAssistance.gov year-over-year obligation swings (fed_foreignassistance). *Harm:* abrupt aid cutoffs shutter clinics and schools mid-year with no wind-down. · caveat: mixing transaction types could double-count; fiscal-year field may need casting.
- **Who got pandemic relief was never recorded.** How blank are the race and ethnicity fields on PPP loans, by state — the reporting hole that makes disparate relief unprovable? — SBA PPP loans (fed_sba_ppp). *Harm:* if who got relief was never recorded, no one can prove the money missed Black and Latino owners. · caveat: the blank rate is the finding — the chart must foreground it, not hide it.
- **Relief followed banking relationships.** Which lenders served only affluent urban borrowers with PPP money, leaving people without banking relationships with nothing? — SBA PPP lender x county with rural/LMI/HubZone indicators (fed_sba_ppp). *Harm:* relief routed through lenders means people without a banking relationship never got any. · caveat: file covers loans of 150k and above only — the small-borrower tail is entirely absent.
- **Dollars per job saved.** Which industries got wildly more public money per job reported than others under PPP? — SBA PPP approval amount / jobs reported by NAICS (fed_sba_ppp). *Harm:* some sectors got many times more public money per worker protected than others did. · caveat: jobs_reported is self-reported and unverified; division blows up on zero/null jobs.
- **A payroll program that paid landlords.** How much of PPP proceeds went to rent, utilities, and mortgage interest rather than payroll, and how much money still sits undisbursed or unresolved years later? — SBA PPP proceeds breakdown, undisbursed amounts, loan status (fed_sba_ppp). *Harm:* a program sold as saving jobs that largely paid rent is a different program than the one Congress described; undisbursed money is relief that never reached a payroll. · caveat: proceeds fields are borrower-declared allocations, not audited spending; status snapshots may be stale.

### finance-and-markets (81)
- **Who moves the financial futures markets.** Which trader class (leveraged funds, dealers, asset managers) builds the biggest and fastest position swings in rate and index futures, and does speculative crowding build before market stress? — CFTC Commitments of Traders, financial futures (fed_cftc_cot_financial). *Harm:* speculative crowding in rate and index futures is what turns a market wobble into a pension loss. · medium · caveat: ~3,163 rows suggests partial history; position columns are untyped passthroughs; mart mis-filed under an education schema; completeness unverified.
- **Small traders squeezed out of futures markets.** Is the nonreportable (small trader) share of open interest shrinking over time, market by market? — CFTC Commitments of Traders futures (fed_cftc_cot_futures). *Harm:* small traders vanishing means price formation is left entirely to institutions. · medium · caveat: partial history; nonreportable is a residual category, not a real trader count.
- **The top-100 corporate snapshot: leanness, concentration, momentum.** Among the 100 largest US companies, how much revenue does each worker carry, how steep is the revenue-concentration curve, and which whole sectors are growing or contracting? — Wikipedia largest US companies (xc_wikipedia_largest_us_companies). *Harm:* concentrated revenue means concentrated pricing power over ordinary buyers; sector-wide contraction is the leading edge of mass layoffs. · medium · caveat: snapshot of 100 rows, no year column, numeric fields may be text; understates the true national tail.
- **Where corporate command sits.** In which handful of metros and states are the headquarters of large US companies and SEC filers physically concentrated, relative to where their harm and payroll land? — Wikipedia top-100 HQs plus SEC DERA filer addresses (xc_wikipedia_largest_us_companies, fed_sec_dera_sub_*, fed_sec_edgar_financials). *Harm:* regions with no headquarters have no local lever over the firms that employ and pollute them. · medium · caveat: needs geocoding of free-text city/state fields (no lat/lon) and address normalization before trust; DERA country fields mis-cast to numbers and null out; row-count mismatch on the financials table suggests partial load.
- **Which industries face public disclosure at all.** Ranked by filings and filers, which SIC industries dominate the public-company record — and which barely appear, meaning they answer to no public disclosure? — SEC EDGAR filings and DERA quarterly submissions (fed_sec_edgar, fed_us_sec_edgar, fed_sec_dera_sub_*, fed_sec_edgar_financials). *Harm:* filing patterns show which industries face real disclosure and which slip through unwatched. · medium · caveat: fed_sec_edgar is a 200-row sample; SIC codes are self-selected and often stale; completeness unverified.
- **Late, bunched, and stuck corporate filings.** How late do companies file after period end, which filer classes chronically file at the wire or weeks past it, and where does the last-48-hours deadline-crush wall land? — SEC EDGAR filing/report dates and DERA submissions (fed_sec_edgar, fed_sec_dera_sub_*). *Harm:* late disclosure is the window where investors and workers fly blind about a company's real condition. · medium · caveat: filed/period dates are untyped text in several marts — the YYYYMMDD epoch parse trap applies; single-quarter slices limit trends.
- **Dual-class structures: companies with many tickers.** Which companies carry multiple ticker symbols under one CIK — the multi-share-class structures that let founders keep control while outsiders carry the risk? — SEC EDGAR company tickers (fed_sec_edgar_company_tickers, fed_sec_edgar_company_tickers_exchange). *Harm:* dual-class structures let founders keep control while outside shareholders carry the risk. · medium · caveat: multiplicity is expected at (CIK, ticker) grain — routine share classes must not be read as anomalies.
- **IPO and prospectus waves.** When do registration and prospectus filings surge, and do offering booms mark the moments retail investors were pulled into the riskiest new issues? — SEC EDGAR full-text/REST filings (fed_us_sec_edgar). *Harm:* offering waves mark when retail investors were pulled into the riskiest new issues. · caveat: ~49k rows may be a partial crawl rather than full EDGAR; completeness unverified.
- **Companies that quietly stop filing.** Which registrants skip annual reports or vanish from the quarterly filing record entirely — going private, collapsing, or going dark — leaving shareholders and workers with no financial picture? — SEC EDGAR annual-report gaps plus stacked DERA quarterly submissions 2024Q4-2026Q1 (fed_us_sec_edgar, fed_sec_dera_sub_*). *Harm:* a company that stops filing has usually gone private, been acquired, or collapsed — and its workers and creditors find out last. · caveat: partial crawl means a missing row may be a collection gap, not a filing gap; only ~6 quarters of DERA coverage, so a gap may be a normal non-filing period.
- **The fast-track disclosure club.** Which industries and size classes get well-known-seasoned-issuer status — the lightest-touch registration path with the least pre-review before the public buys? — DERA submissions WKSI flag (fed_sec_dera_sub_2024q2, fed_sec_dera_sub_2025q4). *Harm:* the lightest disclosure burden goes to the biggest players, whose failures hurt the most people. · medium · caveat: flag vocabulary undocumented; single-quarter snapshots.
- **Who is allowed to say less.** Which industries and filer size classes file only summary-level (untagged) data instead of detailed machine-readable disclosure? — DERA submissions detail flag (fed_sec_dera_sub_2024q3, fed_sec_dera_sub_2024q4). *Harm:* companies filing only summary data cannot be automatically compared to peers — where problems hide longest. · caveat: detail-flag vocabulary undocumented; single-quarter snapshots.
- **Books closed away from December.** Which industries cluster fiscal year ends off the calendar, burying results in quiet news weeks and defeating cross-company comparison? — DERA submissions fiscal-year-end fields (fed_sec_dera_sub_2024q3, fed_sec_dera_sub_2025q2). *Harm:* off-cycle year ends are a small but real way to reduce scrutiny. · medium · caveat: FYE is a four-character text code; thin industries are noisy.
- **Restatement repeat offenders.** Which companies keep re-reporting what they already told the public — the filers whose numbers should never be taken at face value? — DERA submissions previously-reported flag (fed_sec_dera_sub_2025q1). *Harm:* people who traded on the original numbers were trading on numbers the company later took back. · caveat: flag semantics unverified; per-company counts within one quarter may be too small to mean anything.
- **Charges outstanding, creditors unpaid.** Which companies pile up outstanding mortgage charges with none satisfied, by sector and age — where secured lenders get paid and small suppliers never do? — UK Companies House mortgage-charge counts (INT_UK_COMPANIES_HOUSE, intl_uk_companies_house). *Harm:* unsatisfied charges pile up where creditors — often small suppliers — never got paid. · medium · caveat: charge counts are register snapshots or historical totals, not a payment history.
- **The rate environment behind every debt.** What has the full Treasury yield curve done over time — inversions, regime shifts, and the short-rate backdrop that every mortgage, credit card and municipal budget rides on? — Fed H.15 selected interest rates (fed_frb_h15_selected_rates). *Harm:* rate spikes turn affordable debt into foreclosure and bankruptcy; inversions precede the recessions where job and home loss show up. · medium · caveat: no obvious date column — the date appears to sit inside a description field; values stored as text with placeholder codes; utility depends on the date being recoverable.
- **Household versus corporate balance sheets.** Across the flow-of-funds record, which sector is absorbing debt and which is shedding it — and how wide is the gap between household and corporate net worth each cycle? — Fed Z.1 flow of funds (fed_frb_z1_csv). *Harm:* the widening gap between household and corporate balance sheets is the macro backdrop for every harm on this platform. · medium · caveat: columns are raw Fed series codes with no human labels — unusable without a series dictionary; only 304 quarterly rows but hundreds of unlabeled columns.
- **Inequality trajectories worldwide.** How has the Gini coefficient moved per country and region, which countries got measurably more unequal, and where does no inequality measure exist at all? — OWID Gini index (xc_owid_gini). *Harm:* rising inequality shows up as worse health and shorter lives at the bottom; unmeasured inequality cannot even be argued about. · caveat: Gini not numeric-cast (may be text); survey methods differ across countries/years; uneven start/end years make slopes non-comparable without care.
- **Where the world's offshore banking capacity sits.** Which countries host the most FATCA-registered foreign financial institutions — jurisdictions structurally built to hold other people's money? — FATCA FFI list (fed_fatca_ffi). *Harm:* jurisdictions with vastly more registered institutions than population are built to hold hidden money. · caveat: only three real columns — a genuinely thin source; completeness unverified.
- **Ninety years of bank failures and what they cost.** When did American banks fail, what did each wave cost the insurance fund, which resolution strategies cost most per dollar of bank, and did young charters fail fastest? — FDIC failed banks (fed_fdic_failed_banks). *Harm:* each failure spike is a wave of depositors, borrowers and local employers cut adrift. · caveat: losses not inflation-adjusted and null for older records; no denominator of supervised institutions, so supervisor comparisons mislead; resolution categories changed definition over decades.
- **Who bought the failed banks.** Which serial acquirers consolidated whole regions through other banks' failures? — FDIC failed banks acquirer field (fed_fdic_failed_banks). *Harm:* serial acquirers turn local failures into regional banking concentration and fewer local lending options. · caveat: acquirer names are unstandardized text — standardize them (acquirers themselves later failed or merged); a cert-number crosswalk would make it steel.
- **Thirty years of branch closures: the banking deserts.** County by county from 1994 to 2025, where did bank branches disappear — which counties lost every branch, and where are the remaining branches physically? — FDIC Summary of Deposits branch records (fed_fdic_sod_branch_deposits). *Harm:* communities losing every branch lose access to cash, credit and small-business lending. · caveat: branch counts include non-retail service types (filter needed); coordinates may be missing or default centroids; small rural counties dominate percentage rankings without a floor.
- **Deposit and ownership concentration in banking.** What share of all branch deposits do the top holding companies control per survey year, and how many nominally separate banks share one owner? — FDIC SOD holding-company deposits plus FDIC BankFind flags (fed_fdic_sod_branch_deposits, fed_fdic_bank_data). *Harm:* concentrated deposits mean fewer local lenders deciding who gets a mortgage or a business loan. · caveat: holding-company RSSD may be blank for independents, inflating the unaffiliated bucket; BankFind mart is a 10,000-row API slice.
- **Community banks versus the giants.** How has deposit share shifted between community banks and large bank classes, metro versus non-metro, over three decades? — FDIC SOD community-bank flag and bank class (fed_fdic_sod_branch_deposits). *Harm:* if community banks vanish fastest outside metros, rural borrowers lose the lender most likely to say yes. · caveat: community-bank flag definition changed over the survey history.
- **Deposits booked far from home.** Which branches report deposits implausibly large for their location — booking distortions that make lending obligations look met when local money never arrives? — FDIC SOD deposit reporting method (fed_fdic_sod_branch_deposits). *Harm:* deposit-booking distortions make state-level lending obligations look met when local money never arrives. · wild · caveat: requires understanding the deposit reporting-method code, which is unverified.
- **The market participants wired into every venue.** Which trading firms belong to every venue at once, which operate many market identities, and where does the trading industry physically sit? — FINRA MPID list (fed_finra_mpid_list). *Harm:* firms wired into every venue see order flow nobody else sees; one firm operating many market identities is harder to follow. · medium · caveat: flags may be Y/N text; snapshot only, no registration history; location is free text of unknown granularity.
- **Municipal bond gatekeepers and advice deserts.** Which states are served by many municipal securities firms and which by almost none — towns whose only financing advice comes from the people selling them the debt? — MSRB registrants (fed_msrb_registrants). *Harm:* towns with one or two muni dealers pay whatever those dealers charge — residents repay it through taxes and utility bills. · caveat: only 925 rows; state is the registered (HQ) state, not where firms do business; no municipality-count denominator.
- **Advisor and dealer under one roof.** How many municipal-market firms are registered as both advisor and dealer — positioned to advise a town to buy what they themselves sell? — MSRB registrant types (fed_msrb_registrants). *Harm:* firms wearing both hats can advise a town to buy what they sell. · caveat: dual registration must be inferred from the same id under two types — pattern existence unverified.
- **Why credit unions disappear.** What reasons do merging credit unions give for surrendering their charters, how mismatched are the sizes of absorbed vs absorbing institutions, and whose membership rules replace whose? — NCUA charter merger events (fed_ncua_charter_merger_events). *Harm:* every merged-away credit union is a community that lost its own lender and its preferential terms. · caveat: only 27 rows in the mart — far too few to be a full merger history; likely a single snapshot period.
- **Where the poverty-serving lenders actually are.** By state, what share of federally insured credit unions carry a low-income designation — and where does the map leave poor households to payday lenders? — NCUA insured credit union list and call report geography (fed_ncua_federally_insured_cu_list, fed_ncua_call_reports). *Harm:* states with almost no low-income-designated credit unions leave poor households to payday lenders. · caveat: state is mailing-address state, not branch footprint — coverage overstated for multi-branch institutions; single-quarter snapshot.
- **Deposits in, loans not out.** Which credit unions — especially low-income-designated ones — take deposits without lending them back: low loan-to-share ratios and deposit growth outpacing loan growth? — NCUA insured CU list ratios and growth fields (fed_ncua_federally_insured_cu_list). *Harm:* a community's savings parked elsewhere instead of financing local homes and cars. · caveat: ratio and growth fields are text-cast with unverified scale; extreme small-base values dominate.
- **Small credit unions heading for the exit.** Which small, shrinking, thin-capitalized credit unions are on the path to merger — the shortlist of communities about to lose their local lender? — NCUA insured CU list plus call report account codes (fed_ncua_federally_insured_cu_list, fed_ncua_call_reports). *Harm:* members of a failing credit union lose the only lender that would approve them. · caveat: snapshot only; requires the NCUA account-code dictionary to pick the right metrics; regulatory thresholds not in the data.
- **Thirty years of credit union consolidation.** Quarter by quarter since 1994, how many credit unions still report, split by charter type — and which financial disclosures quietly stopped being filed along the way? — NCUA call reports (fed_ncua_call_reports). *Harm:* every credit union that vanishes is a member-owned lender replaced by a for-profit one. · caveat: account-code grain needs deduping to institution-quarter; 30 years of form changes dominate any reporting-gap pattern.
- **Where chartered banks and thrifts survive.** State by state, where are national banks and the remaining thrifts headquartered — and which states have effectively no locally chartered lender of either kind left? — OCC national banks and thrifts (fed_occ_national_banks, fed_occ_thrifts). *Harm:* states with no locally chartered lenders export their deposits and import their credit decisions; thrifts were the mortgage lender of last resort for working families. · medium · caveat: tiny undated snapshots (724 and 218 rows) — no way to show the decline itself; charter numbers are separately namespaced and must not be merged; charter-number-as-age is an unstated assumption.
- **The long consolidation of American banking.** Across establishment and end dates, how did US banking consolidate decade by decade — every closed community bank a town that lost its only local lender? — FDIC BankFind institutions (fed_fdic_bank_data). *Harm:* every closed community bank is a town that lost its only local lender. · caveat: mart is a 10,000-row API slice, explicitly not the full universe, and may skew toward active institutions; date fields untyped.
- **Deposits gathered here, lent somewhere else.** Which institutions gather local deposits without lending locally — capital extraction visible in deposits vs assets? — FDIC BankFind deposits/assets (fed_fdic_bank_data). *Harm:* deposits taken from a community and lent elsewhere is capital extraction from that community. · caveat: 10,000-row slice; the loan side is not in this table, so the extraction claim needs another source.
- **Bank early-warning ratios in a broken source.** Which banks' bad loans exceed their capital cushion and which lend far beyond their deposit base — and, first, the visible finding that this ingest itself broke (rows carrying HTML markup)? — FFIEC call reports probe extract (fed_ffiec_call_reports). *Harm:* a bank whose bad loans exceed its capital fails, and depositors and borrowers in that town absorb it; a broken bank-financials ingest means nobody can check. · medium · caveat: only 302 rows — a probe, not the call report corpus; the doctype_html column shows the scrape captured page markup — source needs re-ingesting before any claim.
- **The roster of institutional money managers.** Who are the institutions filing 13Fs — the entities voting the shares of the companies that employ and house people — how has that population grown over decades, and from which few ZIP codes do they operate? — SEC 13F filers and submissions (fed_sec_13f_filers, fed_sec_13f_submissions, FED_SEC_13F_SUBMISSION). *Harm:* these entities vote the shares in companies that employ and house people, and most of the public has never heard their names. · medium · caveat: manager names are free text with heavy spelling variants; the reporting threshold has not been updated for decades, confounding the growth trend; one state field is mis-cast to a number.
- **Holdings hidden by confidential treatment.** Who files 13F positions under confidential treatment, and does the regulator ever say no — stakes built in secret in companies people work for? — SEC 13F confidentiality fields (fed_sec_13f_filers). *Harm:* confidential holdings mean the public cannot see who is quietly building a stake in their employer. · caveat: confidentiality date fields are text-cast and may be null for the overwhelming majority of rows.
- **Restating what they said they held.** Which managers routinely amend and restate their 13F holdings — making the public ownership record unreadable in real time? — SEC 13F amendment fields (fed_sec_13f_filers, FED_SEC_13F_SUBMISSION, fed_sec_13f_submissions). *Harm:* routine restatement lets a manager time what the public learns and when. · medium · caveat: amendment fields are uncast text; submission-type vocabulary undocumented; the singular submission mart appears to duplicate the positions column list — confirm which table is live.
- **13F late filers.** Which institutional managers consistently file at the last legal moment or later — the public learning who owns what only after the trades that mattered? — SEC 13F period-of-report vs filing date (FED_SEC_13F_SUBMISSION, fed_sec_13f_submissions). *Harm:* late disclosure means the public sees ownership only after it stops mattering. · caveat: both dates are uncast text; deadline rules must be applied externally; singular/plural mart confusion must be resolved first.
- **Common ownership across competitors.** Which securities does nearly every institution hold, and how few managers hold most of any given company — the web of overlapping ownership where the same funds own every competitor in an industry? — SEC 13F holdings and positions (fed_sec_13f_holdings, FED_SEC_13F_POSITIONS). *Harm:* when the same funds own every competitor, competition on price and wages is nobody's interest. · caveat: 101M-202M row tables — expensive to compute, sample by quarter; issuer name is free text (CUSIP is the reliable key); value units changed historically between dollars and thousands.
- **Money without votes.** Where do managers hold big positions while disclaiming voting authority — and where does voting power sit without economic stake? — SEC 13F voting-authority fields (fed_sec_13f_holdings, FED_SEC_13F_POSITIONS). *Harm:* separating money from votes hides who really influences the companies people work for. · caveat: voting-authority fields left uncast as text; inconsistently reported across filers; value scale changed historically.
- **Betting against what they hold.** Which companies carry the heaviest disclosed institutional put positions — who is betting against hospital, housing and utility operators whose customers cannot leave? — SEC 13F put/call fields (fed_sec_13f_holdings, FED_SEC_13F_POSITIONS). *Harm:* heavy short interest in essential-service operators is a signal about companies whose customers cannot leave. · medium · caveat: the put/call field is sparsely used by design; only some managers report derivatives.
- **The delegated-management shell game.** Behind the named 13F filer, who actually controls the shares — the other-manager and investment-discretion chains where the filer is not the decider? — SEC 13F other-manager fields (fed_sec_13f_holdings, FED_SEC_13F_POSITIONS). *Harm:* layered discretion makes it impossible for a worker or pensioner to know who controls their employer's shares. · wild · caveat: othermanager is a positional reference code, not a name — resolve it against the cover-page table or the field is unusable.
- **Audit partners stretched past human limits.** Which individual engagement partners sign more public-company audits than a person can supervise, which sign off in record time, and which firms keep correcting their own engagement records? — PCAOB Form AP filings (fed_pcaob_form_ap_filings). *Harm:* an overloaded audit partner is how a company's books go unchecked — and the pensioners holding the stock pay for the miss. · caveat: partner-id stability across firms unverified; fast is not automatically bad without complexity context; amendment-flag vocabulary undocumented.
- **The audit market's four firms.** How few firms audit the books of nearly every public company — leaving nowhere to go for a genuinely independent second opinion? — PCAOB Form AP firm/issuer counts (fed_pcaob_form_ap_filings). *Harm:* when four firms audit almost everything, industry-wide accounting practices never get challenged. · caveat: member-firm network structures can split or merge firm counts incorrectly.
- **Partners who never rotate.** Which issuers keep the same engagement partner year after year despite the five-year rotation rule written after Enron? — PCAOB Form AP issuer-by-year partner grid (fed_pcaob_form_ap_filings). *Harm:* a partner who never rotates off a client is the exact relationship the rotation rule was written to prevent. · caveat: requires accurate partner ids across years; rotation-rule details are not in the data.
- **Audit work done where the regulator cannot inspect.** How much of US companies' audit work is performed by firms in other jurisdictions — including ones the US regulator cannot inspect? — PCAOB Form AP participant countries and percentages (fed_pcaob_form_ap_filings). *Harm:* audit work in an uninspectable jurisdiction means nobody truly checks the numbers behind American retirement accounts. · caveat: participation percentages stored as text, possibly ranges; issuer country not directly in the table.
- **Registration waves of retail investment vehicles.** When do BDC and closed-end-fund registrations boom — the products launched at market peaks that retail savers buy right before losing money? — SEC BDC and closed-end fund registrations (fed_sec_business_development_company_report, fed_sec_closed_end_fund_information). *Harm:* fund launch waves at market peaks are what retail savers buy right before they lose money; BDC terms flow through to mid-sized employers' workers. · medium · caveat: small rosters (212 and 973 rows); filing_date text-cast with unstated coverage windows.
- **Fund families and their fee-tier share classes.** Which fund complexes run the most share classes, how many fee tiers is one portfolio sliced into, which classes carry no public ticker at all — and where does the industry physically sit? — SEC investment company series/class registry (fed_sec_investment_company_series_class). *Harm:* the same portfolio sold at very different fee levels — and small savers land in the expensive, unquoted tiers. · caveat: fee levels are not in the table — the chart implies but cannot prove the spread; blank ticker may mean not-yet-issued; cik_number is trimmed text needing normalization before joins.
- **Who advises the nation's parked cash.** How few advisors manage the money-market funds where households and small businesses park emergency cash, and how does the government/prime/tax-exempt mix shift month to month? — SEC money market fund information (fed_sec_money_market_fund_information). *Harm:* one advisor stumbling hits everyone's emergency cash at once; category migration is the early tell of funding stress. · caveat: advisor names are free text needing deduplication; report month untyped; small table (1,206 rows).
- **The sub-advisor hidden layer.** Behind the fund's brand name, who actually picks the assets — the sub-advisory layer most fund buyers never learn about? — SEC money market registrant/advisor/sub-advisor chains (fed_sec_money_market_fund_information). *Harm:* the firm actually picking the assets is often not the firm whose name is on the fund. · caveat: sub-advisor likely blank for most rows; sparse graph in a 1,206-row table.
- **Insiders filing late.** Which companies' insiders chronically file past the legal two-day window — retail shareholders trading blind while executives sit on unreported sales? — SEC EDGAR insider reports filing lag (fed_sec_edgar_insiders, FED_SEC_INSIDER_SUBMISSION). *Harm:* retail shareholders trade blind while insiders sit on unreported sales past the legal window. · caveat: period_of_report is untyped text; submissions mart is a single 2025Q1 slice; no transaction amounts in the reports mart.
- **The 10b5-1 legal shield adoption wave.** When did companies and insiders adopt 10b5-1 trading plans — the mechanism that can launder opportunistic selling into pre-scheduled trades? — SEC EDGAR insider reports 10b5-1 flag (fed_sec_edgar_insiders). *Harm:* 10b5-1 plans can launder opportunistic selling into pre-scheduled trades; the adoption curve shows who reached for the shield. · caveat: flag may be sparsely populated or a blank-string sentinel; only exists on newer form versions.
- **Insider filings that keep getting corrected.** Which issuers repeatedly amend insider disclosures — periods where the public record of executive self-dealing was simply wrong? — insider report amendment types (fed_sec_edgar_insiders, FED_SEC_INSIDER_SUBMISSION). *Harm:* every amendment marks a period where the public record was wrong and someone traded against it. · medium · caveat: document-type value set unverified; amendment suffix convention assumed; single-quarter slice on one mart.
- **Registered insiders who never report a trade.** Which insiders file an initial Form 3 and then never a Form 4 — clean, or invisible? — insider filings form-type sequences (fed_sec_edgar_insiders). *Harm:* registered insiders with no follow-up filings are a blind spot in the only public record of executive self-dealing. · wild · caveat: needs insider-person linkage, but the mart carries only issuer CIK — the reporting person may not be identifiable at all.
- **Disclosures timed to be missed.** Do insider filings pile up on Fridays and pre-holiday windows — the classic bury-it dates designed not to inform? — insider filing-date density (fed_sec_edgar_insiders). *Harm:* disclosures timed to be missed are designed not to inform the people they legally protect. · caveat: filing_date is a try_to_date cast — parse failures would silently null rows and skew the density.
- **Options exercised at exactly the right moment.** Which insider derivative exercises cluster far ahead of expiry and deep in the money — information converted into cash — and are the most complex instruments also the latest reported? — SEC insider derivative transactions (FED_SEC_INSIDER_DERIV_TRANS). *Harm:* early exercises clustered before price moves are how executives convert information into cash. · caveat: single quarter (2025Q1); several date fields try_to_date-cast and possibly widely null; true moneyness needs an external market price.
- **What insiders actually do with their equity.** Separating open-market sales from grants and gifts by transaction code, what is the real buy/sell balance of corporate insiders? — SEC insider non-derivative transactions (FED_SEC_INSIDER_NONDERIV_TRANS). *Harm:* open-market selling clustered before bad news is the mechanism retail investors lose money to. · caveat: single quarter; transaction value computed as shares times price and null when either is missing.
- **Same-day selling by the whole executive suite.** On which days does an issuer's entire insider group sell at once — the clearest pre-bad-news pattern there is? — SEC insider non-derivative transactions by day and issuer (FED_SEC_INSIDER_NONDERIV_TRANS). *Harm:* coordinated same-day selling by every insider is the clearest pre-bad-news pattern there is. · caveat: needs the submissions join for issuer identity; one-quarter window limits how many clusters appear.
- **Executives quietly zeroing out their stakes.** Which individuals steadily liquidate their entire holding, transaction by transaction, while telling investors to hold? — SEC insider shares-owned-after paths (FED_SEC_INSIDER_NONDERIV_TRANS). *Harm:* an executive zeroing out their stake while telling investors to hold is the harm. · caveat: requires owner identity from the reporting-owner table; a single quarter is too short for a full drawdown path.
