- **Insiders sitting on many boards.** Which individuals report as insiders at multiple issuers — interlocks that coordinate across companies in ways no single filing reveals? — SEC insider reporting owners (FED_SEC_INSIDER_REPORTINGOWNER). *Harm:* interlocking insiders coordinate across companies in ways no single filing reveals. · caveat: owner CIK population and stability unverified; needs submissions join for issuer identity; single quarter.
- **Where consumer-finance harm concentrates.** Complaints per capita by ZIP — which neighborhoods do debt collectors and servicers work hardest? — CFPB consumer complaints (FED_CFPB_COMPLAINTS). *Harm:* complaint-dense ZIPs are the neighborhoods where debt collectors and servicers work hardest. · caveat: row count differs between catalog and mart comment (34M vs 17M) — suggests a duplicated or partially reloaded table; per-capita needs external population.
- **Companies that never give relief.** Which companies close nearly every complaint without relief — having learned the process costs them nothing — and is the pipeline from receipt to company slowing down? — CFPB complaints company responses and dates (FED_CFPB_COMPLAINTS). *Harm:* a company that closes every complaint without relief has learned the process costs it nothing; delay is extra weeks of a wrongful foreclosure continuing. · caveat: company names are free text with subsidiary variation; response categories changed definition over time; date fields are raw text (known trap); table duplication question above.
- **New harms surfacing in the complaint mix.** Which product-issue cells are rising fast — new ways consumers are being harmed before regulators have a name for them? — CFPB complaints product/issue taxonomy over time (FED_CFPB_COMPLAINTS). *Harm:* a rising issue cell is a new way consumers are being harmed before regulators name it. · caveat: CFPB revised the product/issue taxonomies — cells not comparable across the whole span.
- **Flagged vulnerable, still denied relief.** Do complaints tagged servicemember or older-American get better or worse outcomes than untagged ones? — CFPB complaints tags vs response (FED_CFPB_COMPLAINTS). *Harm:* older Americans and servicemembers flagged as vulnerable and still denied relief are the clearest harm signal in the file. · caveat: tags populated on only a minority of complaints and self-identified.
- **Scripted harms repeating across thousands of complaints.** Do complaint narratives cluster into near-identical language — one company practice hitting thousands of people the same way? — CFPB complaint narratives (FED_CFPB_COMPLAINTS). *Harm:* identical language across thousands of complaints means one practice hitting thousands of people identically. · wild · caveat: narratives are opt-in, present on a minority of rows; text clustering at this scale is heavy compute.
- **The refund-extraction industry.** Where do paid preparers and refund-anticipation products take the biggest cut of poor filers' refunds — and are those exactly the ZIPs with no free (VITA/TCE) tax help? — IRS SOI preparer, RAL/RAC and VITA/TCE fields by ZIP (fed_irs_soi). *Harm:* refund-anticipation products charge triple-digit effective rates to people waiting on their own money. · caveat: RAL/RAC columns discontinued in later SOI years — narrow coverage window; VITA columns sparse; fields untyped.
- **The hollowed-out middle, state by state.** How has the distribution of returns across income brackets shifted per state — where did the middle brackets thin out? — IRS SOI AGI-stub distributions (fed_irs_soi). *Harm:* a state whose middle brackets thin out is one where households moved down, not up. · medium · caveat: bracket definitions shift with inflation across years and must be rebased.
- **Who holds poor countries' debt.** For each debtor country, how has the creditor mix — bilateral, multilateral, private — shifted over four decades, and where did bilateral lending power migrate? — World Bank International Debt Statistics (intl_wb_ids). *Harm:* the creditor mix decides who can force austerity — and whether restructuring is possible when a crisis hits ordinary people. · caveat: the mart wraps country and counterpart names in try_to_number, which will null the text — a modeling bug that likely kills this until fixed; 2025+ columns are projections, not actuals, and that is not encoded in the mart.
- **The debt-service squeeze and the repeat-crisis cycle.** Which countries pay debt service beyond what their economies can carry, and do the same countries cycle through crisis after crisis despite relief programs? — World Bank IDS service vs stock series (intl_wb_ids). *Harm:* when service payments outrun the economy, the cut falls on clinics and teachers, not creditors; repeat crises mean a generation grows up under austerity twice. · caveat: wide year columns must be pivoted; the numeric cast on country codes may destroy ISO3 text; crisis threshold is analyst-defined.
- **Canada's supervised financial institutions.** Who does the Canadian federal regulator actually supervise — by type and industry, which operations are foreign-parented behind local trade names, and which insurers are licensed for which risks? — OSFI regulated financial institutions (intl_osfi_regulated_fi). *Harm:* anyone not on this list is a financial firm nobody federally supervises; customers deal with a friendly trade name while decisions sit in another country. · medium · caveat: only 343 rows, undated snapshot, no trend possible; insurance classes are a delimited free-text list.
- **Trading venue geography and churn.** Where are the world's trading venues registered, and how many opened and shut within a few years — thinly regulated venues gone before any review? — ISO MIC registry (intl_iso_mic_registry). *Harm:* short-lived venues are where thinly regulated trading happens and then disappears before anyone reviews it. · caveat: small registry (2,864 rows); registration country is not necessarily where the matching engine runs; expiry null for live venues by design.
- **Operators running whole families of venues.** Which operating entities run dozens of venue segments under one roof — market power concentrated behind what looks like competition? — ISO MIC registry operating/segment MICs (intl_iso_mic_registry). *Harm:* a single operator running dozens of venue segments concentrates market power behind apparent competition. · caveat: LEI population in the registry is unverified and may be sparse.
- **Neighborhoods where SBA lending fails.** In which zips and counties do SBA-guaranteed loans systematically default and charge off? — SBA 7(a) and 504 loans, FY1991-present (fed_sba_loans). *Harm:* high-default neighborhoods lose the businesses, the jobs, and the owners' personal guarantees together. · caveat: loss rate defined only where chargeoff is populated; still-open loans excluded from the default definition.
- **Lenders originating predictable failure.** Which SBA lenders originate heavily into loans that predictably fail — profiting on origination while borrowers eat the default? — SBA loans lender volume vs chargeoff rate (fed_sba_loans). *Harm:* lenders who profit on origination while borrowers eat the default are a repeatable predatory pattern. · caveat: chargeoff dates may be missing for recent loans; normalize lender names across 35 years of mergers before ranking.
- **Jobs promised per public dollar.** Which industries and places actually convert SBA loan guarantees into the jobs used to justify them? — SBA loans jobs supported vs approval amounts by NAICS and state (fed_sba_loans). *Harm:* loan guarantees are justified as job creation — this shows where that justification is empty. · caveat: jobs_supported is self-reported at application and never verified.
- **Credit that vanishes in downturns.** Does SBA credit disappear for the youngest businesses exactly when recessions hit? — SBA loans approvals by fiscal year, program, business age (fed_sba_loans). *Harm:* credit that disappears in a downturn kills the youngest businesses and their workers first. · medium · caveat: business-age coding likely changed across decades of FOIA releases.
- **Who holds the spectrum.** How concentrated is active spectrum licensing among a handful of entities? — FCC Universal Licensing System (fed_fcc_licensing). *Harm:* concentrated spectrum ownership sets who gets coverage and at what price. · caveat: completeness unverified; normalize entity names first — one company appears under many spellings and FRNs.
- **Spectrum warehoused on dead licenses.** How much spectrum sits on licenses expired years ago but never cancelled, and which service classes are being abandoned? — FCC ULS expiration vs cancellation dates and license status (fed_fcc_licensing). *Harm:* spectrum warehoused on dead licenses is spectrum unavailable to communities with no service. · caveat: null cancellation may just mean still-active; date fields silently null on malformed input.
- **Spectrum deserts.** Which counties have the thinnest active license density per capita — places with no reliable emergency or broadband coverage by license, not just by marketing? — FCC ULS county codes and license status (fed_fcc_licensing). *Harm:* residents of low-license counties have no reliable emergency or broadband coverage. · caveat: fcc_county_code is not FIPS — build the FCC-internal-county-code-to-FIPS crosswalk first.

### corporate-ownership-and-shells (51)
- **Shell-style address clustering behind industrial assets.** Which single mailing addresses host many distinct owner names or facility registrations — shell-layer fingerprints behind plants and permits? — EIA-860 owner addresses plus EPA facility registry addresses (FED_EIA860_4_OWNER, FED_EPA_FRS_FRS_FACILITIES). *Harm:* shell layers between the public and an owner make it impossible to hold anyone to account for local harm. · wild · caveat: unnormalized address strings — needs the address canonicalizer plus a corporate-services-address blocklist; law-firm addresses and genuine industrial parks produce benign false positives.
- **Parent-company pollution rollup (self-reported).** Rolling facilities up by self-reported parent fields, which corporations own the biggest greenhouse and toxic-release footprints? — GHGRP facility parent field plus TRI standardized parents (fed_epa_ghgrp_facility, FED_EPA_TRI_BASIC_2023, FED_EPA_TRI_FACILITY). *Harm:* seeing a parent's whole footprint moves accountability from the plant manager to the corporation. · caveat: parent names are free text (sometimes multiple names per field) — normalize names or use the LEI crosswalk for the hard-ID version; parent-field population unverified.
- **Foreign-owned toxic facilities.** Which toxic-release facilities answer to a foreign parent — the responsible owner outside US jurisdiction? — TRI facility foreign-parent fields (FED_EPA_TRI_FACILITY). *Harm:* when the owner is offshore, the community's leverage over the polluter is thinner. · caveat: foreign-parent fields may be blank on the vast majority of rows.
- **The crosswalk parent leaderboard.** Using the built EPA-to-corporate crosswalk, which ultimate parent companies own the most EPA-regulated facilities? — EPA corporate crosswalk (xc_epa_corporate_crosswalk). *Harm:* facility-level enforcement lets a parent absorb dozens of small fines; the rollup shows the real scale. · caveat: the crosswalk is a match table — parent attribution is only as good as match confidence; exclude low-confidence rows and publish the confidence spread alongside; scale and method vocabulary undocumented.
- **The ownership blind spot.** How many EPA facilities have no identifiable corporate parent at all? — EPA corporate crosswalk unmatched rows (xc_epa_corporate_crosswalk). *Harm:* facilities whose owner cannot be identified are facilities where nobody can be held responsible at the corporate level. · caveat: unmatched may reflect crosswalk gaps rather than genuinely orphan facilities.
- **One company, three unlinked identity systems.** How often does a parent company carry an LEI, a CIK, and a UEI together versus only one — able to be a polluter, a contractor, and a public filer without anyone connecting the three? — EPA corporate crosswalk identifier columns (xc_epa_corporate_crosswalk). *Harm:* unlinked identity systems are how one company's harms stay in separate files. · caveat: identifier columns may be sentinel-masked or blank-string filled — count distinct and sample before trusting fill rates.
- **The staffing-chain shell layer.** Which primary visa-filing employers hide the real worksite employer behind chains of secondary entities? — foreign labor certification disclosures (fed_dol_oflc). *Harm:* Layered staffing chains let the company that actually controls the worksite escape wage and safety liability. · wild · caveat: secondary-entity columns may be mostly blank; ten repeated worksite blocks need unpivoting first.
- **Ownership trees under sanction.** What do the parent-subsidiary structures recorded on designated entities show about how asset freezes get neutralized — subsidiary listed, parent trading on? — UK sanctions parent/subsidiary and registration-number fields (xc_uk_sanctions_list). *Harm:* Sanctioning a subsidiary while the parent trades on is how asset freezes are neutralized in practice. · caveat: parent/subsidiary are free-text packed fields with low expected fill; registration numbers need normalizing.
- **Incorporated in Delaware (or offshore), operating everywhere else.** How many companies are chartered in a state or country they do not physically occupy — the Delaware funnel and the offshore-domiciled slice of US filers — mapped as a flow from legal home to operating home? — SEC EDGAR entities and DERA state-of-incorporation vs business address (fed_sec_edgar, fed_sec_dera_sub_*, fed_sec_edgar_financials). *Harm:* communities host the payroll and the pollution while legal accountability sits in a state or country they have no vote in. · caveat: country-of-incorporation columns are wrongly cast to numbers in several marts and will null out; state fields remain usable.
- **SEC filers that changed their names.** Which filers report a former name and a recent change date — the companies that rebranded, often right after a scandal made the old name unsearchable? — DERA submissions former-name fields (fed_sec_dera_sub_2024q2, fed_sec_dera_sub_2025q3). *Harm:* a company that changes its name after a scandal makes itself unsearchable to the people it harmed. · caveat: former-name fields may be blank for most rows; change-date is uncast text.
- **Companies you cannot serve papers on.** Which filers live behind a mail drop — mailing state different from business state, or almost no address and identifier fields populated at all? — DERA submissions business vs mailing addresses (fed_sec_dera_sub_*, fed_sec_edgar_financials). *Harm:* a company reachable only through a mail drop is a company that is hard for a harmed person to serve papers on. · caveat: address blankness may reflect the extract rather than the filing; country fields mis-cast to numbers; normalize the free-text addresses and add a plausibility filter (corporate-secretary mail handling is often innocuous) before trusting.
- **One filing, forty subsidiaries.** How many filings cover multiple co-registrant legal entities at once, and which corporate groups file as a bundle so no single entity's conduct can be isolated? — DERA submissions co-registrant counts (fed_sec_dera_sub_2024q3, fed_sec_dera_sub_2025q2). *Harm:* a single filing covering forty subsidiaries is forty entities whose individual conduct nobody can isolate. · caveat: the co-registrant list is a packed string needing parsing; count field may be almost always 1.
- **EIN reuse across registrants.** Which employer tax IDs are shared by more than one SEC registrant — sibling entities presenting as unrelated companies under a common tax identity? — DERA submissions EIN column (fed_sec_dera_sub_2025q4). *Harm:* shared tax identities let a corporate family present itself as unrelated separate companies. · wild · caveat: EIN is a documented masking trap on this platform (fake all-nines values) — run COUNT(DISTINCT) plus a value sample before trusting.
- **Addresses hosting dozens of US registrants and fund vehicles.** Which specific office towers, ZIP codes and registered-agent addresses host dozens of SEC filers, business development companies and closed-end funds — the US shell-structure and sponsor-cluster signature? — DERA filer addresses plus BDC and closed-end fund registrations (fed_sec_dera_sub_2026q1, fed_sec_business_development_company_report, fed_sec_closed_end_fund_information). *Harm:* one office running dozens of vehicles is concentration the entity-by-entity view completely hides. · caveat: ZIP formatting inconsistent (5 vs 9 digit); BDC/CEF tables are small (212 and 973 rows); build street-address normalization and label legitimate agents/sponsors before counting.
- **Lapsed and stale entries in the global corporate ID system.** What share of LEIs and of LEI ownership-relationship records have lapsed, gone stale, or passed their renewal date, by country and registrar — meaning the official answer to "who owns this company" is simply out of date? — GLEIF LEI golden copy and relationship records (INTL_GLEIF, INT_GLEIF_RR, intl_gleif_relationships). *Harm:* lapsed identifiers break the audit trail regulators rely on to follow money. · caveat: 3.4M rows with unverified status vocabulary; several registration fields cast with try_to_double and likely nulled.
- **Letterbox jurisdictions: legal home vs real headquarters.** For which countries does the legal-address country diverge from the headquarters country — companies legally domiciled where they have no operations? — GLEIF LEI golden copy address pairs (INTL_GLEIF). *Harm:* companies domiciled where they have no operations are avoiding somebody's tax or regulator. · caveat: fill rate of both country fields unverified at 3.4M-row scale.
- **Havens punching above their weight.** Which micro-jurisdictions host wildly more registered companies per resident than any real economy would produce? — GLEIF LEI counts by country (INTL_GLEIF). *Harm:* tiny jurisdictions hosting millions of companies is the visible signature of the offshore system. · caveat: needs an external population denominator not in the warehouse.
- **Entity death and successor chains.** When entities expire, what reasons are recorded and where do successor-LEI chains lead — the paths by which liabilities get shed while the business continues? — GLEIF entity expiration and successor fields (INTL_GLEIF). *Harm:* following the successor chain is how liabilities get shed while the business continues. · caveat: successor fields are sparse by design; only some dissolutions record them.
- **Registrars that rubber-stamp the world's ownership record.** Which managing registrars (LOUs) control the most LEIs and relationship records, and which accept the weakest validation evidence? — GLEIF managing-LOU and validation fields (INTL_GLEIF, INT_GLEIF_RR). *Harm:* if a registrar rubber-stamps ownership claims, every downstream investigation inherits the lie. · caveat: LOU identifiers and validation-source vocabularies are opaque codes needing a lookup.
- **Corporate ownership trees.** Drawn from parent-child LEI relationships, what does each multinational's full ownership tree look like — how many layers sit between a household brand and its ultimate owner? — GLEIF Level 2 relationship records (INT_GLEIF_RR, intl_gleif_relationships). *Harm:* ownership chains are how a company that harms people in one country keeps its assets where victims cannot reach. · caveat: node IDs are typed and may not all be LEIs; 481k edges need heavy filtering to draw.
- **How deep does ownership go.** What is the distribution of chain depth from ultimate parent to leaf entity across the global LEI graph? — GLEIF relationship records, recursive traversal (intl_gleif_relationships). *Harm:* every extra layer is another step a regulator or claimant must climb before reaching whoever decides. · caveat: cycles and incomplete chains are common in LEI data and would distort depth.
- **Stake sizes: disclosed, hidden, engineered below thresholds.** How often is an ownership percentage actually disclosed versus left as a bare relationship — and do declared stakes pile up just under the 25% and 50% disclosure thresholds? — GLEIF relationship quantifier fields (INT_GLEIF_RR, intl_gleif_relationships). *Harm:* stakes engineered below a reporting threshold are control without the accountability control is supposed to carry. · caveat: quantifier slot-1 fill rate unknown; units may mix percentages with absolute values.
- **Excuses for not naming a parent.** Across 6.3M reporting-exception records, what reasons do entities give for declaring no parent, and does hiding the ultimate parent differ from hiding the immediate one? — GLEIF reporting exceptions (INTL_GLEIF_REPEX). *Harm:* every accepted exception is a company that legally does not have to say who owns it. · caveat: reason fields are enumerated codes needing a lookup; multi-reason rows double-count entities if counted naively.
- **The entities working hardest to stay unowned.** Which LEIs stack multiple exception reasons at once, and what legal provisions do their exception references cite — the loopholes that need closing? — GLEIF reporting exceptions, reasons 1-5 and reference fields (INTL_GLEIF_REPEX). *Harm:* an entity with five stacked excuses for not naming its owner is a deliberate opacity structure. · caveat: trailing reason and reference columns may be almost entirely null.
- **Buildings that host thousands of shells.** Which physical addresses cluster the most offshore entities, officers and service providers — the named buildings where hidden money lives? — ICIJ Offshore Leaks addresses and intermediaries (fed_icij_offshoreleaks_addresses, fed_icij_offshoreleaks_intermediaries). *Harm:* one building holding five thousand companies is the physical address of hidden money. · caveat: leak coverage is what leaked, not what exists — absence is not innocence; normalize free-text address strings first, and counting linked entities needs the relationship edge table.
- **The jurisdiction league table of leaked shells.** Which jurisdictions host the most leaked offshore entities, and how did the geography of secrecy shift between the successive leaks as enforcement pushed money around? — ICIJ Offshore Leaks entities and addresses by jurisdiction and leak (fed_icij_offshoreleaks_entities, fed_icij_offshoreleaks_addresses). *Harm:* a few tiny jurisdictions host the structures that let wealth escape the tax funding schools and hospitals everywhere else. · caveat: counts reflect which providers leaked, not the true global population — the caveat must ride on the chart.
- **When offshore structuring surged.** Timed by incorporation dates and relationship start dates, when did each secrecy haven boom, and which law change elsewhere does each boom follow? — ICIJ entities incorporation dates and relationship start dates (fed_icij_offshoreleaks_entities, fed_icij_offshoreleaks_relationships). *Harm:* each boom follows a law change somewhere else — the timeline maps how money outruns regulation. · caveat: dates are mixed-format text, null on a large share of edges; coverage skewed by which providers leaked.
- **Struck off right after the leak.** Did offshore entities dissolve en masse immediately after each leak's publication — the behavioral proof the structures were doing something their owners did not want seen? — ICIJ entities struck-off/inactivation dates (fed_icij_offshoreleaks_entities). *Harm:* a dissolution spike right after exposure is evidence of concealment. · caveat: leak publication dates must be supplied by hand; struck-off dates may postdate the snapshot and be missing.
- **Offshore entities that changed names.** Where is renaming routine practice among offshore vehicles — entities whose original or former name differs from the current one, breaking the paper trail? — ICIJ entities name/original_name/former_name (fed_icij_offshoreleaks_entities). *Harm:* renaming an offshore vehicle breaks the paper trail linking it to whatever it did before. · medium · caveat: former_name/original_name fill rates unverified and may be near-empty.
- **Where offshore owners live.** By declared country, where do the people behind offshore entities actually reside — which national elites are moving wealth beyond their own tax systems? — ICIJ officers by country (fed_icij_offshoreleaks_officers). *Harm:* shows which national elites move wealth out of reach of their own tax systems. · medium · caveat: country field is multi-value free text, blank on an unknown share of rows.
- **Companies standing in for human owners.** What share of offshore "officers" are companies rather than people, by leak and country — the layering technique that erases the human owner from the record? — ICIJ officers name analysis (fed_icij_offshoreleaks_officers). *Harm:* layering companies as officers is the technique that erases the human owner from the record. · caveat: heuristic classification on name strings only — build and validate a company-vs-person name classifier before trusting.
- **Repeat players across a decade of leaks.** Which intermediaries and which exact relationships appear in multiple leaks (Panama, Paradise, Pandora, Bahamas) — proof that exposure changed nothing? — ICIJ intermediaries by leak and duplicated edges across leaks (fed_icij_offshoreleaks_intermediaries, fed_icij_offshoreleaks_relationships). *Harm:* repeat appearance across leaks means exposure changed nothing for the firms doing it. · wild · caveat: leak-label vocabulary unverified; firms duplicated under name variants; duplicate-edge semantics stated but unverified.
- **The shape of the offshore network.** What does the offshore graph look like — hub-and-spoke concentration where a handful of super-connector nodes control thousands of shells? — ICIJ relationships edges, degree distribution (fed_icij_offshoreleaks_relationships). *Harm:* concentration means a few enablers are single points where accountability could actually bite. · caveat: edges repeat across leaks — degree is inflated without dedup; 3.3M edges need aggressive filtering to draw.
- **Short-lived exotic offshore vehicles.** Among the miscellaneous ICIJ node types, how briefly do the exotic legal forms live, and which havens specialize in them? — ICIJ others nodes (fed_icij_offshoreleaks_others). *Harm:* vehicles that live two years and vanish are built to outrun any investigation. · medium · caveat: tiny table (~3k rows); dates sparse; categories may be too thin to compare.
- **Mailbox addresses hosting thousands of UK and Irish companies.** Which registered addresses and postcodes host industrial-scale company registration in the UK and Ireland — including the addresses where thousands of declared company controllers claim to live? — UK Companies House, UK PSC controller addresses, Ireland CRO (INT_UK_COMPANIES_HOUSE, intl_uk_companies_house, uk_companies_house_psc, intl_ie_cro). *Harm:* mass-registration addresses are the plumbing of the fraud that empties real people's bank accounts — and where enforcement letters go to die. · caveat: PSC table is a truncated ~7M of ~10M load (non-random); a single address splits across text variants — address normalization plus labeling of legitimate formation agents needed before the top of the list is honest.
- **Serial renaming UK companies.** Which UK companies carry the most previous names — ten name changes is a pattern, not housekeeping? — UK Companies House previous-name slots (INT_UK_COMPANIES_HOUSE). *Harm:* renaming is how a company sheds a bad reputation and keeps trading with the same victims. · caveat: ten fixed name slots cap the count — thirty renames looks identical to ten.
- **Companies hiding behind their accounts filings.** Which sectors systematically file accounts late or file dormant/micro-entity accounts — the ways active trading is kept out of the public books? — UK Companies House accounts due dates and account categories (INT_UK_COMPANIES_HOUSE, intl_uk_companies_house). *Harm:* companies that never show real accounts are invisible to everyone they owe money to. · caveat: SIC text is a combined code+description string; account-category vocabulary unverified; date fields may be text.
- **Phoenix lifespans: companies born to die.** In which sectors and legal forms are companies dissolved within a year or two of incorporation — the phoenix-trading signature where debts die and the same business restarts? — UK Companies House lifespan plus Ireland CRO age at dissolution (INT_UK_COMPANIES_HOUSE, intl_ie_cro). *Harm:* short-lived companies in certain sectors are vehicles, not businesses — suppliers and workers eat the losses. · caveat: dissolution date is null for live companies — survivorship must be handled explicitly or the distribution lies.
- **Company formation and death waves.** Month by month, when are companies born and killed in the UK and Ireland — net creation across booms, busts and policy changes? — UK Companies House incorporation/dissolution dates and Ireland CRO incorporation years (intl_uk_companies_house, intl_ie_cro). *Harm:* mass dissolutions mark where jobs and unpaid creditors were left behind. · caveat: UK table (5.7M rows) has no ingestion timestamp — freshness unknown; completeness unverified.
- **Foreign capital routed through Britain.** Which countries of origin stand behind UK-registered companies — Britain as a routing layer that puts ownership one more step from scrutiny? — UK Companies House country-of-origin field (intl_uk_companies_house). *Harm:* routing through Britain is how foreign capital gets one more step from scrutiny. · medium · caveat: country_of_origin fill rate unverified, may be near-empty for domestic firms.
- **Who really controls UK companies — and how vaguely.** Across PSC declarations, how is control most commonly declared, and how often is it the vaguest available category — vagueness there being by design? — UK PSC natures-of-control (uk_companies_house_psc). *Harm:* the stated nature of control is the only public answer to who can make a company act. · caveat: SAMPLE ONLY — ~7.0M of ~10M records from a truncated, non-random load; all totals are undercounts.
- **UK company controllers who live abroad.** How much of UK corporate control is exercised from outside the UK, by country of residence and nationality? — UK PSC country-of-residence (uk_companies_house_psc). *Harm:* overseas controllers are the hardest for UK regulators and claimants to reach when a company causes harm. · caveat: truncated 7M sample; country text is free-form with heavy variant spelling.
- **One person, hundreds of companies.** Which individuals (matched on name plus birth month/year) control the most UK companies — the mass-controller shell-factory signature? — UK PSC individuals (uk_companies_house_psc). *Harm:* one person nominally controlling hundreds of companies is the classic signature behind fraud and wage theft. · caveat: truncated sample undercounts; name+partial-DOB is the only person key and will both merge and split real people — build a person-resolution pass with address corroboration.
- **Control handed off right before the collapse.** How fast is declared control transferred (notified-on to ceased-on), and which companies churn controllers fastest — especially just before failure, when liability lands on someone with nothing to seize? — UK PSC notified/ceased dates (uk_companies_house_psc). *Harm:* rapid controller churn before failure is how liability gets handed to a man of straw. · caveat: dates parsed permissively from text; ceased_on null for live entries by design; truncated sample.
- **Brand families among registered offshore institutions.** Which single brands operate hundreds of registered FATCA vehicles across dozens of jurisdictions, and where does the jurisdiction encoded in the institution's identifier disagree with its reported country? — FATCA FFI names and GIINs (fed_fatca_ffi). *Harm:* one brand with three hundred registered entities across forty jurisdictions is a purpose-built structure, not organic growth. · caveat: name-stem families will contain false positives — needs a validated clustering pass (no parent identifier exists); GIIN internal structure must be confirmed parseable, the identifier-mismatch idea may be a dead end.
- **Trusts and LLCs holding insider stock.** Through which indirect vehicles — trusts, LLCs, family partnerships — do insiders hold and trade stock, obscuring who profits? — SEC insider nature-of-ownership text (FED_SEC_INSIDER_NONDERIV_TRANS). *Harm:* indirect holding structures obscure who actually profits from insider trades. · wild · caveat: free text, null for direct holdings — classify the enormous variation before counting.
- **Aircraft owned through trusts.** How many US aircraft are registered to trusts and LLCs rather than people, and which states function as aircraft ownership shells? — FAA Civil Aircraft Registry (fed_faa_registry / fed_faa_aircraft_registry). *Harm:* anonymous aircraft ownership hides who is flying where, including in enforcement and trafficking cases. · caveat: county/country columns are number-cast and likely nulled; two ingests of this registry exist under different names — completeness unverified; decode type_registrant codes against the FAA codebook and validate trust-detection name patterns on a sample first.
- **One mailbox, hundreds of aircraft.** Which single street addresses host dozens or hundreds of aircraft registrations — the physical footprint of the aircraft-shell industry? — FAA Civil Aircraft Registry (fed_faa_registry). *Harm:* one mailbox holding hundreds of aircraft is the shape of an anonymous-ownership industry. · caveat: legitimate leasing companies will dominate the top of the list — normalize addresses and label known lessors before calling anything a shell; completeness unverified.
- **Co-owner webs behind tail numbers.** Do the other-names fields on aircraft registrations reveal ownership webs where one beneficial owner controls a fleet without appearing on any single registration? — FAA Civil Aircraft Registry other-names fields (fed_faa_registry). *Harm:* layered co-ownership is how aircraft used for questionable purposes stay untraceable to a person. · wild · caveat: other_names fields are mostly blank; name matching will produce false links — name-normalize and manually verify any cluster before naming a person.
- **Sponsors behind the originator brands.** How few sponsors sit behind the many FHA originator storefronts consumers think they chose between? — HUD FHA single-family snapshot, sponsor-to-originator links (fed_hud_fha_sf_portfolio_snapshot). *Harm:* consumers think they chose a lender when often they chose one storefront of the same sponsor. · caveat: sponsor number may be blank for retail originations.
- **Shells holding spectrum.** Which licensee clusters share identical addresses or EINs under different names — splitting holdings to evade concentration limits? — FCC ULS entity name, EIN, FRN, addresses (fed_fcc_licensing). *Harm:* entities splitting holdings across names can evade concentration limits meant to protect consumers. · caveat: the FCC ULS EIN is a known sentinel-masked/blank-string trap on this platform — COUNT(DISTINCT) and value-sample before using; address matching needs normalization.

### nonprofits-and-charities (14)
- **Waves of charity revocations.** When did the IRS strip organizations of exempt status in bulk — the 2011 mass purge and the steady state after, by exemption type? — IRS automatic revocations (fed_irs_auto_revocations, fed_irs_revocation). *Harm:* a revoked nonprofit that keeps soliciting takes donations that are no longer deductible. · caveat: one table sits at exactly 500,000 rows — a probable load cap; revocation dates may be text.
- **Revoked and never reinstated.** How long does reinstatement take when it happens, and which organizations never come back — and if revocation is trivially reversed, is it a deterrent at all? — IRS revocation/reinstatement dates (fed_irs_auto_revocations, fed_irs_revocation). *Harm:* organizations that never return were often the small community groups that could not afford the paperwork. · caveat: reinstatement date likely null for most rows; probable 500k row cap on one copy.
- **Where civic infrastructure collapsed.** Mapped per capita by state and ZIP — including foreign-address cases and the share of register entries in non-active status — where did nonprofit infrastructure quietly die? — IRS revocations geography plus BMF status shares (fed_irs_auto_revocations, fed_irs_revocation, fed_irs_eo_bmf). *Harm:* clusters of revocations mark neighborhoods where the civic safety net quietly collapsed. · caveat: needs external population data for per-capita; probable row cap may bias geography; status-code vocabulary needs an IRS lookup.
- **Deductibility fine print donors never read.** What deductibility statuses do eligible donees actually carry, by state — and how much deductible giving flows to foreign-registered entities? — IRS Pub 78 eligible donees (fed_irs_pub78_eligible_donees). *Harm:* donors relying on a status code they do not understand may lose the deduction they were promised. · medium · caveat: table sits at exactly 500,000 rows — likely truncated well below the real universe; country field may be mostly blank.
- **Charity deserts.** Where are exempt organizations thick and where are they absent, per capita by state and ZIP — the places with services needed and no organizations to provide them? — IRS Pub 78, IRS BMF density, Puerto Rico BMF (fed_irs_pub78_eligible_donees, fed_irs_bmf, FED_IRS_EO_PR). *Harm:* charity deserts mean no local organization stands between a family and a crisis. · caveat: needs external population; probable 500k cap on Pub 78; BMF financials stale and blank for small orgs.
- **Endowment hoarding.** Which organizations sit on large assets while spending little — endowments swelling while services stall? — IRS SOI charity sample and 990 bulk sample (fed_irs_soi_charities, fed_irs_990). *Harm:* foundations hoarding assets are holding money meant to reach people in need. · caveat: both marts are tiny samples (2,450 and 200 rows) — shapes only, nothing generalizes.
- **Which causes hold the charitable money.** By mission category (NTEE) and geography, where do charitable dollars pool — hospitals and universities dwarfing direct services, and nonprofit wealth headquartered far from the communities served? — IRS SOI charities and BMF assets by NTEE (fed_irs_soi_charities, fed_irs_bmf). *Harm:* where charitable dollars pool tells you which harms get addressed and which are ignored. · caveat: NTEE fill rate historically poor; SOI sample is 2,450 rows; BMF amounts stale.
- **Big organizations, light filing duties.** Which large organizations owe no public financial return at all — filing-requirement "none" codes by asset band, plus the group-exemption umbrellas that let hundreds of subordinates skip individual disclosure? — IRS SOI filing codes, BMF filing requirement and group exemption fields, PR BMF (fed_irs_soi_charities, fed_irs_eo_bmf, FED_IRS_EO_PR). *Harm:* large organizations with minimal filing duties are the ones the public can least audit. · caveat: code meanings need the IRS business master file codebook; group exemption number is zero for most orgs.
- **Executive pay against program spend.** Which nonprofits pay leadership more than they spend on programs? — IRS Form 990 bulk data (fed_irs_990). *Harm:* charities paying leadership more than programs are failing the people they raised money for. · caveat: mart holds only 200 rows — a demo sample, nothing generalizes until the corpus is loaded.
- **Nonprofits one bad year from closing.** What does leverage (liabilities to assets) look like across nonprofits by state — which community service providers are financially fragile? — IRS 990 sample plus PR BMF assets vs revenue (fed_irs_990, FED_IRS_EO_PR). *Harm:* a nonprofit that folds takes a community's only service provider with it. · medium · caveat: 200-row sample; BMF financial amounts are stale snapshots.
- **Nonprofits filing late or vanishing from the record.** Which organizations file 990s chronically late, which stop filing entirely while (possibly) still operating, and which formation cohorts survived at all? — IRS 990 e-file index plus BMF ruling-date cohorts (FED_IRS_990_EFILE_INDEX, fed_irs_bmf). *Harm:* an organization that stops filing but keeps operating is spending charitable money in the dark. · caveat: stopping may mean merger or dissolution, not evasion — needs the revocation list to separate; extensions are legal and unflagged, so "late" overstates wrongdoing; ruling date has the YYYYMM epoch parse trap.
- **Foundations displacing charities.** Is charitable wealth shifting toward private foundations (990-PF) and away from public charities — more family control, less public oversight? — IRS 990 e-file index return types plus BMF foundation codes (FED_IRS_990_EFILE_INDEX, fed_irs_eo_bmf). *Harm:* private foundations get the same tax break with far less public accountability. · medium · caveat: return-type and foundation-code vocabularies unverified; BMF amounts stale.
- **One administrator, hundreds of charities.** Which in-care-of names and addresses recur across many exempt organizations — the professional nonprofit administrators and shell-nonprofit clusters no donor sees? — IRS BMF in-care-of and street fields plus shared addresses among revoked orgs (fed_irs_bmf, fed_irs_auto_revocations). *Harm:* one administrator running hundreds of charities is a governance risk no donor sees. · caveat: in_care_of frequently blank; address free text — normalize names/addresses and whitelist registered-agent offices to kill false positives.
- **Revoked charities reappearing under new names.** Which legal and DBA names recur across separate revocations — the same operation dissolving and reforming to shed its record? — IRS revocation list names (fed_irs_revocation). *Harm:* the same operation dissolving and reforming to shed its record is the pattern worth catching. · medium · caveat: name matching fuzzy — build it with address corroboration; dba_name fill rate must be verified first.

### labor-and-workplace (49)
- **Employers who stopped filing injury logs.** Which employers filed OSHA injury summaries in 2023 but disappear from 2024/2025 filings while still operating — reporting fatigue, or something to hide after a bad year? — OSHA 300A summaries, three years (FED_OSHA_ITA_300A_SUMMARY_2023–2025). *Harm:* Workers at firms that went dark right after logging serious injuries lose the only public safety signal. · medium · caveat: ~77% of tax IDs persist year to year, so dropout needs care — closure and ID churn also explain it; confirm the employer still operates before naming. *(Vintages of one dataset — one source under the counting convention; moved from tier 2 on consistency review.)*
- **Who dies in pipeline accidents.** Do pipeline deaths and injuries fall on the public, workers, contractors, or emergency responders? — PHMSA flagged pipeline incidents (FED_PHMSA_FLAGGED_INCIDENTS). *Harm:* contractors and first responders absorb deaths operators report as routine workplace incidents. · caveat: small counts per year; one bad event dominates a year.
- **Certified underpayment.** How often is the offered wage on a certified visa application below the government's own prevailing wage, and which employers systematically file experienced roles at the cheapest wage level? — foreign labor certification disclosures (fed_dol_oflc). *Harm:* Every certified below-market wage is a visa worker legally locked into underpayment by tens of thousands a year. · caveat: prevailing wage stays text while offered wage is cast; pay units (hourly vs yearly) must be normalized; wage-level value set unverified; employer names need normalizing.
- **The geography of seasonal foreign labor.** Where do H-2A agricultural worksites cluster, and how many worker positions are requested in each cluster? — foreign labor certification disclosures (fed_dol_oflc). *Harm:* Dense H-2A clusters are where housing, heat, and wage abuses concentrate on workers with no ability to quit. · caveat: worksite county column is a broken numeric cast (likely all-null); ZIP-to-point geocoding needed.
- **Willful violators still certified.** Do employers already flagged as willful wage-law violators or H-1B dependent keep getting new certifications anyway? — foreign labor certification disclosures (fed_dol_oflc). *Harm:* An employer already found to have willfully violated wage law keeps being handed more workers to violate against. · caveat: the willful-violator flag is cast to double on a likely Y/N text column and may be entirely null — verify before building.
- **County wage floors.** Which counties have structurally low wages for a given industry — the geography of full-time work that does not cover rent? — BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (fed_bls_qcew). *Harm:* counties with structurally low wages are where working full time still does not cover rent. · caveat: disclosure suppression blanks small cells; aggregation-level codes must be filtered to avoid double counting.
- **One-industry counties.** Which counties depend on a single industry for most employment — one plant closure from collapse — and where are establishments dying off for sustained periods? — BLS QCEW industry concentration and establishment counts (fed_bls_qcew). *Harm:* a one-industry county has no cushion when that industry leaves; sustained closure strips jobs and services together. · caveat: suppressed cells understate concentration; quarterly and annual rows are mixed and must be separated.
- **Jobs up, wages down.** Which counties add jobs while pay falls — trading quantity of work for quality of life? — BLS QCEW year-over-year employment and wage changes (fed_bls_qcew). *Harm:* places adding jobs while pay falls are trading quantity of work for quality of life. · caveat: composition shifts can drive both axes; percent-change columns may be sparse.
- **Public versus private pay by county.** Where does public-sector work pay far above or below the local private market? — BLS QCEW ownership codes and average pay (fed_bls_qcew). *Harm:* where public pay is the only decent pay, the private labour market is failing residents. · medium · caveat: industry mix differs between sectors and confounds the gap.
- **Pensions that cannot pay, and how many people are inside.** Which defined-benefit plans sit furthest below full funding, how many participants and retirees stand on that thin ice, and which mature plans have no workforce left to fix it? — Form 5500 Schedule SB actuarial filings (fed_dol_ebsa_form5500_schedule_sb). *Harm:* every point below full funding is a retiree's promised check that may not arrive; counting participants, not plans, shows how many people are exposed. · caveat: funding-percent fields may be text; plan-year coverage unverified.
- **The tiny industry that signs off on pensions.** How few actuarial and preparer firms certify the assumptions behind most of the country's pension plans? — Schedule SB actuary firms and Form 5500 preparer firms (fed_dol_ebsa_form5500_schedule_sb, fed_dol_form5500). *Harm:* a handful of firms certifying everyone's pension assumptions is a single point of failure for retirees. · caveat: preparer fields populated only when a paid preparer was used; plan-number columns have a known 0%-filled trap on this platform; normalize free-text firm names before ranking concentration.
- **Changing the math instead of funding the plan.** Do plans that change actuarial assumptions or methods show up with weaker funding the following year — accounting used to dress up shortfalls? — Schedule SB assumption-change indicators and funding percent (fed_dol_ebsa_form5500_schedule_sb). *Harm:* changing the math instead of funding the plan is how a shortfall stays invisible until it is a retiree's problem. · wild · caveat: change indicators may be sparse; EIN+plan-number linking across consecutive years must be value-verified before trending.
- **Fees rise while the pot shrinks.** Which retirement plans charge rising administrative fees per participant on assets that are falling? — DOL Form 5500 (fed_dol_form5500). *Harm:* retirement savers pay rising fees on a fund that lost money — a direct deduction from workers' retirement. · caveat: only ~33k rows landed against ~800k plans — a partial slice; participant-count categories inconsistent.
- **Plans being wound down, filings coming late.** Where and when do pension plans file final returns (terminations), and who reports late or through the delinquent-filer program? — Form 5500 final-filing flags and receipt dates (fed_dol_form5500). *Harm:* terminations are the moment promised benefits get renegotiated downward; late reporting keeps workers in the dark about their own plan. · caveat: final filing can mean merger, not loss; extensions are legitimate and must be netted out; partial slice.
- **The long decline of organized labor.** How has total union membership declined in unions' own filings, and where do labor institutions still have weight? — DOL OLMS union filings (fed_dol_olms). *Harm:* fewer members means fewer workers with anyone bargaining for their wages and safety. · caveat: form-type mix changes what gets reported; the address is the filing address, not where members work.
- **Union locals in financial trouble or spending oddly.** Which locals report liabilities above assets or shortage amounts, and which spend far more per member than peers? — DOL OLMS assets, liabilities, disbursements, membership (fed_dol_olms). *Harm:* a local going broke stops enforcing the contract; dues spent on overhead is money taken from the workers paying it. · caveat: shortage-amount semantics (embezzlement vs accounting) unverified; short-form filers report less detail.
- **Locals with no audit and no election.** Which unions stopped filing annual reports while still operating, and which go many years without an officer election? — DOL OLMS filing gaps and next-election dates (fed_dol_olms). *Harm:* an unaudited local is where members' dues disappear unwatched; members with no election cannot remove failed leadership. · caveat: a missing filing year may mean dissolution, not evasion; election dates self-reported and often blank.
- **Which rail jobs break people.** Which railroad crafts absorb the most injuries, of what kind and to which body parts, and with how many days lost? — FRA casualty data, 1.15M records (fed_fra_casualties). *Harm:* specific rail crafts absorb injuries at rates their employers have known about for decades; naming how a job maims forces a specific engineering fix. · caveat: job-code vocabulary changes across eras; coded fields need lookups.
- **Railroads and holding companies ranked by casualties.** Which railroads hurt the most workers per year, and does rolling casualties up to the holding company show parents hiding harm inside subsidiaries? — FRA casualties railroad/parent/holding fields (fed_fra_casualties). *Harm:* a parent company can look clean while its worst subsidiary keeps hurting people. · caveat: no employee-hours denominator in the table — raw counts favor big carriers; holding-company fill rate unverified.
- **Post-injury testing as blame-shifting.** Is post-incident drug and alcohol testing applied selectively across railroads to shift blame onto injured workers? — FRA casualties positive test counts (fed_fra_casualties). *Harm:* selective testing shifts blame from the employer's conditions onto the injured worker. · wild · caveat: only positives recorded, not tests administered — a true rate cannot be computed from this table; likely unbuildable as stated.
- **The bodily cost of each mining job.** Which mine occupations destroy which body parts, and does injury risk build across the hours of a shift? — MSHA accidents and injuries (FED_MSHA_ACCIDENTS). *Harm:* fatigue-driven injury peaks late in the shift are an argument about shift length — a policy lever. · caveat: time fields likely text HHMM with overnight wraparound; occupation codes need label cleanup.
- **Rookie miners absorb the worst.** Do fatal and permanent-disability injuries skew toward the least-experienced miners? — MSHA accidents experience fields vs degree of injury (FED_MSHA_ACCIDENTS). *Harm:* the newest miners may absorb the most severe injuries with the least training. · caveat: experience fields may be text or zero-filled; grain is injury record, not worker.
- **Machines that keep hurting miners.** Which equipment makers and models are repeatedly implicated as the source of mine injuries? — MSHA accidents equipment manufacturer/model fields (FED_MSHA_ACCIDENTS). *Harm:* names the machinery repeatedly implicated in miner injuries. · wild · caveat: manufacturer field likely sparse; no denominator of machines in service.
- **Every US mine, including the abandoned ones.** Where are all US mines by status — and where do idled and abandoned mines cluster next to communities carrying the residual hazard? — MSHA mines directory (FED_MSHA_MINES). *Harm:* communities living next to idled and abandoned mines carry the residual hazard. · caveat: lat/lon may be null or zero for many mines; status labels need grouping.
- **Who controls the mines.** How few controlling companies own most US mines — the handful that set safety culture for most miners? — MSHA mines controller names and ids (FED_MSHA_MINES). *Harm:* a handful of controllers set safety culture for most US miners. · caveat: only the current controller is in the file — historic ownership is missing.
- **Mines without miner representation.** In which states do mines report no miners' representative and no safety committee? — MSHA mines representation and committee indicators (FED_MSHA_MINES). *Harm:* miners without a representative have no safe channel to report hazards. · caveat: indicator blanks may mean unknown rather than no.
- **Miscategorized gassy mines, and ownership flips before closure.** Are mines classified low-gas while liberating high methane volumes, and do mines change hands shortly before going idle — stranding cleanup and benefit obligations? — MSHA mines methane liberation, gas category, controller and status dates (FED_MSHA_MINES). *Harm:* a mis-categorised gassy mine is an explosion waiting for the men underground; late ownership flips strand obligations on workers and the public. · wild · caveat: methane fields populated only for underground coal; only current controller held, so churn history is missing.
- **The penalty discount machine.** How far below the proposed penalty do mine operators actually pay, and does contesting a violation function as a routine discount for well-lawyered operators? — MSHA violations penalty/paid/contest fields, operator rollup via MSHA mines (FED_MSHA_VIOLATIONS, FED_MSHA_MINES). *Harm:* every discounted dollar is enforcement pressure that never reached the operator who endangered miners. · caveat: money fields arrive as text; open and pending dockets look like unpaid; the wedge could be timing, not evasion.
- **Repeat offenders, trivial fines.** Which controllers rack up the most significant-and-substantial violations while paying small average penalties, and how has enforcement intensity shifted across administrations? — MSHA violations S&S counts and penalties by year (FED_MSHA_VIOLATIONS). *Harm:* operators who keep endangering miners while paying trivial fines face no real deterrent. · caveat: no production/hours denominator — counts confound activity with enforcement; group inconsistent controller name spellings before ranking.
- **Days living with a cited hazard.** How long do dangerous mine conditions persist between citation and fix, and do high-negligence violations linger longest? — MSHA violations issue date to termination date, negligence level (FED_MSHA_VIOLATIONS). *Harm:* miners keep working in a hazard for every day between citation and fix. · caveat: the issue-date column is cast with a numeric function in the model — parsing may fail.
- **Injuries per hour worked, industry by industry and employer by employer.** Using OSHA 300A's own hours-worked and headcount fields, what are injury and death rates per 200k hours by industry, state, and employer size across the 2023-2025 filings — and which employers' rates dwarf their NAICS peers? — OSHA ITA 300A summaries 2023-2025, ~1.2M establishment-years (FED_OSHA_ITA_300A_SUMMARY_2023/2024/2025). *Harm:* raw injury counts flatter giant employers; rate-per-hour finds the genuinely dangerous workplaces, which most workers never see compared. · caveat: numeric fields uncast (may be text); self-reported with known underreporting and non-filers invisible; 2025 file may be a partial year.
- **Implausibly clean injury records.** Which large employers in hazardous industries report zero or near-zero injuries far below their industry norm, and who amended their numbers downward after filing? — OSHA 300A zero-injury flags and change reasons (FED_OSHA_ITA_300A_SUMMARY_*). *Harm:* an employer hiding injuries in a hazardous industry is hiding harm from the workers it happened to; post-hoc downward revisions quietly disappear a worker's injury from the record. · caveat: genuinely safe employers will be flagged alongside suspicious ones; zero-flag semantics and change-reason fill unverified.
- **Industries that maim versus scrape.** Which industries produce rare-but-devastating injuries (long days-away per case) versus frequent minor ones — the split counts-based enforcement misses? — OSHA 300A days away and case counts by industry (FED_OSHA_ITA_300A_SUMMARY_*). *Harm:* rare-but-devastating industries get overlooked by counts-based enforcement even though they ruin more lives per incident. · caveat: uncast numeric fields; small-denominator industries fly to the corners.
- **The slow harms: occupational illness fingerprints.** Which industries produce skin disorders, respiratory disease, poisonings, and hearing loss — and where does noise-damage geography concentrate? — OSHA 300A illness columns, zip-level hearing loss (FED_OSHA_ITA_300A_SUMMARY_*). *Harm:* occupational illness is slow invisible harm that shows up years later as deafness or lung disease — this names the industries producing it. · caveat: illness columns heavily zero and known-underreported relative to injuries; zips may be malformed.
- **Do small workplaces kill more.** Do small establishments have far higher fatality rates than large ones — meaning the inspection regime is aimed at the wrong employers? — OSHA 300A size bands vs deaths (FED_OSHA_ITA_300A_SUMMARY_*). *Harm:* if small workplaces kill at higher rates, inspections are pointed at the wrong doors. · caveat: deaths rare per establishment (mostly zero rows); size-band coding undocumented.
- **Temp and contract workers' invisible risk.** Do contract and staffing establishments report injuries differently from direct employers? — OSHA 300A establishment type (FED_OSHA_ITA_300A_SUMMARY_*). *Harm:* temp and contract workers are widely believed to absorb the worst risk while appearing on nobody's injury log. · caveat: establishment-type coding undocumented — may not distinguish staffing arrangements at all.
- **Corporate families behind the injuries.** Which corporate groups, rolled up by parent company name and EIN, carry the largest total injury burden across hundreds of sites? — OSHA 300A company name, EIN, establishment ids (FED_OSHA_ITA_300A_SUMMARY_*). *Harm:* establishment-level reporting hides that one corporation may be responsible for thousands of injuries. · caveat: EIN listed as a key but unverified — COUNT(DISTINCT) + value-sample it (may be masked/blank) and normalize company names first.
- **What actually injures workers.** Which events, sources, and injury natures — machines, falls, substances, by body part and industry — hurt the most people, per the case-level record? — OSHA ITA case detail 2023-2025 (fed_osha_ita_case_detail_2023/2024/2025). *Harm:* naming the specific machines, falls, and substances turns an abstract injury count into a fixable list. · caveat: classification fields are model predictions (_pred suffix) of unknown accuracy; each year file is row-capped (500k/500k/330k) — truncation bias.
- **Injuries by hour of shift.** Does injury risk build through hours nine to twelve of a shift — making shift-length rules the direct cost? — OSHA case detail time started work vs time of incident (fed_osha_ita_case_detail_*). *Harm:* if injuries spike late in long shifts, shift-length rules are directly costing workers their bodies. · caveat: time fields are inconsistently formatted text with a large unknown share.
- **Which job titles absorb the harm.** Which occupations (SOC codes) take the most injuries and the worst outcomes — including restricted-duty outcomes that keep cases off the serious log? — OSHA case detail SOC codes and incident outcomes (fed_osha_ita_case_detail_*). *Harm:* putting a job title on the injury is how a reader recognizes their own work in the data; restricted duty can hide a still-hurt worker. · caveat: occupation codes are machine-predicted with confidence scores — unreviewed low-confidence codes may dominate.
- **Dying weeks after the accident.** How many workers die days or weeks after their workplace incident — deaths excluded from fatality headlines — and which injuries end careers with 180+ days away? — OSHA case detail incident date vs date of death, days-away tail (fed_osha_ita_case_detail_*). *Harm:* delayed deaths understate the true toll of a workplace; a worker with 180 days away usually never returns to that job or income. · caveat: date-of-death fill unknown; days-away may be form-capped, truncating the tail artificially.
- **The seasonal injury calendar.** Do heat and season drive repeating injury waves in outdoor industries? — OSHA case detail incident dates by industry (fed_osha_ita_case_detail_*). *Harm:* summer heat spikes in outdoor industries are a preventable, repeating, named cause of worker harm. · caveat: row caps could bias any seasonal pattern.
- **Amputation geography.** Where do amputation and crush injuries cluster — the map of where machine-guarding rules are not enforced? — OSHA case detail predicted injury nature by state/zip (fed_osha_ita_case_detail_*). *Harm:* amputations are life-changing and largely preventable with guarding; their geography maps unenforced rules. · caveat: relies on predicted nature codes; zip-level sparse; row cap could distort geography.
- **Same employer, same injury, again and again.** Which establishments produce multiple cases of the identical predicted accident type within a year — and across all three years of filings? — OSHA case detail 2023-2025, establishment id x predicted event code (fed_osha_ita_case_detail_*). *Harm:* three straight years of the same accident at the same site means the harm is a management choice, not bad luck. · caveat: all three year files are row-capped — an employer may be missing purely from truncation; verify establishment-id stability across annual files before cross-year claims.
- **Workers' own words.** What do the free-text incident narratives — the closest thing to the injured person's own account — say about what happened, and where do injuries happen off-premises in enforcement gaps? — OSHA case detail narrative and location free-text fields (fed_osha_ita_case_detail_*). *Harm:* the narratives are the closest thing in the data to the injured person's own account of what was done to them. · wild · caveat: narratives may be heavily redacted or blank; text analysis at this scale is a big lift; row caps.
- **Machine-guessed occupation codes under the claims.** How much of the injury record's occupation coding is a low-confidence machine guess that no human reviewed — the shaky floor under every which-workers-get-hurt claim? — OSHA case detail SOC probability and reviewed flags (fed_osha_ita_case_detail_*). *Harm:* if the occupation attached to an injury is a guess, every downstream claim about which workers get hurt is shaky. · caveat: probability field may be text; reviewed-flag vocabulary undocumented.
- **The pension backstop's own accounting.** When did the federal pension insurer absorb its biggest waves of failed plans, how do the single-employer and multiemployer programs diverge, where are insured participants concentrated, and which statistical series quietly stopped being published? — PBGC pension insurance data tables (fed_pbgc_data). *Harm:* every claim is a group of retirees whose promised pension got capped; multiemployer members faced cuts single-employer members did not. · caveat: tall metric table — metric names must be filtered carefully and units differ by row; state present only for some tables; series absence may reflect the ingest.
- **Pensions lost, by year and place.** How many workers' plans were taken over by the federal insurer each year since 1974, where did the failures land geographically, and how long did workers wait in limbo between termination and takeover? — PBGC trusteed plans (fed_pbgc_trusteed_plans). *Harm:* every point is thousands of workers whose promised pension was cut to an insurance cap; a multi-year gap is years of retirees not knowing what their check will be. · caveat: participant column is misspelled at source; date parse may fail on some rows; sponsor state is headquarters, not where workers were.
- **Employers who failed workers repeatedly.** Which employers (by EIN) have more than one pension plan taken over by the federal insurer? — PBGC trusteed plans EIN, sponsor name, plan number (fed_pbgc_trusteed_plans). *Harm:* same employer, multiple broken promises, no visible consequence. · medium · caveat: sponsor names change through bankruptcy; COUNT(DISTINCT) + sample the EIN column first — older cases may be blank or masked.

### housing-and-real-estate (36)
- **Does the racial mortgage denial gap survive the lender's own controls.** Within one market and one loan product, are Black and Latino applicants denied at higher rates than white applicants with the same income — and does the gap survive debt-to-income, loan-to-value and credit-score-type controls in the modern data? — CFPB HMDA historic LAR 2015-2017, modern LAR sample, and DC-2023 loan-level sample (fed_cfpb_hmda_historic, fed_cfpb_hmda_lar, fed_cfpb_hmda). *Harm:* this is the numeric shape of modern redlining — families denied a mortgage their income supported; if the gap survives the lender's own stated risk controls, the excuse collapses. · caveat: historic file has income as the only control (suggestive, not causal); modern mart is a 17,474-row sample and the loan-level mart a DC-2023 slice — the model files themselves ban lending-pattern claims until a full corpus lands.
- **Denial reasons clustered in minority neighborhoods.** Which stated denial reasons — credit history, collateral, debt-to-income — concentrate in majority-minority tracts or are assigned differently to different demographic groups for similar applications? — HMDA denial reasons vs tract minority share and applicant group (fed_cfpb_hmda_historic, fed_cfpb_hmda). *Harm:* credit-history and collateral denials concentrated in minority tracts are the mechanism, not the excuse; if the same reason is disproportionately assigned to one group, the reason code itself is doing discriminatory work. · caveat: denial-reason reporting was optional for some agencies — coverage varies by regulator; historic is 2015-2017 only; loan-level mart is a DC-2023 sample and reasons are coded numerics needing a codebook.
- **High-cost credit funneled into poor neighborhoods.** Where do high-rate-spread and HOEPA-flagged loans concentrate relative to tract income and minority share? — HMDA historic rate spread and HOEPA status (fed_cfpb_hmda_historic). *Harm:* high-cost lending strips wealth from the exact neighborhoods with the least of it. · caveat: rate spread only reported above a threshold — most loans blank by design; 2015-2017 only.
- **Lenders whose entire book avoids minority tracts.** Which lenders never lend in minority neighborhoods at all — redlining by absence, whether or not anyone is ever formally denied? — HMDA historic lender tract profiles (fed_cfpb_hmda_historic). *Harm:* a lender that never lends in a neighborhood is redlining whether or not it ever denies anyone. · caveat: respondent_id is only unique within agency_code — must pair the two; 2015-2017 only.
- **Who buys the loan right after closing.** Which lenders originate to immediately sell, and to whom — the originate-to-sell chain that removes any incentive to care whether the borrower can pay? — HMDA historic purchaser type (fed_cfpb_hmda_historic). *Harm:* originate-to-sell removes the lender's incentive to care whether the borrower can pay. · medium · caveat: purchaser only recorded for loans sold within the same calendar year.
- **Priced differently at the closing table.** Do rate spreads, closing costs, origination charges and discount points differ by borrower race and sex for otherwise similar loans — and do costs climb as tract minority share rises? — HMDA modern LAR cost fields plus DC-2023 loan-level rate/cost fields (fed_cfpb_hmda_lar, fed_cfpb_hmda). *Harm:* identical loans priced differently at closing is wealth extraction that never shows up in the interest rate — a direct transfer out of those households. · caveat: 17k-row sample plus a DC-2023 slice; cost fields exempt from reporting for some institution classes and often blank for exempt lenders.
- **The algorithm that denies by group.** Do particular automated underwriting systems produce more denials for particular racial groups — discrimination nobody has to sign their name to? — HMDA modern LAR AUS fields (fed_cfpb_hmda_lar). *Harm:* an algorithm that denies one group more often is discrimination nobody signs. · caveat: 17k-row sample far too small for subgroup claims; AUS fields frequently blank; needs the full corpus before any claim.
- **The worst terms sold to the poorest homebuyers.** How do interest rates, terms and prepayment penalties on manufactured-home loans compare to site-built loans, by borrower group? — HMDA modern LAR construction-method fields (fed_cfpb_hmda_lar). *Harm:* manufactured-home buyers are the poorest homebuyers and are routinely sold the worst terms in the market. · caveat: small sample — manufactured-home rows may be a handful of records.
- **Who drinks from the Federal Home Loan Banks.** Who is actually in the federal housing-liquidity system — banks, credit unions, or increasingly insurers who borrow cheap housing money without making home loans — by district, over time, and on the map? — FHFA FHLB membership (fed_fhfa_fhlb_membership). *Harm:* a housing liquidity system dominated by insurers rather than local lenders is not funding homes. · caveat: member-type codes unexplained; no exit dates so churn is invisible; id columns may be blank rather than null — distinct-count check needed.
- **Redlining in effect — lender tract fingerprints.** Do multiple lenders independently skip the same neighborhoods, producing collective redlining no single lender did alone? — HMDA lender x census tract approval rates (fed_cfpb_hmda). *Harm:* neighborhoods every lender skips are redlined in effect even where no lender did it alone. · caveat: DC-only sample means few lenders and thin tracts; LEI population unverified.
- **Where housing wealth never grows.** Which counties' house-price indexes flatlined for two decades while others multiplied — the geography of who builds wealth by owning? — FHFA House Price Index master file (fed_fhfa_hpi). *Harm:* people in flat-index counties build no housing wealth while owners elsewhere gain hundreds of thousands for free. · caveat: index bases differ by series (1980/1991/1995) — cross-series comparison needs rebasing; county series are annual only.
- **The housing volatility belt.** Which counties suffer the largest peak-to-trough price crashes — where homeowners are most exposed to going underwater? — FHFA HPI peak-to-trough drops by county (fed_fhfa_hpi). *Harm:* households in high-volatility counties lose their equity in downturns and are the first to fall underwater. · caveat: FHFA place_id is not raw FIPS at every level — mapping requires deriving FIPS; early periods have base-value artifacts.
- **Price cliffs between adjacent tracts.** Where do adjacent census tracts show hard price gaps — the invisible lines where property value falls off a cliff? — FHFA HPI tract-level series (fed_fhfa_hpi). *Harm:* a hard price line between adjacent blocks is usually a boundary someone drew, and the people on the wrong side inherit it. · wild · caveat: tract series are annual and sparse; needs external tract-adjacency geometry and a verified place_id-to-FIPS derivation before trust.
- **Metros in chronic mortgage distress.** Which metros carry persistently high delinquency rather than one-off shocks? — FHFA National Mortgage Database public-use file, 19M rows (fed_fhfa_nmdb). *Harm:* persistently high delinquency metros are places where families are one paycheck from losing the house. · caveat: statistic names are a long free-text catalog — a value inventory is required before picking a series.
- **New loans written into distressed markets.** Where do lenders keep originating heavily into markets whose existing loan book is already distressed? — FHFA NMDB origination vs performance statistic families (fed_fhfa_nmdb). *Harm:* fresh lending into a distressed market sets up the next foreclosure wave on the same families. · caveat: requires matching two statistic families that may not share geography or period grain.
- **What the federal price picture cannot see.** Which places and questions fall outside the federal house-price and mortgage samples — where the index is unreliable, seasonal adjustment diverges, and publication lags a year behind reality? — FHFA HPI coverage/standard errors and NMDB release lag (fed_fhfa_hpi, fed_fhfa_nmdb). *Harm:* communities with no reliable price index are invisible to the mortgage and appraisal system that uses it; local harms invisible in a 5% national sample never reach policy. · medium · caveat: standard-error fields may be mostly blank; release-date parsing may be widely null.
- **Subsidized housing sited in the poorest tracts.** Is federally assisted housing systematically sited in the highest-poverty, most segregated tracts? — HUD assisted housing projects, tract poverty and minority context (fed_hud_assisted_housing_projects). *Harm:* siting subsidized housing only in high-poverty tracts locks families into the conditions the subsidy was meant to escape. · caveat: tract stats are contextual attachments repeating across projects in the same tract.
- **Who actually lives in HUD housing.** How do tenant profiles (female-headed, disabled, elderly, minority share) differ across HUD programs, and does the unit stock match family sizes or overcrowd them? — HUD assisted housing projects demographics and bedroom mix (fed_hud_assisted_housing_projects). *Harm:* the least-funded programs often serve the most vulnerable people; a family of six in a two-bedroom is an inventory problem lived out by children. · caveat: percent columns suppressed for small projects — blank is not zero; crowding must be inferred, the overhoused measure runs the other way.
- **Years on the waitlist.** Where do families queue years for a subsidized unit and where do they walk in? — HUD assisted housing projects months-waiting field (fed_hud_assisted_housing_projects). *Harm:* years on a waitlist is years in unsafe or unaffordable housing for a real family. · caveat: months_waiting is the average prior wait of current tenants, not current queue length — very easy to misread.
- **Projects HUD stopped hearing from.** Which assisted-housing projects have not reported to HUD for months or years — tenants nobody is watching? — HUD assisted housing projects months since report, percent reported (fed_hud_assisted_housing_projects). *Harm:* unreported projects are tenants whose conditions nobody at HUD is watching. · caveat: reporting gaps may reflect program rules rather than neglect — program context is essential to avoid a false accusation.
- **When the subsidy does not close the gap.** In which programs and places does subsidy plus tenant income still not cover rent — the gap the household eats? — HUD assisted housing projects income, rent, subsidy per month (fed_hud_assisted_housing_projects). *Harm:* when the subsidy does not close the gap, the household eats the difference out of food and medicine. · caveat: project-level averages hide the worst-off households inside each project.
- **HUD's own data holes, and the unused EIN.** Which HUD programs publish almost no data by geography or year, and does the organization-EIN field that would connect landlords to their other conduct actually carry values? — HUD open data index, 77 rows (fed_hud_data). *Harm:* programs with no published data cannot be audited, so their failures land on tenants unseen; without a usable landlord id, HUD money cannot be traced to conduct. · medium · caveat: 77 rows — a thin index, not program data; COUNT(DISTINCT) + value-sample the EIN column before believing any fill rate (known platform trap).
- **Same federal guarantee, different price.** Which FHA originators charge more for the identical government-backed loan, and does the insured rate differ by county for the same endorsement period? — HUD FHA single-family portfolio snapshot (fed_hud_fha_sf_portfolio_snapshot). *Harm:* same federal guarantee, different price depending on lender and zip code, is textbook modern redlining. · caveat: snapshot only — rate differences may reflect time period; county names without FIPS are ambiguous.
- **Where federal multifamily money goes and what it builds.** Which states get federal multifamily commitments, how much refinances existing buildings versus builds new units, and is cost per unit rising? — HUD multifamily firm commitments (fed_hud_mf_firm_commitments). *Harm:* if most federal money refinances existing buildings at rising cost per unit, each federal dollar houses fewer families. · caveat: activity grouping needs program-code interpretation; zero unit counts must be filtered from ratios; fiscal coverage unverified.
- **Lenders capturing the multifamily insurance.** How concentrated is the federal multifamily insurance program among a few lenders, and how many subsidies must be stacked to make one affordable building pencil? — HUD MF firm commitments lender names and subsidy flags (fed_hud_mf_firm_commitments). *Harm:* a handful of lenders steering federal insurance decide which projects get built; five stacked subsidies per deal reveal broken affordable-housing economics. · caveat: flag columns may be Y/N text or blank rather than boolean; normalize free-text lender names before ranking.
- **The Section 8 expiration cliff.** How many assisted units sit on contracts expiring in the next few years, which get only one-year renewals, and which contracts have already terminated? — HUD multifamily Section 8 contracts (fed_hud_mf_section8_contracts). *Harm:* every expiring contract is a set of households who may lose their rent protection; short-term renewals keep tenants in permanent uncertainty. · caveat: contracts are routinely renewed — expiration is a risk signal, not a guaranteed loss.
