- **Subsidized rents above market.** Where do subsidized contract rents exceed local fair-market benchmarks, housing fewer families per federal dollar? — HUD Section 8 contracts rent-to-FMR ratio (fed_hud_mf_section8_contracts). *Harm:* above-market subsidized rents mean fewer families housed for the same federal dollar. · caveat: ratio definition and vintage unverified.
- **No room for families.** How scarce are three-plus-bedroom subsidized units relative to studios and one-bedrooms? — HUD Section 8 contracts bedroom-count unit fields (fed_hud_mf_section8_contracts). *Harm:* large families cannot use a stock of studios, so they stay on waitlists forever. · caveat: bedroom counts may be zero-filled where unreported.
- **Empty public units amid waitlists.** Which large housing authorities sit on vacant units while families wait? — HUD public housing authorities (fed_hud_public_housing_authorities). *Harm:* empty public housing units while families sleep in cars is the sharpest form of this harm. · caveat: vacancy may reflect units offline for renovation rather than mismanagement.
- **Capital starvation and living conditions.** Which authorities get the least repair money per unit, and where did operating spend drop sharply year over year? — HUD PHA capital and operating funds (fed_hud_public_housing_authorities). *Harm:* underfunded capital budgets are why public housing tenants live with mold, leaks, and broken elevators. · caveat: only two periods available — a change snapshot, not a trend; designation vocabulary unverified.
- **Troubled authorities and who depends on them.** Which authorities are designated troubled, weighted by how many elderly, disabled, and child residents depend on them — and which authorities fail even to report? — HUD PHA performance designation and resident composition (fed_hud_public_housing_authorities). *Harm:* a troubled designation means the people most dependent on housing are being failed by their landlord of last resort. · caveat: designation may be stale versus the snapshot; composition percentages self-reported.
- **The 1930s redline grades, mapped and ranked.** What did the HOLC grading system look like nationally — which cities and states were graded most punitively, down to the street lines where best flipped to hazardous? — Mapping Inequality HOLC polygons (fed_mapping_inequality). *Harm:* every D-graded neighborhood is a place where federal policy told lenders not to invest, and residents paid for generations. · caveat: 1,155 rows suggests partial or city-level coverage; geometry may be text needing parsing; only ~200 surveyed cities exist.
- **The language of the downgrade.** What explicit racial and ethnic terms in the HOLC area descriptions justified the A-versus-D grades? — Mapping Inequality area descriptions (fed_mapping_inequality). *Harm:* the written justifications name the residents whose presence was itself treated as a reason to deny credit. · caveat: description field likely nested/semi-structured; text-mining quality unverified.
- **The rural affordability cliff, mapped.** Where is the rural subsidized housing stock, and how many units lose their affordability protection on known dates as restrictive clauses and tax credits expire? — USDA RD multifamily active projects (fed_usda_rd_mfh_active_projects). *Harm:* every expiring clause is a specific number of rural households who can be priced out of their home on a known date. · caveat: date parsing assumes one fixed format — other formats become null and understate the cliff; lat/long parsed from text.
- **The landlords of rural subsidized housing.** Which management companies control most of the rural subsidized stock? — USDA RD MFH management names and borrower ids (fed_usda_rd_mfh_active_projects). *Harm:* a handful of firms control the housing of tens of thousands of low-income rural tenants with nowhere else to go. · caveat: management name is free text — dedupe it or key on borrower_id after verifying that column.
- **Does the rural stock match its tenants.** Does accessible and family-sized rural housing exist where it is needed — or do accessible units sit vacant while family units are absent entirely? — USDA RD MFH vacant units, accessible units, bedroom mix by county (fed_usda_rd_mfh_active_projects). *Harm:* disabled rural tenants have the thinnest housing options of anyone; families with children get squeezed out wherever the mix skews small. · caveat: vacancy is an undated snapshot; FIPS text-trimming may break leading zeros.

### food-and-agriculture (5)
- **Speculation in food commodity futures.** Is the speculative (noncommercial) share of wheat, corn and other food contracts rising ahead of price spikes, and how does positioning shift across harvest cycles? — CFTC Commitments of Traders, futures (fed_cftc_cot_futures). *Harm:* speculation in food futures shows up as grocery prices in the poorest households worldwide. · caveat: ~16,764 rows is likely partial history; commodity grouping must be parsed from market-name text; completeness unverified.
- **Two generations of chronic hunger.** Which countries show persistent or worsening undernourishment across sixty years, and how deep does insecurity run (severe vs moderate)? — FAOSTAT food security indicators (intl_fao_faostat_food_security). *Harm:* persistent dark bands are populations hungry for two generations; reversal means more people hungry now than a decade ago. · caveat: aggregate rows (World, Africa) must be filtered; indicators must be pinned; estimated-vs-reported flags should be shown.
- **How much of the hunger statistic is modelled.** What share of the world's hunger numbers are statistical estimates rather than surveys, and in which countries? — FAOSTAT food security data flags (intl_fao_faostat_food_security). *Harm:* modelled hunger figures can hide fast-moving crises in the countries least able to survey. · wild · caveat: flag coding needs the publisher's legend.
- **Who is starving right now, and who is next.** How many people sit in each IPC famine phase per country, what share of each nation is in crisis, what do official projections say will worsen, and which crises have gone unassessed too long? — IPC Global Acute Food Insecurity (intl_ipc_food_insecurity_global). *Harm:* Phase 5 is people starving to death right now; an unassessed crisis gets no aid appeal and no attention. · caveat: country column is number-cast (labels may be broken); 735-row landing looks national-level only; current-vs-projection must be parsed from text.
- **What the world's food statistics do not cover.** Which parts of the food system are richly measured and which are thin or stale in the FAO's own catalog? — FAOSTAT dataset catalog, 69 rows (intl_fao_faostat). *Harm:* under-measured parts of the food system are where hunger goes unnoticed. · medium · caveat: catalog of datasets, not data; update-date field untyped.

### transport-and-vehicles (25)
- **Who is building EV charging.** Which utilities report alternative-fuel-vehicle activity, and whose customers pay grid costs but get no charging infrastructure? — EIA-861 utility data (FED_EIA861_UTILITY_DATA). *Harm:* absent utilities leave customers without infrastructure they still pay grid costs for. · medium · caveat: two similarly named columns with unclear distinction.
- **The aging and lapsed fleet.** Which owner categories fly the oldest airframes, and how many aircraft fly on expired or about-to-lapse registrations nobody is formally responsible for? — FAA Civil Aircraft Registry (fed_faa_registry). *Harm:* old airframes in commercial-adjacent categories and lapsed registrations put passengers on planes outside the tracking system. · medium · caveat: year and date fields are untyped passthroughs; status codes need the FAA codebook; completeness unverified.
- **Vessel pressure on coastal communities.** Where do vessels loiter outside designated anchorages and which traffic lanes hug populated shorelines — the idling-emissions and collision exposure map? — NOAA AIS speed category, positions, vessel types (fed_noaa_ais). *Harm:* loitering tankers and heavy lanes next to port towns mean emissions and unregulated transfers where people live. · medium · caveat: designated-anchorage boundaries are not in the source; 2024 only.
- **The deadliest crossings, named.** Which specific grade crossings have killed and injured the most people over decades, and who dies there by age and sex? — FRA grade crossing incidents (fed_fra_crossing_incidents). *Harm:* a crossing that has killed five people over twenty years is a fixable intersection nobody fixed. · caveat: no lat/lon in the table — a true point map needs a crossing-inventory join; age/sex fields sparse and railroad-recorded.
- **Warning devices versus deaths.** Do passive, unprotected crossings kill at higher rates per incident than gated ones? — FRA crossing incidents warning device types vs outcomes (fed_fra_crossing_incidents). *Harm:* communities that never got gates know which crossings they are. · caveat: incidents only — no denominator of crossings by warning type.
- **Blind crossings, blamed drivers.** How often does driver error coincide with a crossing the driver could not see down — blame moved off the railroad and onto the dead? — FRA crossing incidents view obstruction x highway user action (fed_fra_crossing_incidents). *Harm:* blaming the driver at a blind crossing moves liability off the railroad and onto the dead. · caveat: both fields are railroad-reported after the fact — a bias that must be stated on the chart.
- **The price of quiet zones.** Do whistle-ban crossings show more collisions and deaths than comparable crossings — the tradeoff communities were sold? — FRA crossing incidents whistle-ban flag over years (fed_fra_crossing_incidents). *Harm:* quiet zones trade noise for risk, and the people who bear the risk did not always get the vote. · caveat: ban-flag fill unverified; no denominator of quiet-zone crossings.
- **Every hazmat derailment, mapped.** Where have trains derailed and released hazardous materials, and how many people were evacuated each time — every East Palestine-shaped event in the record? — FRA rail equipment accidents (fed_fra_equipment_accidents). *Harm:* every dot is a town told to leave its homes because a train came apart. · caveat: lat/lon fill unverified across history — older records likely lack coordinates.
- **What derails each railroad.** Which carriers derail from track defects (under-maintenance) versus human factors versus equipment? — FRA equipment accidents primary cause by railroad (fed_fra_equipment_accidents). *Harm:* a railroad whose accidents are mostly track defects is under-maintaining infrastructure that runs through towns. · caveat: cause codes are self-reported by the railroad, with a known bias toward human-factor attribution.
- **Crew fatigue before the wreck.** How many hours had engineers and conductors been on duty when their trains crashed? — FRA equipment accidents hours-on-duty fields (fed_fra_equipment_accidents). *Harm:* crews worked past exhaustion are a scheduling decision made by management and paid for by everyone on the train. · caveat: no baseline of non-accident shifts — this is the accident distribution, not relative risk.
- **Do longer, heavier trains do more damage.** Do longer and heavier trains produce worse damage and more injuries per accident — the human cost of the efficiency push? — FRA equipment accidents car counts, tonnage, speed vs damage (fed_fra_equipment_accidents). *Harm:* if longer heavier trains produce worse outcomes, the industry's efficiency push has a body count. · caveat: no exposure denominator; damage cost self-reported and not inflation-adjusted.
- **Reporting just under the threshold.** Do railroad damage estimates pile up suspiciously just below the federal reporting threshold — managing the number instead of the risk? — FRA equipment accidents damage-cost distribution (fed_fra_equipment_accidents). *Harm:* bunching under the threshold means railroads are managing the number instead of the risk. · wild · caveat: the threshold changes over time and is not in the data — uninterpretable without the threshold schedule.
- **Who bears aviation accident injuries.** Who gets hurt in plane crashes — crew, passengers, and people on the ground who never boarded — how survivable have accidents become, and which few mass-casualty events carry most of the loss? — NTSB aviation injury and events tables (fed_ntsb_aviation_injury, fed_ntsb_aviation_events). *Harm:* ground casualties and cabin crew never chose the risk; a flat survivability curve means decades of safety spending never reached the seats. · caveat: injury grain is event x aircraft x category — double-counting is easy; the injury table's only date is a record-change date, the real event date is in the events table.
- **Who edits the injury record.** Which accounts revise official aviation injury counts, and when — after the first number is already public? — NTSB injury table last-change user and date (fed_ntsb_aviation_injury). *Harm:* late revisions to fatality counts matter because the first published number is the one the public remembers. · wild · caveat: only the latest change is stored — no full revision history; userid may be masked.
- **Repeat-crash operators.** Which operators appear in multiple accident records — including whether the lightly-regulated homebuilt lane carries more lethal outcomes than certified aircraft? — NTSB aircraft table operator names, certificates, homebuilt flags (fed_ntsb_aviation_aircraft). *Harm:* repeat-crash operators keep flying paying passengers between incidents. · caveat: heavy spelling variation and no operator id — dedupe free-text operator names first; homebuilt/damage flag encodings unverified.
- **Inspection gaps before crashes.** How long since the last inspection when aircraft crash, by inspection type and rule part? — NTSB aircraft table last-inspection dates with the events table for accident dates (fed_ntsb_aviation_aircraft, fed_ntsb_aviation_events). *Harm:* maintenance gaps that end in wreckage are a regulatory failure, not bad luck. · caveat: inspection dates may be sparse.
- **Emergency beacons that fail.** Which emergency locator beacon makes and models most often fail to help locate the wreck? — NTSB aircraft table ELT fields (fed_ntsb_aviation_aircraft). *Harm:* a beacon that fails is the difference between rescue and death by exposure. · caveat: ELT fields likely populated only for fully investigated accidents.
- **Repeat crash corridors.** Which airports and corridors show repeat accident clusters, and do weather, light, and season predict which flights kill? — NTSB events table coordinates, weather, light conditions (fed_ntsb_aviation_events). *Harm:* communities under repeat crash corridors bear a risk they never chose; night and instrument-condition flying kills at rates regulation could address. · caveat: decimal coordinates' fill unknown; visibility/ceiling are text; only a rolling window loaded, truncating long trends.
- **Which carmakers generate injuries, not gripes.** Which vehicle manufacturers' complaints disproportionately involve crashes, fires, injuries, and deaths — and how long does harm sit unreported before reaching the regulator? — NHTSA ODI consumer complaints, 1995-present (FED_NHTSA_COMPLAINTS). *Harm:* some makers generate complaints; others generate injuries — the mix is the story. · caveat: complaint volume tracks fleet size and needs a registration denominator; consumer-entered failure dates unreliable; use the consumer-safety model, not the transport-schema copy with unnamed columns.
- **Complaint deserts.** In which states do people apparently never complain about vehicles — more likely never knowing they can — so their defects get less regulatory attention? — NHTSA complaints per-capita by state (FED_NHTSA_COMPLAINTS). *Harm:* under-reported regions get less regulatory attention for the same defects. · medium · caveat: needs an external vehicle-registration denominator; state field may be blank on many rows.
- **Lethal model-year cohorts.** Which component and model-year combinations show concentrated fatal-complaint rates — known lethal cohorts still on the road? — NHTSA complaints component x model year x fatality flags (FED_NHTSA_COMPLAINTS). *Harm:* buyers of a specific model year are unknowingly driving a known lethal cohort. · caveat: component text is free-form and needs grouping; model_year is text.
- **How long defect probes stay open.** How long do NHTSA investigations stay open by manufacturer and component, and does regulator attention track market share or familiarity? — NHTSA ODI investigations (FED_NHTSA_INVESTIGATIONS). *Harm:* every extra month a probe stays open is a month the defective vehicles keep driving. · caveat: grain is investigation-recall link, not investigation — group by action number first; open probes need censoring treatment.
- **Who triggers recalls.** Are recalls driven by regulator investigations or manufacturer self-reports, and how has that mix shifted? — NHTSA ODI recalls trigger and influence fields (FED_NHTSA_RECALLS). *Harm:* when makers never self-report, the regulator is the only thing between a defect and a driver. · caveat: influence coding may be inconsistent across decades; unit counts are manufacturer estimates.
- **Defects sold for years before the letter.** How long were defective vehicles manufactured and sold before the recall notice, and how many total units per maker were exposed? — NHTSA recalls manufacture-date spans vs notification dates (FED_NHTSA_RECALLS). *Harm:* cars built years before the warning are already on the used market with owners who never got the letter. · caveat: manufacture-date fields are untyped passthroughs; units double-count if summed naively across campaign-product rows.
- **Remedy language that fixes nothing.** Which manufacturers use vague recall remedy language — the inspections that fix nothing? — NHTSA recalls corrective action and consequence text (FED_NHTSA_RECALLS). *Harm:* vague remedy language is how a recall becomes an inspection that fixes nothing. · wild · caveat: requires text grouping that does not exist in the mart; interpretation is subjective.

### disasters-and-emergency (28)
- **Where extreme weather kills.** Which hazard types kill the most people per event, and in which counties does extreme weather keep killing — the quiet heat and flood deaths versus the televised tornadoes? — NOAA storm events database (fed_noaa_storm_events). *Harm:* repeated fatal-weather counties are places where warning and shelter systems keep failing. · caveat: mart shows 69,801 rows vs a 1.78M catalog claim — the landed slice may be one year; forecast-zone rows (type Z) must be dropped before any FIPS county read.
- **Property damage versus lives lost.** Which hazards destroy property and which destroy people — and do the people-killing hazards attract the least recovery money? — NOAA storm events (fed_noaa_storm_events). *Harm:* hazards that kill without destroying much property attract the least recovery money. · caveat: damage fields are text with K/M/B suffixes needing parsing; no inflation adjustment; coverage caveat applies.
- **Overnight events kill more.** Do tornadoes and flash floods that strike overnight kill at higher rates because warnings never reach sleeping people? — NOAA storm events (fed_noaa_storm_events). *Harm:* overnight events kill more because people are asleep and warnings do not reach them. · caveat: times are local-zone and need normalizing; coverage caveat applies.
- **Tornado track corridors.** Which specific communities keep sitting in tornado paths, drawn as actual begin-to-end swaths? — NOAA storm events (fed_noaa_storm_events). *Harm:* track corridors show which communities keep sitting in the path. · medium · caveat: end coordinates often missing for weaker events.
- **How weather warnings differ by office.** Do forecast offices use severity language differently for the same danger, and how much lead time do hazards actually get? — Weather.gov API alerts snapshot (fed_noaa_weather_api). *Harm:* inconsistent severity language means the same danger reads differently depending on where you live. · medium · caveat: only 287 rows — a single live-API snapshot, not a history.
- **The failing-dam cohort.** Which high-hazard dams are rated poor or unsatisfactory, how much water do they hold, and is the 1950s–60s build boom the failing generation? — National Inventory of Dams (fed_nid_dams). *Harm:* these are the structures whose failure kills people, already flagged as failing. · caveat: condition assessment is blank for many dams; absence is not safety.
- **Dams overdue for inspection.** Which high-hazard dams have gone longest past their inspection schedule? — National Inventory of Dams (fed_nid_dams). *Harm:* where inspections stopped is where a preventable failure is most likely. · caveat: last-inspection null share unknown; inspection frequency is free text.
- **Who owns the riskiest dams.** Are high-hazard dams owned by private and local owners who lack the money federal owners have? — National Inventory of Dams (fed_nid_dams). *Harm:* residents downstream carry the risk of owners who cannot afford repairs. · caveat: owner types multi-value; primary-owner coding unverified.
- **High hazard, no emergency plan.** What share of high-hazard dams have no emergency action plan, state by state? — National Inventory of Dams (fed_nid_dams). *Harm:* no plan means no warning for the towns downstream when it goes. · caveat: EAP flag derived from a YES string; blanks may be misread as no.
- **Soft soil multiplies the shaking.** Where do high seismic hazard and soft soil coincide — the cheapest land absorbing the deadliest collapses? — GEM global seismic hazard model (intl_gem_hazard). *Harm:* soft-soil neighborhoods — often the cheapest land — absorb disproportionate quake damage. · wild · caveat: only 12 rows landed — almost certainly a model registry sample, not the hazard grid; unusable until the real grid is loaded.
- **Countries with no seismic hazard model.** Which countries have no published seismic hazard model at all? — GEM seismic hazard model registry (intl_gem_hazard). *Harm:* no hazard model means no building code, so residents build blind. · medium · caveat: the country column is wrapped in a numeric cast that nulls it — geography must come from FIPS or model ID.
- **The same software keeps getting broken into.** Which vendors and which decades-old weakness classes dominate the catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities? — CISA known exploited vulnerabilities (fed_cisa_kev). *Harm:* Hospitals and utilities run this software; repeat vendors and repeat avoidable mistakes keep exposing the public's systems. · medium · caveat: no install-base denominator, so big vendors naturally top the list; weakness field is a delimited list, partly blank on older entries.
- **The patch clock.** How long are the windows between a flaw being catalogued as exploited and its federal remediation deadline — and are they shrinking? — CISA known exploited vulnerabilities (fed_cisa_kev). *Harm:* Every day of the window is a day federal systems holding citizen data stay open. · medium · caveat: due date is a deadline, not a compliance record — the catalog cannot show who actually patched.
- **Exploits gone criminal.** Is the exploited-vulnerability landscape increasingly ransomware-monetized, month over month? — CISA KEV ransomware flags (fed_cisa_kev). *Harm:* Ransomware-linked flaws are the ones that shut down clinics and school districts. · medium · caveat: additions reflect agency attention as much as real-world exploitation.
- **Ransomware aims at life-critical services.** Which criminal crews deliberately target which sectors — and are attacks on hospitals, water, energy, and schools rising? — ransomware victim tracker (xc_ransomwarelive_victims). *Harm:* Sector specialization means specific hospitals, schools, and utilities are being deliberately targeted; patients and residents lose service when they are locked out. · caveat: sector labels are loose free text needing hand-mapping; victim names are attacker-claimed; the country column is a broken numeric cast.
- **Takedowns that change nothing.** When a ransomware gang is taken down, how fast does a rebrand appear in its place? — ransomware victim tracker (xc_ransomwarelive_victims). *Harm:* When a takedown is followed instantly by a rebrand, the disruption did not protect anyone. · caveat: rebrand linkage is inference, not data; crowdsourced collection has gaps when the project was offline.
- **Days before your data goes public.** How little time do victim organizations get between attack discovery and public leak, by sector? — ransomware victim tracker (xc_ransomwarelive_victims). *Harm:* Victim organizations are given very little time before their data goes public. · medium · caveat: discovered is when the tracker saw the post, not the attack; both date fields uncast text.
- **Disaster money that arrives late.** For awards carrying disaster emergency fund codes, how long is the gap between award action and performance start — how many months do people live in damaged housing waiting? — USASpending assistance disaster fund codes and dates (FED_USASPENDING_ASSISTANCE_FULL). *Harm:* every month of delay in disaster money is a month of people living in damaged housing. · caveat: DEF codes are a concatenated multi-value text field; dates are untyped passthroughs.
- **Hazards the network cannot see.** Where do shallow low-magnitude quakes do damage without warnings, and where is the seismic monitoring network too thin to count events at all? — USGS Earthquake Catalog depth, magnitude, station count, azimuthal gap (fed_usgs_earthquakes). *Harm:* under-monitored regions get undercounted hazard, which becomes under-regulated building and drilling. · wild · caveat: depth/magnitude are untyped passthroughs; network-quality fields blank on older records.
- **Where disaster aid systematically does not land.** In which counties are disaster-aid registrations found ineligible at the highest rates, and for what stated reasons? — FEMA Individual Assistance housing registrations (fed_fema_ia_housing_registrations). *Harm:* households whose homes flooded and who got nothing are the clearest harm the data can show. · caveat: mart is a 12% truncated load, not a random sample — geography may be skewed.
- **Aid awarded versus loss verified.** How far below verified losses do actual awards fall, how often do households hit the assistance cap, and how large is the unmet need FEMA itself records? — FEMA IA registrations verified loss, awards, caps, unmet need (fed_fema_ia_housing_registrations). *Harm:* unmet need is the government's own count of harm it chose not to cover; short assistance windows push families back into unstable housing before repairs finish. · caveat: truncated 12% load understates totals; verified-loss fields may be zero for uninspected registrations.
- **Renters get less than owners.** After the same disasters and at similar damage levels, are renters structurally awarded less than homeowners? — FEMA IA registrations own/rent, damage levels, awards (fed_fema_ia_housing_registrations). *Harm:* renters displaced by the same storm may be structurally awarded less than their homeowner neighbors. · caveat: owner and renter damage-level scales differ, so the comparison needs care; truncated load.
- **Who the aid process itself fails.** Are poorer applicants disproportionately ruled insufficiently damaged at inspection, and what happens to households with elderly members or access and functional needs? — FEMA IA registrations income bands, inspection outcomes, access-needs flags (fed_fema_ia_housing_registrations). *Harm:* if low-income and least-mobile applicants are the ones ruled out at inspection, the process itself is the harm. · medium · caveat: income self-reported and heavily missing; access-needs flag sparsely recorded; truncated load.
- **Communities where flood insurance is not available.** Which communities never joined or left the National Flood Insurance Program, leaving residents unable to buy federal flood insurance at all? — FEMA NFIP community status book (fed_fema_nfip_community_status_book). *Harm:* residents of non-participating communities are uninsurable against the flood that is coming. · caveat: community-to-geography mapping is name-only, no coordinates.
- **Flood maps decades out of date.** How many communities are being priced and permitted off flood maps from the 1970s-80s? — NFIP community status effective map dates (fed_fema_nfip_community_status_book). *Harm:* homes built to a 1980s flood map flood in a 2020s storm, and the owners had no warning. · caveat: map date parsed from messy text with two-digit years — parse failures likely.
- **Who gets the flood discount.** Which states' communities earn premium discounts through the community rating system, and how many communities have no rating at all? — NFIP community status CRS class and discounts (fed_fema_nfip_community_status_book). *Harm:* discounts reward communities with staff to do paperwork while poorer places pay full premiums. · caveat: most communities likely unrated — averages must exclude them explicitly.
- **Tribal communities in the flood program.** Do tribal communities participate less, sit on older flood maps, and hold worse ratings than non-tribal peers? — NFIP community status tribal flag (fed_fema_nfip_community_status_book). *Harm:* if tribal communities have older maps and no discounts, flood risk falls hardest where it is least funded. · caveat: tribal flag population unverified; tribal community count may be small.
- **The critical-infrastructure inventory and its staleness.** Where does critical infrastructure sit, who owns it, which counties have none of a given facility type, and how out of date is the national inventory? — DHS HIFLD (fed_dhs_hifld). *Harm:* emergency planners routing around facilities that closed years ago put lives at risk; facility deserts mean people travel for basic services. · medium · caveat: the mart is explicitly a 500-row sample of one layer — absence is a sampling artifact until relanded.

### science-education-reference (44)
- **Where NIH money never goes.** Which states and congressional districts have absorbed almost no biomedical research money over 26 years? — NIH RePORTER awards FY2000-FY2026 (fed_nih_reporter). *Harm:* never-funded regions get no local research capacity, no trial access, and no clinical spillover. · caveat: per-capita needs an external population denominator; congressional district formatting inconsistent across years.
- **The same hundred institutions.** How concentrated is NIH funding among a small set of institutions, and is the concentration tightening? — NIH RePORTER awards by organization (fed_nih_reporter). *Harm:* concentration decides which diseases and which populations get studied at all. · caveat: organization names have spelling variants; UEI may be sparse for older fiscal years.
- **The indirect-cost skim.** Which institutions convert the largest slice of research grants into overhead rather than science? — NIH RePORTER indirect vs direct costs (fed_nih_reporter). *Harm:* every overhead dollar is a dollar not spent on the science patients are waiting for. · caveat: indirect cost fields may be null on many award types — the ratio is meaningless where direct cost is blank.
- **Crisis research money: wave in, wave out.** Where did COVID and stimulus research money land, and what happened to those recipients after the wave passed? — NIH RePORTER covid/arra flags (fed_nih_reporter). *Harm:* crisis money that vanishes leaves the same under-resourced institutions worse off than before. · medium · caveat: covid_response and arra_funded may be sparse text flags rather than clean booleans.
- **Study sections as gatekeepers.** Do specific peer-review panels reliably fund the same small set of institutions — review capture inside the grant machine? — NIH RePORTER study sections vs funded organizations (fed_nih_reporter). *Harm:* peer-review capture means outsider institutions and unfashionable diseases never get to the table. · wild · caveat: study section fields may be blank for contracts and renewals; the network may be too dense to read.
- **Debt without earnings.** Which colleges put students in the high-debt, low-earnings quadrant — paying for a credential that never pays them back? — College Scorecard institution file (fed_ed_college_scorecard_institution). *Harm:* students in that quadrant carry unpayable debt for a degree that never returns it. · caveat: earnings/debt cover federally aided students only; suppression at small schools; file vintage unverified.
- **Where student borrowers default.** Which sectors and Pell-share bands concentrate loan defaults — the borrowing that ends in wage garnishment? — College Scorecard default rates, control type, Pell share (fed_ed_college_scorecard_institution). *Harm:* default follows a borrower for life through wage garnishment and credit destruction. · caveat: default-rate definitions changed over time; file vintage unverified.
- **Tuition in versus teaching out.** Which schools collect far more tuition per student than they spend on instruction? — College Scorecard instructional spend vs tuition revenue per FTE (fed_ed_college_scorecard_institution). *Harm:* when tuition dollars do not reach the classroom, students borrowed for overhead. · caveat: per-student accounting varies by sector; both fields' casts unverified.
- **Minority-serving institutions underfunded twice.** Do HBCUs, tribal, and Hispanic-serving institutions get less instructional funding and produce worse outcomes than similar-size peers? — College Scorecard MSI flags, spend, completion, earnings (fed_ed_college_scorecard_institution). *Harm:* underfunded minority-serving schools produce worse outcomes for students the country underinvested in twice. · caveat: peer matching needs care; suppression removes many tribal colleges.
- **Closed campuses and stranded students.** Where have colleges closed, and what kind of institutions strand students with debt and credits nobody will accept? — College Scorecard operating flag, coordinates, control type (fed_ed_college_scorecard_institution). *Harm:* a closure strands enrolled students with debt and credits nobody will accept. · caveat: operating flag is a snapshot with no closure date; coordinate population unverified.
- **Charging the poorest students the most.** Which schools combine high net price with a high share of Pell students — bills their students cannot actually carry? — College Scorecard net price, Pell share, locale (fed_ed_college_scorecard_institution). *Harm:* a high net price on a Pell-heavy campus is a bill the students cannot actually carry. · caveat: two separate net-price columns must be combined correctly by control type.
- **Chronic absence and subgroup gaps in schools.** Where do chronic absenteeism and low graduation coincide, and how far apart do student subgroups sit inside the same systems? — EDFacts (fed_ed_edfacts). *Harm:* chronically absent students are the ones the system is losing; subgroup gaps are children educated to different standards in the same building. · medium · caveat: only 33 rows landed — a stub; unusable until re-ingested; grain (state/district/school) unclear.
- **Fields of study that vanished from the taxonomy.** Which academic program codes were deleted or reclassified in the 2020 CIP revision, making whole fields statistically invisible? — NCES CIP codes (fed_ed_nces_cip_codes). *Harm:* reclassification breaks the time series any student-outcome study depends on. · medium · caveat: single-revision snapshot; a reference table, so the harm is indirect.
- **Genomic reference coverage imbalance.** How lopsided is genomic reference coverage across species and ancestries — who gets worse diagnostics because their references are thin? — Ensembl genome browser API (intl_embl_ensembl). *Harm:* under-studied species and ancestries get worse diagnostics and worse conservation decisions. · medium · caveat: 643-row API probe, not the Ensembl corpus — cannot support coverage claims until relanded.
- **When each place was last mapped.** When was each part of the country last surveyed at scale, which regions only ever got coarse coverage, and which historical place names have vanished from modern records? — USGS historical topographic map collection (fed_usgs_topoview). *Harm:* places last mapped decades ago are the places federal attention left; erased towns are often Black, Indigenous, or company towns displaced and unrecorded. · medium · caveat: 250-row sample; publication date left as raw text; the vanished-names variant needs an external modern gazetteer.
- **Which incarceration camps are documented.** Which WWII Japanese American incarceration camps are rizchly documented in the archive and which are nearly forgotten, and what kinds of evidence survive from which period? — Densho Digital Repository (fed_densho_ddr). *Harm:* camps with thin documentation are the ones whose survivors' experience is hardest to prove and easiest to deny. · caveat: only 25 rows in the mart — a sample of the repository; unusable for coverage claims until relanded.
- **Whose voice the Southern archive preserves.** Is the digitised record of the American South mostly planter-class literature or first-person narrative, and whose works survive in volume? — Documenting the American South (fed_docsouth). *Harm:* if the accessible Southern archive is mostly white-authored writing, the accessible history is the enslavers' version. · caveat: 144 rows may be a fraction of the corpus; author names inconsistent; publication dates likely free text.
- **The internal slave trade: routes, ports, mortality.** Which intra-American trafficking routes killed the highest share of captives, and which buying and selling ports formed the internal network? — SlaveVoyages Intra-American database, 11.5k voyages (fed_slavevoyages_intraamerican). *Harm:* route-level mortality puts a number on how many people specific merchants killed in transit. · caveat: many voyage variables sparsely populated; imputed columns mix estimate with record; port codes need a lookup.
- **The trade that continued after the ban.** How did the internal American trade in enslaved people continue and grow after the transatlantic ban, and which named captains ran repeat voyages? — SlaveVoyages Intra-American year, flag, captain fields (fed_slavevoyages_intraamerican). *Harm:* naming the repeat operators moves the record from an abstract system to individual accountable people. · caveat: captain names inconsistently spelled — entity-resolve spellings before naming repeat operators; year missing for many voyages.
- **The death toll of the crossing.** How many people died in the transatlantic crossing — the gap between embarked and disembarked — and did longer routes and worse conditions kill proportionally more, compared against crew deaths on the same ships? — Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (fed_slavevoyages_transatlantic). *Harm:* the distance between embarked and disembarked is roughly two million people who died at sea; comparing crew and captive death rates removes the excuse of unavoidable conditions. · caveat: imputed columns mix documented values with estimates; duration must be derived and is null for most voyages; crew deaths sparsely recorded.
- **Who carried the trade, and who they carried.** Which nations' ships dominated the trade in which eras, and when did traffickers fill ships with children? — Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database flag nation and child-ratio variables (fed_slavevoyages_transatlantic). *Harm:* naming which still-existing states carried the most people assigns responsibility; the rising child share was a measurable trafficker choice. · caveat: flag coding needs a lookup and flags of convenience distort attribution; child-ratio columns have multiple denominators — picking wrong distorts everything.
- **Where the enslaved were landed.** Which present-day American ports and cities received how many captives? — Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database arrival ports (fed_slavevoyages_transatlantic). *Harm:* naming arrival ports connects present-day cities to the specific number of people landed there in chains. · caveat: port codes need a geographic lookup not present in the table.
- **How the WPA interviewers shaped the archive.** Where did the 1936-38 WPA interviewers go relative to where formerly enslaved people actually lived, who held the pen, whose accounts were cut short, and which themes were never indexed? — WPA Slave Narratives (fed_wpa_slave_narratives). *Harm:* the only federal record of survivor testimony was filtered through a small set of government interviewers who chose what got written down — and whole populations are missing from it. · caveat: only 100 rows in the mart against ~2,300 narratives — likely a sample; interviewer and date fields may be sparse.
- **Most-renamed places, and who names them.** Which geographic features carry the most name variants — the most contested pasts — and which agencies and publishers control the official name record? — USGS GNIS all names (fed_usgs_gnis_all_names). *Harm:* renaming is how a place's history gets edited; the authority that writes the name writes the history. · caveat: variants include spelling noise, not just genuine renamings; citation dates may be null for most historical records.
- **Who maintains the species record, and is it rotting.** How few people curate the national taxonomy (ITIS), how stale are its records and expert rosters, and is the pace of describing new organisms rising or collapsing? — ITIS comments, experts, taxonomic units, author lookups (fed_itis_* family). *Harm:* a national reference maintained by a handful of experts is fragile public infrastructure; unnamed organisms get no protection. · medium · caveat: update timestamps may be bulk-stamped at load, which would flatten every timeline; catalogue-entry dates are not species-description dates.
- **Where life is and is not catalogued.** Which regions and US jurisdictions have almost no catalogued species — including single-region species that one spill or clearcut could erase entirely? — ITIS geographic divisions and jurisdictions (fed_itis_geographic_div, fed_itis_jurisdiction). *Harm:* regions with no catalogued species are regions where environmental harm happens unnoticed because nobody named what was lost; US territories with no records get no environmental-review protection. · caveat: coverage reflects US research priorities, not real biodiversity; single-division records may reflect thin recording, not true narrow range.
- **Unfinished corners of the tree of life.** Where does the official tree of life stop short — shallow branches, giant unsorted buckets of hundreds of species under one parent, taxa with uncertain parentage — the organisms legally invisible for protection? — ITIS hierarchy and taxonomic units (fed_itis_hierarchy, fed_itis_taxonomic_units). *Harm:* giant unsorted buckets are unfinished science that leaves species legally invisible; statutes require a named species. · caveat: depth is partly a ranking-convention artifact; children counts' computation unverified.
- **The thin evidence under species protection.** How many species rest on a single citation, which handful of century-old documents underwrite thousands of records, how much of the bibliography is untraceable, and how much of the list is flagged low-credibility or incomplete by the catalogue itself? — ITIS reference links, publications, credibility/completeness ratings (fed_itis_* family). *Harm:* single-citation and low-credibility species are the ones that can be challenged out of protection, and nobody outside the field knows which they are. · caveat: rating fields may be dominated by one default value; evidence counts may be inflated by duplicate document ids; date fields possibly text.
- **Renamed species slipping through statutes.** Which organisms have been renamed many times — synonym chains and mass-renaming waves that let protections written under old names lapse by accident? — ITIS synonym links and unaccept reasons (fed_itis_synonym_links, fed_itis_taxonomic_units). *Harm:* heavily-renamed species slip between statutes written under old names, so protections lapse by accident. · caveat: whether synonym chains are flattened to the final accepted name is unverified; update dates may be bulk-stamped.
- **One name, many animals.** Which common names are shared by many distinct species — the loophole in seafood, timber, and wildlife-trade labelling — and which names lack any supporting document? — ITIS vernaculars and vernacular reference links (fed_itis_* family). *Harm:* ambiguous common names are how a fish gets sold under a protected species' name with nobody able to check. · caveat: case and punctuation variants must be normalized or collisions are undercounted; the unevidenced denominator needs the vernaculars table.
- **Whose languages name the natural world.** How heavily does the national species catalogue lean on English over Indigenous and other languages, which non-English names are denied approval, and which species have no common name at all — and so never enter a public comment period? — ITIS vernaculars language and approval flags (fed_itis_* family). *Harm:* species that only have Indigenous names are invisible to an English-only record, and so are the communities who depend on them. · caveat: language values are free text; near-zero Indigenous coverage may itself be the finding; approval-flag vocabulary unverified.
- **Untranslatable ocean history.** How badly does the legacy NOAA ocean-species code crosswalk collapse or orphan old codes — losing the historical fisheries data that proves long-run decline? — ITIS NODC legacy id crosswalk (fed_itis_nodc_ids). *Harm:* untranslatable historical ocean data is lost evidence about fisheries collapse that coastal communities lived through. · caveat: unmatched codes may simply not be loaded, making the gap invisible rather than measurable.
- **Who named the world.** How concentrated is taxonomic naming authority — the small set of historical individuals whose judgments still define what counts as a species and what gets protected? — ITIS taxon author lookups (fed_itis_taxon_authors_lkp, fed_itis_strippedauthor). *Harm:* concentration means a few institutions and individuals decided what counts as a species in US law. · medium · caveat: free-text author strings with embedded years — normalize citation strings first, one person appears many ways and the stripped-author key collapses distinct people; kingdom links may be largely null.
- **Research funder registry churn.** Which research funders merged, vanished, or appear under duplicate identities in the registry that money-trail analyses depend on? — Crossref funder registry (xc_crossref_funder_registry). *Harm:* duplicate funder identities let the same money appear as two independent sources of support. · medium · caveat: genuinely thin source — three usable columns, no dates; replacement links mostly null.
- **Study plans the public cannot check.** How many preregistered study plans are embargoed or withdrawn — hidden through exactly the period when results get published? — OSF registrations (xc_osf_registrations). *Harm:* embargoed and withdrawn preregistrations are studies whose plans the public cannot check against the published result. · wild · caveat: 10-row sample — a shape check, not a finding; unusable until the full registry lands.
- **Why papers get retracted.** What share of retractions are fabrication, plagiarism, and paper-mill activity versus honest error, how is that mix trending, and are the corrections themselves paywalled away from the people misled? — Retraction Watch database, 71k records (xc_retraction_watch_database / fed_retraction_watch). *Harm:* retractions for fabrication mean patients and policymakers acted on findings that were never real; a paywalled correction never reaches the misled. · caveat: reasons are delimited multi-value strings whose vocabulary changed over time; paywalled-flag reliability unverified; two ingests of this database exist.
- **How long bad science stays live.** How many years pass between publication and retraction, by subject and publisher — and which publishers retract slowest relative to their volume? — Retraction Watch publication vs retraction dates (xc_retraction_watch_database). *Harm:* every year between publication and retraction is a year of clinicians and policymakers citing something false. · caveat: dates parsed from M/D/YYYY text — failures bias toward recent records; raw counts favor big journals without a papers-published denominator (defamation risk).
- **Where research-integrity failures cluster.** Which countries and institutions produce the most retractions — systemic publish-or-perish pressure versus individual bad actors? — Retraction Watch countries and institutions fields (xc_retraction_watch_database). *Harm:* systemic pressure falls hardest on early-career researchers in the countries at the top of this map. · caveat: free-text multi-value fields — explode the delimited country/institution lists and attribute fractionally; counts will be noisy.
- **Repeat-retraction authors.** Which authors appear in dozens of retraction records — careers and students built on work that was never sound? — Retraction Watch author lists (xc_retraction_watch_database). *Harm:* a researcher with dozens of retractions has trained students on work that was never sound. · caveat: the author field is a delimited free-text list with no id and common names merge distinct people — manual verification per name before naming anyone (defamation risk).
- **The world map of research capacity.** Where do the world's 135k registered research organisations physically sit, which countries have almost none, and when did each region build its institutions? — ROR research organizations registry (xc_ror_research_organizations). *Harm:* regions with no registered research organisations are regions whose problems nobody is funded to study — they depend on outsiders to define what gets researched about them. · caveat: registry coverage itself is uneven; coordinates may be city centroids; established-year null for a large share.
- **The identifier fabric under accountability.** Which countries' research organisations lack crosswalk identifiers (GRID, ISNI, Wikidata, FundRef) — invisible to every automated accountability system built on those ids? — ROR external identifier columns (xc_ror_research_organizations). *Harm:* organisations missing crosswalk identifiers cannot be followed across systems. · caveat: naive fill checks will mislead — COUNT(DISTINCT) + value-sample the identifier columns, blanks may be empty strings rather than nulls.
- **Widely read, never reviewed.** Which heavily-downloaded preprints never pass peer review, which fields' work stalls forever in preprint, and whose funding is behind the fast science? — bioRxiv/medRxiv preprints (xc_biorxiv_medrxiv). *Harm:* public health decisions get made off widely-read work that never survived review. · caveat: only 432 rows — a metadata sample; is_published depends on DOI-match completeness; funding fields often blank.
- **NSF award patterns.** How are NSF awards distributed across programs, project lengths, and named program officers — including how much discretion sits with individual officials? — NSF award search API (fed_nsf_awards). *Harm:* small-award programs are where new and minority-serving institutions get in; shrinking them closes the door. · medium · caveat: 125-row sample — conclusions cannot generalize until the real corpus lands.
- **AI harm reports are accelerating.** Are reported AI incidents and controversies accelerating year over year, and does the curve track major model deployments? — OWID annual AI incidents, 14 rows (xc_owid_ai_incidents_annual). *Harm:* each count is a real person misidentified, denied, or injured by an automated decision. · medium · caveat: 14-row derived aggregate with no drilldown; model-release annotations would be hand-added context.

### crosscutting-catalog (59)
- **Where the public health record goes dark.** Which populations, places, and conditions are systematically suppressed or blanked in official health data — the map of who is statistically invisible? — suppression/flag fields across Part D, CDC surveys, county injury, suicide, WONDER, NNDSS, home-health (FED_CMS_PARTD_PRESCRIBER_DRUG, fed_cdc_health_insurance, fed_cdc_anxiety_depression, fed_cdc_injury_violence_county, fed_cdc_suicide_rates, fed_cdc_wonder, fed_cdc_nndss_weekly_2024, fed_cms_home_health). *Harm:* chronically suppressed groups are invisible in every policy debate about them; nobody funds what nobody counts. · caveat: flag semantics vary per source and must be decoded (suppressed vs zero vs missing) or the chart lies; some suppression is legitimate small-cell privacy protection.
- **Which populations are measured worst.** Where are the official numbers statistically almost meaningless — wide confidence intervals, methodology breaks, after-the-fact revisions? — CI-width fields and revision histories (fed_cdc_anxiety_depression, fed_cdc_injury_violence_county, xc_guttmacher_monthly_abortion). *Harm:* populations measured with huge error bars can be safely ignored by policymakers. · medium · caveat: CI columns may be text; survey phase-change dates and their meaning are not documented in the tables.
- **What CDC measures — and where measurement stops.** Which states, topics, and geographic grains have almost no public health data at all — including the near-total absence of anything below state level? — CDC data portal catalog (fed_cdc_data_portal). *Harm:* states with thin data cannot be held to account for outcomes nobody measures. · medium · caveat: 15,000 rows is a portal sample — gaps may reflect the crawl, not real coverage.
- **Abandoned surveillance series.** Which public health data series did CDC quietly stop updating? — CDC data portal last-updated dates (fed_cdc_data_portal). *Harm:* an abandoned surveillance series means an ongoing harm stops being counted. · caveat: updated_at may be a crawl timestamp rather than a true dataset refresh date.
- **Name collisions in the provider record.** How many distinct providers share the exact same name across rosters — the ambiguity that breaks every name-based match? — name-only rosters and referral lists (fed_cms_fiscal_intermediary_shared_system_attending_and_rendering, fed_cms_order_and_referring, fed_cms_medicare_fee_for_service_public_provider_enrollment). *Harm:* name collisions are how a sanctioned provider keeps billing under a clean identity — and how innocent same-named providers get smeared. · medium · caveat: duplicate names are usually genuinely different people — a data-quality exhibit, not an accusation.
- **Which health identifiers are real.** Across the health record, which ID columns are actually populated and distinct — and which read as full but are sentinel-masked or blank (the NPPES EIN problem)? — identifier profiling across NPPES, Open Payments roster, LEIE, CMS catalog (fed_cms_nppes, fed_cms_open_payments_profile_supplement, fed_hhs_oig_leie, fed_cms_main). *Harm:* a payment or a ban that cannot be tied to a licensed provider is one no patient can look up and no system can enforce. · caveat: requires column-level profiling, not plain queries; this is the platform's known sentinel-mask trap made visible.
- **Can chemical harm be traced across registries?** Which substance classes have working crosswalks (CAS, RxCUI, PubChem, CompTox) and which are names only? — FDA substance registry crosswalk and structure fields (fed_fda_unii_gsrs_substances). *Harm:* substances with no crosswalk cannot be tracked from a drug label to an environmental release, so harm goes unlinked. · medium · caveat: identifier columns may hold blanks rather than nulls — needs distinct-value checks; structureless entries may be legitimately non-chemical.
- **What CMS publishes, and how it goes stale.** How much of the published Medicare record is refreshed annually versus never, and how fragmented is it across publishing offices? — CMS dataset catalog (fed_cms_main). *Harm:* never-refreshed datasets let outdated provider and spending information drive real decisions. · medium · caveat: catalog of only 158 rows — describes datasets, not people.
- **Polluters the public cannot locate or identify.** Which regulated facilities and case records lack usable coordinates, registry IDs, or even labeled columns? — NPDES geocodes, case-facility registry IDs, NRC unlabeled columns, USGS water qualifiers (fed_epa_npdes_icis_facilities, fed_epa_icis_fec_case_facilities, fed_uscg_nrc_incident_reports, fed_usgs_water). *Harm:* you cannot organize against a plant whose location or identity the government never recorded. · medium · caveat: missing data may be a load-vintage artifact rather than a true records gap; registry IDs may be sentinel-masked — count distinct before trusting.
- **The watershed reference layer.** What does the HUC-8 subbasin atlas look like — names, areas, state spans — the unit every water-harm story must aggregate to? — USGS watershed boundary dataset (FED_USGS_WBD_HUC8). *Harm:* without the reference layer, no water story can be aggregated to the unit that actually shares the water. · medium · caveat: attributes only — no geometry column landed; drawing real boundaries needs a shapefile that may not be on the platform.
- **How much can the crosswalk be trusted.** What is the distribution of match confidence by method in the EPA corporate crosswalk, and how many rows sit flagged for human review? — EPA corporate crosswalk (xc_epa_corporate_crosswalk). *Harm:* overclaiming a corporate link would smear the wrong company; the confidence spread is the honesty check that must run before any parent leaderboard. · caveat: confidence scale and review-flag semantics undocumented.
- **The Envirofacts slice reality check.** What does the 5,000-row Envirofacts API sample actually contain — and why must nobody analyze it as environmental data? — EPA Envirofacts API sample (fed_epa_envirofacts). *Harm:* treating a sample as the full dataset produces confidently wrong conclusions about who is polluting. · medium · caveat: model comment says explicitly: 5,000-row slice, blank facility IDs — shape-testing data only.
- **The justice record that isn't there.** Which parts of the public justice and immigration record are landed but unusable — and what does each gap hide? The known husks: border encounters is 9 summary rows; the DHS statistics tables are a dozen incompatible sheets stacked in one table; the DHS yearbook is a 27-row index with broken country casts; the immigration-court table has one real column out of a rich FOIA corpus; FDIC bank enforcement is ~15 rows of raw text; DOJ fraud settlements is 12 rows; US Courts caseload is a 50-row table index; the CourtListener judge registry carries unresolved aliases; Oyez is a 25-row sample. — the husk inventory across those marts (fed_cbp_encounters, fed_dhs_ohss, fed_dhs_yearbook, fed_eoir_case_data, fed_fdic_enforcement, fed_doj_fca_settlements, fed_uscourts_stats, fed_courtlistener_judges, fed_oyez). *Harm:* When the only public record of how people are treated is a husk, no one outside the agency can audit that treatment — the gap itself is the finding, and it protects every downstream claim from being built on sand. · caveat: purely diagnostic; needs upstream release comparisons to state each gap precisely; most of these sources also carry "completeness unverified."
- **Party-label churn as an analysis hazard.** How much has party naming churned in state election records, and how does the publisher's simplification distort long-run analysis built on it? — MEDSL Senate returns, detailed vs simplified party fields (fed_medsl_senate_returns). *Harm:* Inconsistent party labelling is how election analysis quietly goes wrong downstream. · wild · caveat: diagnostic rather than a public story; depends on the publisher's own simplification choices.
- **Members invisible to the watchdogs.** Which members of Congress are missing which external identifiers (FEC, OpenSecrets, ICPSR, Wikidata, Ballotpedia) — who cannot be tracked by accountability datasets? — congress-legislators id crosswalk fields (fed_congress_legislators). *Harm:* Members missing from money or vote datasets are members who cannot be tracked by watchdogs. · caveat: IDs may be sentinel-blank strings rather than nulls — check distinct values before trusting fill rates.
- **Know what the API sample is.** What exactly does the 500-row FEC API slice contain — so nobody ever publishes it as national truth, and so the messiness of donor free-text fields is understood before the 84M-row file is touched? — OpenFEC API sample mart (fed_fec_api). *Harm:* Knowing the sample is a sample stops a 500-row artifact being published as a national number. · medium · caveat: explicitly a default-page sample; not analytically usable for findings.
- **The memo-code trap.** What share of FEC transactions carry memo flags — the rows automated trackers double-count or miss, corrupting every published total? — FEC committee-to-candidate memo fields (fed_fec_committee_to_candidate). *Harm:* Memo-flagged rows are money that automated trackers double-count or miss entirely. · medium · caveat: memo semantics in FEC files are notoriously subtle; misreading them produces wrong totals.
- **The linkage coverage hole.** What share of candidate-committee linkages actually resolve to a known candidate and committee, cycle by cycle — how big is the hole in the money-tracing chain? — FEC candidate-committee linkage (fed_fec_bulk_linkages). *Harm:* An unresolvable link is a dollar that cannot be traced to a candidate — a hole in the accountability chain. · caveat: the 2026 file is described as resolving only ~57% — measure before use.
- **Election-year mismatch flags.** How often do the candidate election year and the FEC election year disagree in the linkage file — routine convention, data defect, or money raised for one race spent on another? — FEC linkage year fields (fed_fec_bulk_linkages). *Harm:* Mismatched election years can hide money raised for one race being spent on another. · medium · caveat: may be a routine FEC convention rather than a signal; needs a rule check first.
- **Name the unnamed FEC columns.** What do the unnamed positional columns (c1..c27) in the multi-cycle FEC marts actually hold — the decoding that unblocks the candidate registry, committee registry, and PAC balance sheet? — FEC multi-cycle candidate master, committee master, and PAC summary (FED_FEC_CANDIDATES, FED_FEC_COMMITTEES, FED_FEC_PAC_SUMMARY). *Harm:* Until these registries are readable, every dollar traced to them dead-ends and nobody can audit who ran. · caveat: likely mirrors the named bulk-file layouts, but that mapping is unverified — recover the official headers.
- **Stub loads pretending to be sources.** Which nominally held sources are actually tiny probe loads — FAA data portal (4 rows), Brazil (10), Ghana (10), NASA APIs (54 rows of unparsed JSON), BTS catalog (21), EDFacts (33), GDELT (1,015), Densho (25), NARA WRA (38), Rumsey (10), OSF (10), plus Spain's mercantile gazette (28), the GFI illicit-flows estimates (25) and the ADB project corpus (41) — so nobody builds a finding on a stub? — the sources named plus the catalog registry (CATALOG, intl_es_borme, intl_gfi_trade, intl_adb_data). *Harm:* a stub mistaken for coverage produces confident findings about a record we do not actually hold — while the questions the stubs would carry (Spanish corporate churn, money drained from poor countries, stalled development projects) go unasked. · caveat: row counts read from model metadata, not re-verified; GFI and ADB country columns are additionally wrapped in try_to_number, nulling country names.
- **Where sources die on the way in.** How many sources sit at each lifecycle stage (scouted, queued, landed, sampled, empty, failed, modeled), and which domains are only half-ingested? — platform catalog registry (CATALOG). *Harm:* every source stuck short of modeled is a public record nobody can search yet. · caveat: lifecycle is a derived expression; 249 of 558 modeled rows have a blank primary domain, so the biggest bar may be "unknown".
- **The 10,000-row wall and the round numbers that smell like caps.** How much of the library is a capped portal-probe sample masquerading as a source — several tables at exactly 500,000 rows (Pub 78, auto-revocations, OSHA case detail, CourtListener investments header, Google political ads), contracts at exactly 20M, deposits at exactly 10,000 — and what would the full sizes be? — CATALOG landed/mart row counts, sample flags, volume notes. *Harm:* a capped sample looks like full coverage to a reader; every truncated source silently biases toward whatever sorted first — never the representative records, and the missing rows are the people left out of the story. · caveat: caps are inferred from run messages and round-number rules, not measured against upstream totals; volume notes are free text.
- **Why ingestion fails.** What actually stops sources from landing — dead links, auth walls, parse errors, timeouts, page caps — and how many retries does each source cost? — CATALOG run history (status, messages, run ids). *Harm:* each failure family is a category of public record the platform cannot see at all. · caveat: messages are free text — grouping is judgement; retries conflate our loader bugs with publisher obstruction.
- **Walls between the public and its record.** Which sources sit behind API keys, logins, fees, restrictive licences, or hostile formats — and which publishers make their public record hardest to take? — CATALOG access method, auth, cost, licence, format fields. *Harm:* every wall is a public record the public functionally cannot read; a publisher at the top of an obstruction index is choosing who gets to look. · caveat: auth/cost/licence are sparsely filled free text; any composite obstruction score is invented weighting.
- **Data held but never modeled or read.** Which landed sources have no working model — and which modeled sources have never once been queried by anything downstream? — CATALOG landed vs mart row counts, lineage where it exists. *Harm:* data sitting unmodelled is evidence collected and shelved; an unread dataset is a harm nobody checked for. · caveat: mart existence derives from a name-parsing rule that misses multi-source marts; usage lineage may not be recorded anywhere.
- **Models that silently drop or fake data.** Which marts hold far fewer rows than their landings (silent row loss), which are 1-3-row stubs reported as modeled, and which ingests logged success over nearly-empty tables? — CATALOG landed vs mart rows, density probes, statuses. *Harm:* silent row loss quietly deletes the people in those rows from every finding; a green ingest over an empty table records a blind spot as coverage. · caveat: some marts legitimately aggregate; the stub heuristic catches legitimate small reference tables; density probes sample columns.
- **Duplicates, orphans, and twins.** Which landing tables have no registry entry, which source ids differ only by case or prefix, and which pairs of sources hold the same upstream dataset twice? — CATALOG ids, names, URLs, publishers. *Harm:* double-counting the same filings inflates any pattern built on them; an undocumented table cannot be provenance-checked. · caveat: duplicate detection from name/URL similarity is fuzzy; orphan counts are role-relative.
- **The unbuilt library.** How big is the backlog of scouted and queued sources, how long has each waited, and what would the library look like fully built? — CATALOG lifecycle, timestamps, volume estimates. *Harm:* a source that waits years in the queue is a harm nobody is watching for that long. · medium · caveat: registry timestamps may reflect one bulk import; full-size estimates barely exist for unlanded sources.
- **Where the library's mass actually is.** How concentrated are the library's rows in a handful of corpora, and how long is the tail of tiny sources — with broken loads hiding among legitimate small tables? — CATALOG mart row counts. *Harm:* if the platform's bulk is a few federal spending files, its blind spots are everything else; row counts flatter thin evidence. · caveat: row count says nothing about population coverage; metadata alone cannot separate small-by-design from broken.
- **Does coverage track harm or convenience.** Do the domains with the most sources and rows match the domains where the most people get hurt — or did the easy ingests win over the high-priority ones? — CATALOG domains, priority tiers, accountability-relevance ratings, lifecycle. *Harm:* when only the easy sources land, coverage tracks convenience rather than harm — and under-covered high-harm domains are exactly where nobody is watching. · caveat: the harm-scale axis is external editorial judgement, not warehouse data, and must be labelled as such; relevance field is free text.
- **Whole domains we simply do not hold.** Which subject areas — insurance, agriculture, social security, local policing — have zero or near-zero sources, the platform's deliberate blind-spot list? — CATALOG domain counts diffed against an expected-domain list. *Harm:* naming what we cannot see is the only honest way to publish what we can. · caveat: the expected-domain list is a judgement call; blank domains on ~45% of modeled rows skew everything until classification finishes.
- **The unclassified pile.** How many sources have no domain label or only a low-confidence machine guess — data no investigator will ever think to search? — CATALOG domain, confidence, label source. *Harm:* a misfiled source is invisible to the person who needed it. · caveat: 67 modeled rows explicitly unclassified and 249 blank.
- **Which IDs bridge the most sources.** Which standard join keys appear across the most sources, which key pairs co-occur (making crosswalks possible), and which rare keys are single points of failure? — CATALOG standard join-key claims per source. *Harm:* the keys at the top decide which connections the platform can even make; when one source carries a key alone, one dead loader severs a line of inquiry. · caveat: registry claims — a listed key may be blank or masked in the actual table.
- **How much of the library joins by guesswork.** What share of sources can only be joined by name and address, which big tables rest on provisional unverified key tiers, and which large name-only corpora carry the biggest false-match liability? — CATALOG join-key tiers, provisional flags, name-only sources by size. *Harm:* name-only joins produce false matches, and a false match can name the wrong person. · caveat: NAME appears as a key on 158 modeled sources — the crowd is the point.
- **Islands that connect to nothing.** Which sources carry no standard join key at all — readable but never connectable to any other record? — CATALOG empty join-key arrays. *Harm:* an unconnectable source can never show that the same actor appears elsewhere. · caveat: blank key arrays may reflect unfinished tagging rather than truly keyless data.
- **The resolution ceiling of the library.** What geographic grain can each source actually support — point, zip, tract, county, state — and how many zip-coded sources are tract-blind, blocking demographic overlays? — CATALOG coordinate/geometry/zip/tract key claims. *Harm:* coarse grain hides local concentration, which is where disparate impact usually lives; zips are too coarse to prove which communities bear the cost. · caveat: grain inferred from registry key tags, not measured columns; 81 sources claim ZIP against one claiming census tract.
- **Where the platform can actually see.** How is coverage split across federal, state, local, and international levels and across the fifty states — is this in practice a federal-only platform with unlit states? — CATALOG jurisdiction and geographic scope (~404 of 558 modeled ids are federal). *Harm:* most harm is administered locally, and local records are where the platform is thinnest; people in unlit states get no accountability journalism from it at all. · caveat: level-of-government comes from id prefix conventions; scope fields are free text; per-capita reads need external population.
- **What kinds of actors the platform can see.** Which entity types (organisations, places, facilities, people, vessels, aircraft) does the library cover, and in which domains is individual-level harm structurally invisible because no person-grain source exists? — CATALOG entity-type tags (~40 modeled sources claim person grain). *Harm:* if a domain holds no person-level records, individual harm in it is structurally invisible. · caveat: entity-type values have a long tail of one-offs needing folding; row counts are not distinct people.
- **What can ever support a trend claim.** Which sources carry events over time versus only current-state snapshots, and which have no usable time axis at all? — CATALOG and freshness ledger event flags and recency columns. *Harm:* snapshot-only domains can never show that things are getting worse — only that they exist. · caveat: event flags are registry claims; a null recency column may mean the builder failed to find one.
- **How current the library really is.** What is each source's freshness state, how many days behind is each domain, and how much of the library would be out of date on publication? — source freshness ledger (SOURCE_FRESHNESS). *Harm:* reporting off stale data accuses people using facts that have since changed. · caveat: freshness is only as good as the recency-column pick; unknown may dominate; static/annual sources distort the tail.
- **The load-stamp trap.** Which sources look freshly loaded but hold years-old data, which are clocked off a load stamp instead of an event date, and which marts were last built before their source's latest ingest? — SOURCE_FRESHNESS load date vs data-through date; CATALOG mart timestamps. *Harm:* a fresh-looking load over two-year-old data makes a reader think they are seeing today; a stale mart serves yesterday's numbers under today's date. · caveat: mart timestamps bump on metadata-only changes — a noisy signal, not proof.
- **Publishers that break their own cadence — and who reports slowest.** Which publishers' actual data lag diverges furthest from their stated update cadence, which sources died entirely or were never re-ingested, and — measuring the gap between the newest event in each source and its release cadence — which agencies' "current" public data is actually months or years stale, leaving which harm domains flying blindest in time? — SOURCE_FRESHNESS promised vs measured cadence, row counts, run history; max event dates vs ingest timestamps (CATALOG). *Harm:* agencies that miss their own publishing cadence are agencies hiding in the delay; a nursing-home deficiency published 18 months late protects nobody choosing a home today; when a public dataset disappears, the accountability it enabled disappears with it. · caveat: stated cadence is a registry free-text claim; a zero row count may be a failed measurement; run history may be truncated across rebuilds; publisher lag must be separated from the platform's own ingest lag — only one is the agency's fault.
- **Keys that look full and are blank.** Across every profiled table, which detected key columns are actually empty, sentinel-masked, or placeholder junk (all-nines EINs, blank-string IMOs, 0%-filled plan numbers) — and ranked by agency, who publishes the least usable register? — column catalog key-populated percentages plus per-source COUNT(DISTINCT)+sample checks (COLUMN_CATALOG, CATALOG JOIN_KEYS_STD). *Harm:* a key that looks full and is blank produces confident findings built on nothing — it has already happened twice on this platform; masked keys are how accountability joins die, and naming the agencies that do it is itself an accountability story. · caveat: the column catalog may only cover pack tables, not every mart; fill rates are sampled, not full scans.
- **The blank space in the library.** How much of the library's cells are empty — including fields the publisher deliberately blanked (the redaction surface) and columns whose meaning is only a machine guess? — COLUMN_CATALOG fill rates, empty chart-role columns, gloss provenance. *Harm:* blank fields are missing people and missing outcomes; deliberate blanks are the shape of what an agency decided the public may not know; a misunderstood column makes a chart say something the data never said. · caveat: cannot distinguish deliberate redaction from genuinely optional fields; sparse columns may look empty at sample time.
- **The shape of the connection graph.** What does the platform's whole wiring look like — which sources are hubs everything leans on, which clusters are islands talking only to themselves, and is the graph held together by real IDs or by names? — connection edge store (CONNECT_EDGES). *Harm:* the shape of the graph is the shape of what can be held accountable across silos; a graph held together by name matching will eventually accuse the wrong person. · caveat: edge confidence is explicitly uncalibrated; some edges are coincidental overlap.
- **Bridges nobody walks.** Which verified high-overlap edges are exploited by no model or lens — wired but unwalked questions about who repeats across systems? — CONNECT_EDGES cross-referenced with mart lineage. *Harm:* every unused bridge is a question nobody has asked about actors who repeat across systems. · caveat: lineage may not be captured on disk — may need new instrumentation.
- **Do the edge labels mean anything.** Does measured match rate actually track declared edge tier and confidence, how thin are the thinnest claimed connections, and what share of each source's key values resolve to a spine entity at all? — CONNECT_EDGES match rates, tiers, confidence, spine resolution; rejected-wiring lists. *Harm:* thin overlaps presented as connections manufacture relationships that do not exist; rows that never resolve are people and firms the platform can never follow. · caveat: confidence documented as uncalibrated; spine scope is a hand-written spec list — absence may mean unwired, not unmatchable; reject evidence lives in a possibly stale CSV.
- **Degrees of separation between domains.** How many join hops separate each pair of domains — how far is a campaign donation from a nursing-home death in the graph? — CONNECT_EDGES plus source-domain mapping. *Harm:* long paths mean the money and the harm can never be shown in the same sentence. · caveat: paths through weak edges may be illusory; requires the domain mapping to be finished.
